items.title: Students' Knowledge of Personalised Learning: How AI Can Help?

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Personalised learning aims to align instruction with students' needs, interests, and motivation through responsive learning environments. However, many students demonstrate limited understanding of this concept, often associating it only with self‐paced learning or technology use. Such misconceptions weaken classroom implementation and may reduce student engagement and self‐regulation. This study aims to calibrate students' understanding of personalised learning and examine how artificial intelligence (AI) can be leveraged, directly and indirectly, to address key areas of misunderstanding and enhance effective implementation. The study involved 450 high school students aged 16–18 from selected schools in Kedah, Penang, and Perak, using a purposive sampling approach. Data were collected through a questionnaire administered during class after participants were briefed on the concept of personalised learning and the study purpose. Validity and reliability of the assessed constructs were evaluated using factor loadings ( λ ), average variance extracted (AVE), Cronbach's alpha ( α ), and composite reliability (CR), with acceptable thresholds of λ > 0.50, AVE > 0.50, α > 0.60, and CR > 0.60. Students' knowledge scores were analysed to identify aspects of personalised learning that were well understood and those requiring further clarification, providing an empirical basis for targeted instructional interventions. The findings indicate that the measurement model demonstrated adequate reliability and validity. Students strongly associated personalised learning with needs‐based differentiation, particularly in project‐based and mixed‐ability contexts, but showed weaker understanding of learner autonomy, self‐paced learning, and digital facilitation. These results reveal a conceptual gap between theory and practice. Practical AI‐based strategies are proposed to enhance learning effectiveness and support adaptive, self‐regulated learning environments.

items.title: Beyond the Pyramid: Bloom’s Taxonomy Meets Generative AI

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Generative AI (Gen AI) has exposed and intensified a long-standing gap between academic products, such as papers and presentations, and the learning processes those products are often assumed to represent. The gap between process and product was always there, and had been widening for a while. This article examines how several pre-AI frameworks no longer adequately account for this shift. We first review earlier efforts to expand Bloom’s cognitive focus, including the models of Marzano and Kendall and L. Dee Fink. We then examine post-AI frameworks such as Michelle Kassorla’s Inverted Bloom’s Taxonomy and Tina Austin’s UnBlooms™ framework. Together, these frameworks suggest that GenAI exposes fundamental weaknesses in existing assessment structures and necessitates a rethinking of how evidence of learning is defined in AI-mediated contexts. How should learning taxonomies and assessment frameworks be reconfigured when GenAI weakens the traditional assumption that academic products reliably demonstrate student learning? Through a conceptual/theoretical analysis of pre-AI and post-AI learning frameworks, we examine how Bloom’s Taxonomy, Marzano and Kendall’s New Taxonomy, Fink’s Significant Learning, Inverted Bloom’s, and UnBlooms™ account for process, product, agency, and metacognition in Higher Education.

items.title: The epistemic limits of generative AI disclosure in scholarly authorship

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Generative AI disclosure is commonly treated as a means of making manuscript production transparent. This article argues that its epistemic value is more limited. Authors may accurately report observable operations, retained outputs, and verification procedures, but functional labels such as “language polishing” or “idea generation” cannot fully reconstruct the causal contribution of AI to a finished manuscript. Nevertheless, such descriptions may strongly influence scholarly evaluation. To examine this asymmetry, the article develops the readerly distraction model, distinguishing justified provenance monitoring from disproportionate attention to features insufficiently related to the disclosed operation. Readerly distraction is analytically distinct from evaluative stigma, although disproportionate monitoring may contribute to negative perceptions of originality, competence, or trustworthiness. The model generates testable predictions concerning attention allocation, comprehension, and evaluation, including comparisons between AI assistance and functionally equivalent human mediation. The article further proposes epistemically proportionate reporting through three complementary categories: methodological reporting, governance reporting, and production-provenance disclosure. Reporting requirements should reflect the role of adopted outputs, their epistemic risks, and the procedures used to verify them rather than the quantity of AI involvement. Finally, the article develops accountable judgment as a standard of authorship comprising understanding, verification, decision authority, and answerability. Unlike nominal responsibility, accountable judgment requires capacities and procedures that can be examined when scholarly claims are challenged. Together, these proposals seek to preserve meaningful transparency without allowing speculative technological provenance to displace the evaluation of evidence and reasoning.

items.title:
ChatGPT as an Instructor’s Assistant for Generating
Chemistry Images: A Study Using ChatGPT Images 2.0

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence tools such as ChatGPT are increasingly being explored as assistants for chemistry instructors, including the preparation of teaching materials. Here, we examined whether ChatGPT, using Images 2.0, can generate scientifically correct images for first-year undergraduate chemistry students, focusing on visual and symbolic representations central to the discipline. A total of 444 images covering six chemistry areas were generated. Short, minimally descriptive prompts were used first; when important errors appeared, more detailed corrective prompts were introduced. We also generated instructional infographics combining several representations to explain chemical concepts. Scientific accuracy depended strongly on image complexity, with simpler orbitals, titration curves, and molecular structures generally performing better than more demanding examples. When the six categories were equally weighted, 43.5% of basic-prompt images, 45.6% of images from corrective prompts, and only 8.3% of instructional infographics were directly usable. Embedded text was generally more accurate than the images. Expert checking therefore remains essential before classroom use.

items.title: Longitudinal association between AI dependence and pre-service teachers’ critical thinking disposition: the role of AI self-efficacy and perceived stress

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into teacher education has brought both opportunities and challenges. While AI tools are increasingly accessible to pre-service teachers, excessive dependence on AI may inadvertently undermine their critical thinking disposition—a key competency in professional development. Based on social cognitive theory, this study investigates the influence of AI dependence on pre-service teachers’ critical thinking disposition, with a particular focus on the mediating role of AI self-efficacy and the moderating role of perceived stress. A three-phase longitudinal design was employed. The study tracked 461 pre-service teachers from Jiangxi Province, China. Data were analyzed using structural equation modeling (SEM) to examine the hypothesized relationships, including the mediation effect of AI self-efficacy and the first-stage moderating effect of perceived stress. Results showed that AI dependence significantly and negatively predicted pre-service teachers’ critical thinking disposition. AI self-efficacy partially mediated this negative association. Furthermore, perceived stress significantly moderated the first stage of the mediation process, such that the negative association between AI dependence and AI self-efficacy was stronger among pre-service teachers with higher levels of perceived stress. The conditional indirect effect was stronger at higher levels of perceived stress, and the index of moderated mediation was significant. The second-stage moderation was not significant. These findings highlight the potential risks associated with excessive AI dependence in teacher education: over-reliance on AI may undermine pre-service teachers’ critical thinking disposition partly through reduced AI self-efficacy. Moreover, perceived stress amplifies the negative indirect effect by moderating the first stage of the mediation process. This study extends social cognitive theory to the context of AI use and provides practical implications for promoting balanced AI engagement and critical thinking development in teacher training programs.

items.title: Between AI usage and academic procrastination among college students through anxiety, self-control, and ai guilt

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: The increasing integration of AI tools in higher education has raised questions about how AI usage is associated with students’ academic behaviors. While AI can enhance efficiency, it may also be associated with greater academic procrastination. Existing studies have explored AI use and learning outcomes, but the psychological pathways underlying this association remain underexamined. Drawing on Self-Regulated Learning Theory and Moral Emotion Theory, this study examined the indirect roles of academic anxiety and self-control in the relationship between AI usage and academic procrastination, while also assessing whether AI guilt moderated these associations. In this cross-sectional survey, 782 students were recruited from two public universities in Guangxi, China, which were selected based on accessibility. Mediation and moderated mediation analyses were performed using PROCESS Models 4 and 7 in SPSS. The results showed that AI usage was positively associated with academic procrastination. Academic anxiety and self-control both showed significant indirect associations, with completely standardized estimates of 0.129 and 0.119, respectively. Together, these indirect associations accounted for approximately 54.87% of the total association. In addition, AI guilt moderated the associations between AI usage and academic anxiety and self-control. Specifically, the positive association between AI usage and academic anxiety was weaker at higher levels of AI guilt, as was the negative association between AI usage and self-control. Within the scope of the variables examined, these findings provide context-specific evidence concerning selected emotional, behavioral, and moral-evaluative processes relevant to the associations among AI usage, academic anxiety, self-control, and academic procrastination among students at the participating universities.

items.title: Associations of managers’ AI literacy with innovative work behavior and work well-being through AI job crafting and psychological needs satisfaction

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Learning to use AI is not the same as benefiting from it. As artificial intelligence becomes embedded in knowledge work, its implications are often discussed in contrasting terms—potential productivity gains and risks to well-being—raising the question of whether AI literacy is associated with both performance-related behavior and well-being. Conceptualizing AI literacy as a learnable competence, this study examines how AI literacy is associated with what managers achieve and how they experience their work. Managers here are examined as adult learners whose roles may provide opportunities to apply AI-related competence in their work. Drawing on the Job Demands–Resources perspective and Self-Determination Theory, survey data from 322 managers experienced with generative AI were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. AI literacy was positively associated with AI job crafting, and AI job crafting was positively associated with psychological needs satisfaction (autonomy and competence satisfaction). AI literacy, AI job crafting, and psychological needs satisfaction were also significantly associated with innovative work behavior and work well-being, and the proposed indirect associations were statistically significant.

items.abstract_text: Australia’s growing demand for science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) skills contrasts with stagnant tertiary participation and persistent inequities. This brief review examines barriers to inclusive tertiary STEM education and the potential for artificial intelligence (AI) to support Universal Design for Learning. AI can provide multimodal content, personalised scaffolding, flexible participation and assessment, and support for self-regulated and collaborative learning. Effective adoption therefore requires institutional governance, AI proficiency and sustained educator judgement. Further longitudinal research in Australian tertiary STEM settings is needed to identify which tools reduce barriers, for whom and under what conditions.

items.title: Performance without capability: generative AI and the validity of assessment in higher education

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has altered how assessment supports learning and evidences achievement in higher education. Early institutional responses concentrated on academic integrity, detection, and task redesign, while a rapidly expanding empirical literature documents the contingent benefits and trade-offs of AI-mediated learning. This conceptual paper develops an assessment-specific framework organised around two dimensions: the distribution of learning-relevant cognitive responsibility and the visibility of student process. GenAI can operate as an engagement amplifier when it supports cognitive and metacognitive activity while preserving student responsibility for the intellectual work that matters, or as a cognitive substitute when it displaces that work while enabling successful task completion. The framework distinguishes immediate AI-supported performance from durable capability, whether demonstrated independently or with GenAI, and connects this distinction to the validity of inferences drawn from assessment evidence. Rather than proposing a universal solution to what has been called the wicked problem of AI and assessment, the framework offers an evaluative lens for judging how particular assessment configurations distribute cognitive responsibility and make student thinking visible, and whether the resulting evidence can support defensible claims about achievement. This reframing informs assessment judgements without prescribing a single model for all higher education contexts.

items.title: Co-Creating Value with Generative AI in Later Life: A Qualitative Diary Study of Older Adults’ Everyday Appropriation

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) presents both opportunities and challenges for later life, with its benefits depending on how older adults appropriate, evaluate, and regulate its use rather than on technical capability alone. Existing research has focused primarily on technology acceptance, offering limited insight into how GenAI becomes valuable after adoption. Drawing on a socio-technical appropriation perspective, this study conducted a 14-day qualitative diary study with 16 community-dwelling older adults to examine everyday GenAI use. Thematic analysis identified four interconnected forms of appropriation: functional, creative, and relational appropriation, which co-created functional, experiential, and relational value; and critical appropriation, which regulated these forms of value while preserving human agency. We propose the GenAI Appropriation and Value Co-creation Framework (GAVC), explaining how older adults transform GenAI into a capability-expanding resource that supports later-life well-being. The framework advances appropriation theory and informs GenAI system design and literacy initiatives that foster active, productive aging.

items.title: From policy to pedagogy: a thinking-centered framework for epistemic agency in AI-enabled higher education

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education has challenged longstanding assumptions about the relationship between academic performance and student learning. When AI can generate essays, analyses, explanations and solutions, final products may no longer provide sufficient evidence that students engaged in the reasoning processes those products are intended to represent. This conceptual and theoretical paper proposes the IDEA framework as a thinking-centered approach to AI-enabled pedagogy. Drawing on scholarship in learning theory, reasoning, assessment and generative AI, the framework distinguishes among critical, systematic and creative thinking and connects these capacities to deductive, inductive and abductive reasoning. It further incorporates epistemic offloading and epistemic agency to examine how cognitive responsibility is distributed between learners and AI. The framework considers assignment structure, disciplinary context and learner development to determine when AI should be restricted, guided, or integrated. It also emphasizes making student reasoning, judgment, reflection and intellectual ownership visible. By shifting the focus from regulating AI use to identifying the cognitive and epistemic work that must remain meaningfully with the learner, IDEA provides a concept-to-application model for aligning generative AI with the purposes of teaching, assessment and curriculum in higher education.

items.title: Does Generative AI Enhance or Erode Critical Thinking in Music Education?

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Critical thinking has been a cornerstone of education. Some wonder what these technological advancements will do to people’s thinking and, more specifically, to critical thinking. In this chapter, we look at some of the potential affordances and limitations to critical thinking regarding artificial intelligence (AI) and how educators might respond. We address three aspects of critical thinking as outlined by research. First, critical thinking is the capacity to problem-solve. AI has the potential to help solve problems, although it might also erode one’s abilities, what some researchers call “cognitive offloading.” Second, critical thinking is a social process where people come together to think and challenge ideas. AI and newer technologies in general might bring people together; however, they might lead to what we are calling social offloading. Third, critical thinking is dependent on a diversity of ideas. Generative AI has the potential to synthesize a diversity of information and provide greater access; however, its models and algorithms may slowly limit this diversity. We situate these conceptions of critical thinking in concert with AI and provide pedagogical considerations for music educators to move toward a more process-based approach to critical thinking. This includes creating purposeful moments for students to work collaboratively—or to gather—and think critically, while also using AI tools.

items.title: Weather warnings for a multilingual nation: The role of applied linguistics in the National Weather Service’s AI Language Translation Program

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract The National Weather Service (NWS) recently developed an AI-powered neural machine translation system to deliver potentially life-saving weather warnings to the 68.8 million Americans who speak a language other than English at home. This forum piece makes the case that applied linguistics and sociolinguistics have a vital and largely untapped role in the continued development of this technology. First, dialect and register variation across multilingual groups demands ongoing sociolinguistic attention, as translation differences affect how people understand and conceptualize risk. Second, the metrics NWS uses to evaluate translation quality leave communicative effectiveness unmeasured, and demographic categories used to identify target audiences miss the breadth of bilingual experience, both of which applied linguistics and sociolinguistics have the tools to address. Third, indigenous, oral-tradition, and signed languages present challenges that corpus-based training cannot resolve alone, and reaching these groups will take community linguistic fieldwork and delivery beyond text. Warnings are only as effective as their comprehension, and applied linguistics can increase understanding and action during extreme weather events across a multilingual nation.

items.title: The boundaries of copyright law in regulating AI-generated content: lessons from the UK

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: Journal of Intellectual Property Law & Practice
items.abstract_text: Abstract Section 9(3) of the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 attributes authorship of a computer-generated work to the person who undertakes the arrangements necessary for its creation. The rapid development of generative AI has renewed attention to this provision, yet its legal function remains uncertain. In particular, its relationship with the originality requirement is unresolved, and it is unclear whether section 9(3) should be understood as an authorship rule or as a mechanism for protecting investment in authorless outputs. This article reassesses section 9(3) through doctrinal and comparative analysis. It argues that AI-assisted works involving sufficient human creative contribution can be accommodated within the existing framework of human authorship and originality. Comparative experience from China and the United States supports this conclusion. The potential independent role of section 9(3) should therefore be confined to the genuinely authorless AI-generated outputs. Protection of such outputs, however, cannot be justified merely because copyright is unavailable. The article argues that the future of section 9(3) should depend on whether it continues to serve a distinct and defensible social or economic function. Until the legal position is clarified or changed, courts should first apply general copyright principles and avoid assuming that section 9(3) automatically displaces the originality requirement. If special protection for authorless outputs is retained in the future, its scope and duration should be designed in accordance with the specific policy objectives that such protection is intended to serve.

items.abstract_text: Abstract The CIViC (Clinical Interpretations of Variants in Cancer) knowledgebase (https://civicdb.org) remains one of the few free, unrestricted knowledgebases for the distribution of somatic cancer variant interpretations. CIViC leverages public curation and expert moderation to address the bottleneck problem of cancer variant interpretation for patient care. As the curation platform for ClinGen Somatic Cancer, the CIViC knowledge model is informed by multiple experts across disparate fields in cancer and, in turn, acts as a model for cancer variant classification and representation. In order to capture a wider range of genomic variations, several updates to CIViC’s data and curation model have been made with a focus on maintaining familiar workflows and user interface layouts. A new top-level entity called the Feature represents Genes, Fusions, Regions for large-scale structural variations, and Factors for genome-wide biomarkers. Accompanying Variants capture information unique to each genomic event. Molecular Profiles enable the curation of complex combinations of these Variants. CIViC has also developed a system for approval and submission of Assertions to ClinVar, guidance for the use of AI in curation and moderation of content, and additional capabilities such as source retraction monitoring and an advanced query builder.

items.title: Content licensing strategy in AI–publisher coopetition: the role of asymmetric comparative advantages and citation intensity

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: Asia Pacific Journal of Marketing and Logistics
items.abstract_text: Purpose This study examines strategic content licensing between a generative artificial intelligence (AI) platform and a digital news publisher in digital news markets, an important issue for understanding where AI platforms rely on publisher content while competing for user attention. It analyzes how citation intensity shapes licensing incentives, pricing, user diversion and welfare. Design/methodology/approach We develop a game-theoretic model of two-dimensional horizontal differentiation in which the AI platform has a comparative advantage in content integration and the publisher has a comparative advantage in factual accuracy. The model examines how citation intensity, hallucination risk, user preference correlation and per-use royalty jointly determine equilibrium outcomes. Findings Licensing between AI platforms and publishers arises from a trade-off between two countervailing forces: entry displacement and engagement expansion. Content licensing requires sufficiently high citation intensity; mutual gains additionally require low preference correlation. The pricing effects of citation intensity are nonmonotonic. Subscription prices can rise or fall depending on the strength of citation relative to royalty costs. User diversion is shaped by the balance between referral traffic expansion and direct substitution. Welfare improves only when engagement expansion dominates entry displacement. Originality/value This study models AI–publisher licensing in a two-dimensional Hotelling framework of asymmetric comparative advantages, conceptualizing citation intensity as a content-composition variable that shapes output quality, user traffic and royalty payments beyond existing display-level constructs.

items.title: Explainable AI for tail-risk forecasting in cryptocurrencies: evidence from green and energy-intensive assets for risk-aware investment decisions

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Purpose This study aims to develop an explainable deep learning framework for forecasting tail risk and volatility in cryptocurrency markets, with a particular focus on differences between energy-intensive and ESG-oriented digital assets. It aims to assess how volatility dynamics and downside risk exposure vary across environmental profiles and market regimes and how these differences can inform risk-aware investment decisions. Design/methodology/approach The proposed framework uses a quantile long short-term memory model to estimate predictive quantiles and Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR), enabling the modeling of asymmetric, fat-tailed and regime-dependent risks. The analysis focuses on four cryptocurrencies – Bitcoin and Litecoin (energy-intensive) and Algorand and Chia (lower-energy alternatives). The model integrates SHapley Additive exPlanations-based explainability and a regime classification (calm vs stress). Robustness is assessed using 20-, 40- and 60-day rolling evaluation windows, while predictive performance is evaluated through coverage rates, hit ratios and Kupiec and Christoffersen back testing procedures. Findings The results reveal substantial heterogeneity across the four cryptocurrencies rather than a uniform green-versus-energy-intensive ranking. Chia records the lowest Q50 root mean squared error (0.00149) and mean absolute error (MAE) (0.00119), whereas Algorand has the lowest full-sample CVaR (0.0293) and Litecoin the highest (0.0411). Regime results are also asymmetric: Bitcoin’s Q10 violation rate rises from 8.74% in calm periods to 11.74% in stress periods, while Litecoin and Algorand record more Q10 violations in calm than in stress regimes. Chia combines the lowest global Q10 violation frequency (2.98%) with the highest mean CVaR violation loss (0.127419), showing that infrequent breaches can still be severe. These findings support asset-specific tail-risk monitoring and cautious use of energy-profile information in risk-aware investment decisions. Originality/value This study contributes to the literature by integrating quantile-based deep learning, explainable artificial intelligence, regime-specific diagnostics and sustainability considerations into a unified risk-forecasting framework. Its main value lies in complementing connectedness and spillover studies with interpretable, asset-level distributional forecasts and formal tail-risk backtesting. The results provide decision-support information for risk monitoring and portfolio analysis, but do not imply that lower-energy cryptocurrencies are universally safer or that the observed differences are causal.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management
items.abstract_text: Purpose Despite widespread adoption of AI agents in restaurant and gastronomic tourism settings across Asia, practitioners consistently observe a counterintuitive pattern: increasing AI service involvement initially enhances but subsequently undermines tourist experience quality. This study aims to term this the “AI engagement paradox” and introduce algorithmic hospitality congruence (AHC), a new second-order construct to theorise and empirically confirm the inverted-U relationship between AI congruence and gastronomic tourist experience quality (GTEQ). Design/methodology/approach A sequential exploratory mixed-methods design was used across three Asian markets (Hong Kong, Singapore, Bangkok). Phase 1 comprised 24 semi-structured interviews using the critical incident technique to develop AHC construct items. Phase 2 involved a quantitative survey (N = 412). AHC was grounded in cognitive load theory (CLT). Polynomial regression with response surface methodology confirmed the inverted-U effect; partial least squares structural equation modelling validated the construct. Common-method-bias mitigation and endogeneity-robustness checks used temporal separation, Harman’s single-factor test with a marker variable and Gaussian copula endogeneity correction. Findings AHC comprising culinary AI precision (CAP), emotional service resonance and cultural contextual fit (CCF) demonstrated robust construct and discriminant validity. AHC exhibited a significant inverted-U effect on GTEQ. Cultural collectivism steepened the negative slope, while digital literacy shifted the tipping point rightward. Research limitations/implications This study delivers empirically grounded deployment guidance for hospitality operators in AI-integrated gastronomic settings. The validated 15-item AHC scale provides a diagnostic instrument for monitoring AI-experience alignment. Operators are advised to benchmark their AHC composite score against the estimated tipping-point zone (4.18–5.04 on a seven-point scale), differentiate deployment intensity by tourist digital literacy, apply conservative ceiling margins for high-collectivist segments and treat CCF as a foundational design requirement rather than a localisation afterthought. Digital literacy investment is reframed as a direct hospitality revenue strategy. Originality/value This is among the first studies to theorise and empirically confirm an inverted-U effect of AI congruence in gastronomic tourism. AHC is rigorously differentiated from five related constructs and grounded in CLT from the outset. The findings challenge the linear AI benefit assumption dominant in hospitality AI research and provide indicative deployment guidance for practitioners.

items.abstract_text: Purpose This study examines how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transformed into research value within Southeast Asian universities by investigating the institutional and adaptive mechanisms linking technological capability to perceived research excellence and technology commercialization success. Design/methodology/approach Drawing upon institutional theory and dynamic capability theory, the study develops the Institutionally Regulated Research Adaptability framework and tests it using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). Data were collected from 2,371 respondents across 170 universities in eleven Southeast Asian countries, with institutional-level aggregation supported through within-group agreement and interclass correlation diagnostics. Findings The results demonstrate that institutional AI regulatory capacity exerts stronger effects on adaptive academic reconfiguration than foundational technological capability conditions. Dynamic research agility emerged as the strongest predictor of perceived research value realization. The proposed negative moderating effect of excessive regulatory readiness was not supported; instead, regulatory structures reinforced adaptive responsiveness. Importance–performance map analysis further identified dynamic research agility and regulatory-ethical framework readiness as the most critical strategic intervention priorities. Research limitations/implications The cross-sectional design limits causal inference, while institutional aggregation may mask within-university variation. Future research should employ longitudinal designs and comparative multi-group analyses to examine national-level institutional heterogeneity across higher education systems. Practical implications Universities should prioritize institutional AI governance maturity, strengthen adaptive research agility, and strategically align faculty capability development with regulatory frameworks to translate AI capability into sustainable research and commercialization outcomes. Social implications The study highlights how institutionally coordinated AI integration can strengthen regional research ecosystems, support responsible digital transformation, and enhance Southeast Asia's academic innovation capacity within emerging knowledge economies. Originality/value This study advances AI-in-higher-education scholarship by shifting analytical focus from technology adoption to institutionally coordinated value transformation. It introduces institutionally regulated research adaptability as a novel explanatory mechanism and provides one of the first large-scale multilevel empirical examinations of GenAI-enabled research transformation across Southeast Asian higher education systems.

items.abstract_text: Purpose This paper aims to reframe board gender diversity as a strategic governance capability rather than a symbolic initiative or universal performance lever. It explains inconsistent diversity–performance findings and clarifies when diversity may strengthen oversight in algorithmically mediated environments. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on structured evidence mapping and interdisciplinary research in corporate governance, leadership, efficiency economics, organizational demography and artificial intelligence (AI) governance, the paper develops a structured integrative conceptual synthesis focused on power, expertise–authority alignment and technological oversight. Findings Diversity effects are contingent rather than automatic. Board gender diversity is most likely to strengthen governance when three enabling conditions are present: representation thresholds that convert presence into voice, expertise aligned with authority and inclusive power structures that enable challenge. Under algorithmic complexity, these conditions may strengthen oversight of bias, explainability, privacy, cybersecurity, vendor dependence and technocratic capture. Practical implications Boards and policymakers should move beyond numerical representation to structural influence. Diverse directors should occupy consequential committees, have relevant expertise and decision rights and be supported by practices that enable challenge. Boards should evaluate participation, committee assignments and technology-governance structures so diversity contributes to accountability, risk oversight and resilience rather than symbolic compliance. Social implications Representation-focused reforms are insufficient when formal inclusion does not produce influence. More substantively inclusive governance can strengthen accountability and stakeholder responsiveness in algorithmic organizational environments. Originality/value The paper moves beyond the business-case debate by integrating intersectionality, governance, efficiency and AI-governance perspectives into a mechanism-based framework showing how board diversity becomes a strategic governance capability under algorithmic complexity.

items.title: Designing transparency in AI influencer marketing: a consumer–agency architecture

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Purpose The purpose of this study is to develop an understanding of AI influencer transparency and its effects on affective and cognitive trust, engagement and consumer well-being. Design/methodology/approach This paper presents a conceptual synthesis of influencer marketing, consumer psychology and human–algorithm interaction research. Findings This paper introduces the Consumer–Agency Architecture (CAA) framework, distinguishing between information, control and provenance transparency. CAA posits that effects of transparency on consumer outcomes are driven by reductions in reactance, whether affective or cognitive. Information transparency primarily mitigates affective reactance; control transparency reduces cognitive reactance; and provenance transparency can attenuate both. Lower reactance, in turn, can support the formation of affective and cognitive trust, engagement and consumer well-being. The framework further identifies boundary conditions that either strengthen or weaken the relationship between transparency and reactance. Research limitations/implications This paper proposes a conceptual framework that remains to be empirically tested. It also posits that transparency effects in AI influencer marketing are primarily driven by reactance, not gains in perceived authenticity. The developed model also assumes that transparency forms have distinct rather than additive or even nonlinear effects on cognitive and affective reactance. Such assumptions could be tested in future work. Practical implications Brands and platforms should treat transparency as a portfolio of design levers rather than a single disclosure: match the specific type of transparency to the focal objective, anticipate trade-offs and avoid one-size-fits-all transparency that can erode trust. Social implications CAA provides a consumer-welfare lens for governing AI-influencer ecosystems by clarifying how transparency can support consumer agency. Originality/value CAA frames transparency in AI-influencer marketing as a means of respecting and protecting consumer agency, offering a mechanism-based foundation for designing ethically grounded, trust-sustaining AI-mediated brand relationships.

items.abstract_text: Purpose This study aims to examine how artificial intelligence (AI) is associated with changes in entrepreneurship education in emerging economies, focusing on entrepreneurial competencies, student cognition, venture originality and early graduate behavior. Design/methodology/approach The study uses a multisource, multicohort quasi-experimental design. Principal analyses draw on an approximately 900-student longitudinal survey and a preliminary 18-month graduate follow-up. Published evidence on educator perspectives and on 150 business plans with 45 interviews across three Chinese universities is used only for contextual triangulation and is not pooled with the study-specific statistical analyses. Findings In the principal student analyses, generative AI was associated with stronger opportunity recognition but lower divergent thinking and higher confirmation bias. Predictive analytics was associated with more evidence-based evaluation, while structured intelligent tutoring was associated with stronger metacognitive reflection. Published business-plan evidence is used only to contextualize homogenization. The 18-month venture-creation differences were not statistically significant and remain exploratory. Research limitations/implications The nonrandomized design, incomplete wave-specific attrition information, unavailable matching diagnostics, reliance on published contextual evidence for homogenization and educator perspectives and short follow-up period limit causal claims and cross-context generalization. Future studies should use controlled designs, complete longitudinal reporting, longer graduate tracking and cross-country comparisons. Practical implications Educators should require prompt logs, independent evidence checks, revision rationales and originality rubrics that reward local validation, assumption testing, judgment and distinctive venture logic. Social implications In emerging economies, AI can broaden access to entrepreneurial feedback and market knowledge, but inadequate guidance may yield generic ventures detached from local needs. Originality/value The study extends entrepreneurship education ecosystem thinking by treating AI as an active mediator of cognition and venture artifact production whose educational role depends on tool function, assessment design and institutional governance.

items.venue: Journal of Hospitality and Tourism Insights
items.abstract_text: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) digital humans, developed to mimic humans, have emerged as promoters in marketing. Although existing studies have identified that AI digital humans' anthropomorphism shapes marketing outcomes, the multidimensionality of anthropomorphism remains underexplored. Focusing on historical figure-inspired AI digital humans in tourism destination marketing, this study examines how their multiple anthropomorphic features influence consumers' responses under the Computers are Social Actors and Media are Social Actors paradigms. Design/methodology/approach An online survey (N = 435) was conducted in 2026. Respondents completed a questionnaire after watching a typical travel vlog featuring a historical figure-based AI digital human. Findings We revealed that voice, behavior and mental anthropomorphism influence consumers' parasocial interactions with AI digital humans, which subsequently affect consumers' attitudes toward tourism destinations. Mental anthropomorphism mediates appearance, voice and behavior anthropomorphism's effects on parasocial interactions. Furthermore, mental anthropomorphism's effect is conditioned by consumers' familiarity with the AI digital human's historical figure prototype. Research limitations/implications This study extends existing research by demonstrating that AI digital humans' multiple anthropomorphic features shape consumers' parasocial interactions, with historical figure familiarity serving as a moderator. However, nonprobability sampling and a single cultural context restrict generalizability, warranting cross-cultural research with probability sampling in the future. Practical implications This study provides practical insight into developing AI digital humans in tourism marketing. Marketers should systematically optimize their human-likeness across voice, behavioral and mental traits, while considering consumers' individual differences. Originality/value This study fills the research gap in AI digital humans by unpacking the multidimensionality of anthropomorphism and showing that its effects are contingent on consumers' traits.

items.abstract_text: Purpose While organizational knowledge conversion (OKC) is central to value creation, its translation into individual employee performance remains insufficiently understood, particularly in artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled contexts where knowledge is abundant but must be appropriately adapted and ethically applied to generate meaningful outcomes. items.abstract_text: Peer code review is widely used in programming and software engineering education, but its instructional value depends on the quality of student feedback rather than review completion alone. In large classes, instructors can readily monitor participation but lack scalable methods for assessing whether feedback is relevant, concrete, and constructive, limiting opportunities for timely instructional intervention. To address this gap, this study developed and evaluated the review engagement graph (REG), an instructor-focused learning analytics dashboard that integrates multilabel artificial intelligence classification of feedback quality with interactive network visualization. REG operationalizes feedback quality across three independent dimensions and translates five recurring visual patterns into corresponding pedagogical actions while preserving instructor judgment. The system was evaluated in two studies. Study 1 compared seven classification models spanning traditional machine learning, deep learning, fine-tuned transformers, and prompted large language models using 2,398 peer review comments independently annotated by two experts. Fine-tuned RoBERTa achieved the strongest overall performance, with a macro F1 score of 0.828. Study 2 evaluated REG with instructors and teaching assistants through scenario-based sessions. REG achieved a mean System Usability Scale score of 81.13, exceeding the benchmark of 68, and a mean perceived usefulness (PU) score of 4.31 out of 5. These findings demonstrate that AI-classified feedback quality indicators can be transformed into actionable visual evidence through a pattern-to-action framework that supports timely and informed instructor decision-making.

Phase 1 generated 967 participant reply messages from 61 unique individuals and 101,980 $Degen distributed. Using historical DEGEN/USD closes at the beginning and end of the 9–22 January reward phase as a broad valuation bracket, the aggregate token budget was on the order of US$111–152; this is not a transaction-time weighted valuation. The findings carry implications for platform economics, AI governance, and token incentive design.

items.venue: ACM Transactions on Computing for Healthcare
items.abstract_text: Connected health integrates sensors, mobile devices, and information technology to realize the real-time collection and transmission of medical data, providing patients with more personalized and efficient medical services. In this context, medical image segmentation technology plays a vital role as a key digital medicine tool in connected health. However, its effective deployment across diverse clinical settings and data sources remains challenging due to inherent variations in imaging modalities, patient demographics, and device characteristics. Currently, connected health requires highly efficient AI models for real-world medical applications. The versatility of the model across diverse environments is of great significance. Domain Generalization (DG) has emerged as a crucial solution to address these challenges of connected health. Previous work focuses on the domain similarity calculation on the final layer output of the backbone model, which ignores the impact of the multi-scale features. In this article, we proposed a Domain Pyramid Attention Network (DPANet), which aims to transfer knowledge from source domains to unseen domains for medical image segmentation at a multi-scale level. The overarching goal is to enhance the efficiency of connected health systems through this innovative knowledge transfer mechanism. DPANet is capable of learning multi-scale similarity between two kinds of domains through a Domain Similarity Pyramid Attention Module (DSPAM). We also designed Domain Prototypes (DP), which can enhance the flexibility of the knowledge pre-extracted from source domains for better transferability. A simple fusion method is adopted to merge the multi-scale features for the final segmentation prediction. DPANet is evaluated on Brain Tumor segmentation and Retina Fundus segmentation tasks, achieving an average Dice improvement of 1.14% and 0.98% on these two tasks, respectively.

items.abstract_text: While large language models (LLMs) have captured global attention for their linguistic abilities, our work harnesses their power to overcome traditional barriers in querying Linked Data (LD) and Resource Description Framework (RDF) triplestores. This article presents an innovative framework that integrates LLMs into conversational user interfaces (UIs), enabling the dynamic generation of precise SPARQL queries without the necessity for constant retraining. Most conversational UI models struggle with adaptability as they require frequent retraining whenever datasets are updated or expanded. This limitation impedes their effectiveness as general-purpose extraction tools. To address this challenge, our approach 1 seamlessly incorporates LLMs into the conversational UI process, fostering a more sophisticated understanding and interpretation of user queries and enhancing overall responsiveness. By leveraging the advanced natural language processing capabilities of LLMs, our method improves RDF entity extraction in web systems that utilise conventional chatbots. Furthermore, it extends the functionality of these chatbots, allowing them to respond directly to queries based on the RDF schema while providing an assistive interface that deepens understanding of the dataset and its underlying domain. This facilitates the extraction of more meaningful information. By adopting this approach, interactions become more refined and context-sensitive, a crucial advancement for managing the intricate query structures commonly found in RDF datasets and Linked Open Data (LOD) endpoints. We have evaluated our approach in practical settings by assessing the tool’s ability to address complex queries and to answer general ecological queries, with the outputs evaluated by human experts. The results demonstrate a notable improvement in system expressiveness and response accuracy, showcasing the potential of LLMs to transform information retrieval. The findings not only confirm their adaptability in enhancing existing systems but also open up exciting possibilities for their deployment in specialised web information domains, paving the way for future research in this evolving field.

items.venue: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
items.abstract_text: Deep learning (DL) frameworks such as TensorFlow and PyTorch have powered major AI advancements, yet their reliance on third-party libraries introduces critical, understudied security risks. This article examines dependency management in these frameworks, focusing on dependency characteristics, associated vulnerabilities, and mitigation strategies. We analyze 448 libraries, 8,641 dependency-related commits, and 72 vulnerabilities, using GitHub APIs, official package sites, NVD/CWE databases, and a developer survey. Our findings show that while both frameworks share similar dependency types, PyTorch has more dependencies with less frequent updates. Both exhibit substantial vulnerabilities—42 in TensorFlow and 30 in PyTorch—almost half of which are high or critical severity, many unresolved. Notably, cumulative vulnerability exposure events reach 9,653 for TensorFlow and 627 for PyTorch, largely due to repeated removal and reintroduction of vulnerable dependencies. We also reveal that most security fixes occur incidentally alongside dependency optimization or compatibility improvements. Only 12% of changes explicitly address security, despite 90% of developers acknowledging its importance, reflecting limited experience, over-reliance on dependencies, and unclear accountability. This study sheds light on dependency management practices in DL frameworks, highlighting critical security risks and offering actionable guidance to strengthen DL ecosystem security and resilience.

items.venue: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
items.abstract_text: Context . Code refactoring improves software quality without changing external behavior. Despite its advantages, its benefits are hindered by the considerable cost of time, resources, and continuous effort it demands. Aim . Understanding why developers refactor, and which metrics capture these motivations, may support wider and more effective use of refactoring in practice. Method . We performed a large-scale empirical study to analyze developers’ refactoring activity, leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) to identify underlying motivations from version control data, comparing our findings with previous motivations reported in the literature. Results . LLMs matched human judgment in 80% of cases, but aligned with literature-based motivations in only 47%. They enriched 22% of motivations with more detailed rationale, often highlighting readability, clarity, and structural improvements. Most motivations were pragmatic, focused on simplification and maintainability. While metrics related to developer experience and code readability ranked highest, their correlation with motivation categories was weak. Conclusions . We conclude that LLMs effectively capture surface-level motivations but struggle with architectural reasoning. Their value lies in providing localized explanations, which, when combined with software metrics, can form hybrid approaches. Such integration offers a promising path toward prioritizing refactoring more systematically and balancing short-term improvements with long-term architectural goals.

items.title: BlockKD3A: A Web3-Native Framework for Decentralized Collaborative AI and User-Generated Model Assets

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: ACM Transactions on Multimedia Computing, Communications, and Applications
items.abstract_text: User-generated model assets in Web3 demand verifiable provenance, clear attribution, and dependable coordination across organizational boundaries without centralizing data. However, real-world deployments still face persistent challenges. Even algorithmically robust methods like KD3A often lack auditable coordination, failure resilience, and reproducible artifact lineage. These limitations make training brittle and results difficult to audit amidst node churn, adversarial behavior, and system heterogeneity. We introduce BlockKD3A, a hybrid on-chain/off-chain framework that operationalizes KD3A with three key system guarantees: (i) auditable coordination, achieved via smart contracts that record training state, model content identifiers (CIDs), and Consensus Focus (CF)-based attribution; (ii) reliability, through a transaction-safe client and failure-aware orchestration that applies nonnegative CF clipping, supports zero-CF fallback, and avoids blocking on stragglers; and (iii) reproducibility, enabled by content-addressable packaging and unified telemetry that couples machine learning metrics with blockchain events. In 9 end-to-end deployments (40 epochs per target), BlockKD3A delivered near-centralized performance, 96.74% macro-average accuracy on Office-Caltech10, and 89.40% on DigitFive—substantially outperforming representative federated baselines. Coordination remained efficient and predictable, with only 13 blockchain transactions across all 9 deployments, bounded gas costs per write (125,972–298,405), and stable epoch timings even under partial participation. By integrating KD3A’s algorithm-native attribution with on-chain provenance and robust execution, BlockKD3A closes the gap between decentralized learning algorithms and reliable system deployment, providing auditability, predictable cost envelopes, and transferable engineering patterns for verifiable user-generated model assets.

items.abstract_text: Artificial Intelligence (AI) techniques are driving increasing volumes of reliability-sensitive Service Function Chain (SFC) requests from applications such as autonomous driving, smart manufacturing, and intelligent healthcare. These applications require not only feasible deployment but also continuous service availability under failures, disruptions, and uncertainty. Existing reliable SFC deployment studies have largely relied on rule-based approaches, which provide explicit formulations and interpretable decision rules but often struggle with dynamic, large-scale, and multi-objective requirements involving reliability, latency, cost, and security. AI-driven solutions therefore offer a promising direction for enabling adaptive and data-driven deployment decisions. This survey first clarifies the workflow of SFC deployment and the distinction between conventional and reliable SFC deployment. We then review rule-based reliable SFC deployment, analyzing its major design rationales, representative solution paradigms, and limitations. Building on this analysis, we examine AI-driven methodologies for reliable SFC deployment, with a particular focus on deep reinforcement learning approaches, which dominate the existing literature. Finally, we discuss open challenges and future directions toward adaptive, robust, and scalable reliable SFC deployment.

items.abstract_text: Spiritual AI is a nascent area of HCI research exploring how generative AI can augment spiritual experiences. Research to date has focused on speculative design, but actual AI use for spiritual purposes remains unexplored. To address this gap, this research explored how AI is used in daily life, specifically for spiritual growth in a Christian tradition. This research was inspired by and based on the first author’s experience, as well as collaborative ethnographic research with 20 participants who publicly identify as Christians. Our findings show how AI was used for spiritual practices across three areas – growth in knowledge, faith, and godliness – and how AI both supported and conflicted with practices such as Bible study and prayer. Based on these findings, we propose a revised notion of spiritual AI that is grounded in lived spiritual practice, rather than augmented experience, and present an agenda for future HCI research.

items.abstract_text: This paper reports on a qualitative study with 12 experts across dermatology and radiology about the risk of AI-induced skill erosion. Integrating AI tools (e.g., visual diagnosis, generative scribes) into medical workflows introduces the risk of AI-induced skill erosion among experts despite short-term efficiency gains. While existing literature focuses on short-term behavioral phenomena like automation bias and real-time accuracy, it fails to capture how continuous AI integration alters what clinicians consider essential skills and reshapes professional identity over time. We conducted 12 semi-structured interviews and speculative design workbook activities with expert radiologists and dermatologists. From this study, we derived the Human-AI Clinical Skill Framework, which maps how modular, unitary, and dynamic skill philosophies intersect with mechanical, integrative, and translational skill tiers, and what it means for clinical expertise in an AI-powered practice. We conclude with design principles for integrating AI into medical tools to mitigate skill erosion.

items.abstract_text: Most generative AI interfaces organise interaction as a linear conversational thread. However, open-ended collaborative knowledge work often requires comparing alternatives, revisiting ideas, and negotiating direction over time. We designed and studied ThoughtPaths, a multi-branch generative AI interface that produces three parallel response trajectories—balanced, critical, and provocative—and maintains them as persistent, navigable structures. Through a qualitative study with five groups (three dyads, two triads; N = 12), we examine how knowledge workers use these branches to expand and redirect exploration, surface assumptions through contrast, and coordinate decisions by revisiting earlier trajectories. We found that persistent divergence supported negotiated interaction while introducing challenges in managing cognitive load. This work contributes an open-source prototype, an empirical account of collaborative practices, and design implications for generative AI interfaces that support knowledge work.

items.abstract_text: Limited access to mental health support due to infrastructural limitations and workforce shortages has contributed to growing interest in the use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) for scalable mental health support. Despite their promise, these technologies pose risks, such as hallucinations and misalignment with local experiences of mental health challenges in the Global South. While there is growing attention to safety and harm mitigation, limited research has examined how cultural representation, linguistic coverage, and dataset provenance shape these technologies, particularly for Global South populations, and how cultural sensitivity can be improved to support mental health care. This systematic review synthesises 29 empirical studies published between 2020 and April 2026, predominantly concerning conversational GenAI for mental health. Using a keyword-based search strategy, critical narrative synthesis, and reflexive deductive thematic analysis, we examined how GenAI systems encode cultural assumptions. Our findings reveal representational gaps, limited culturally grounded narratives, and predominantly additive adaptation, whereby cultural elements are introduced while underlying Western diagnostic and therapeutic frameworks generally remain unchanged. Also, we consolidate cross-study evidence into strategies that have implications for clinical and non-clinical collaborative practices for mental health support. Lastly, we outline implications for Human-Centred AI and Computer-Supported Cooperative Work and directions for culturally grounded conversational GenAI that supports equitable mental health care.

items.title: A Single-Center Retrospective Analysis of Artificial Intelligence-Based Emotion Recognition Systems for Attention-Regulation Training in Children with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Introduction: Children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) often experience attention instability and emotion dysregulation. Existing interventions typically lack real-time responsiveness and ecological validity. This study retrospectively examined historical training records from an AI-assisted closed-loop system integrating emotion recognition and behavioral feedback for attention regulation in children with ADHD. Methods: This single-center retrospective analysis included historical training records from 60 children with ADHD who had completed either AI-assisted attention training or conventional attention training between 2021 and 2024. The AI-assisted training-record group comprised children whose archived records included 12 sessions of integrated cognitive training involving Go/No-Go, CPT, and Flanker tasks with real-time AI-generated feedback based on task performance and facial-emotion monitoring. The conventional training-record group completed the same attention tasks without AI-based feedback. Assessments included task performance, Conners Continuous Performance Test, 3rd Edition (CPT-3), teacher ratings, and emotion metrics, analyzed using linear mixed-effects models, linear growth modeling, and structural equation modeling (SEM). Results: Compared with conventional training records, AI-assisted training records showed greater pre-post changes in reaction time (RT), RT variability, and task accuracy, together with fewer commission errors in CPT-3. Post-feedback behavioral recovery was observed in 78.3% of feedback events. Teacher ratings showed consistent pre-post improvements across attention maintenance, emotional regulation, and task execution. Negative emotion labels decreased from 42.3% to 24.6% (p = 0.003). SEM supported an associative pathway linking emotion recognition frequency, feedback frequency, and RT reduction (95% CI: 0.15-0.38). Conclusions: The retrospective findings suggest that AI-assisted closed-loop training records were associated with favorable changes in attention and emotional-state indicators in children with ADHD. These exploratory results support further prospective, externally validated studies before broader clinical or educational implementation.

items.abstract_text: Digital platforms have become sites of mourning, remembrance, and continuing bonds with the dead. Yet the temporal consequences of platformed commemoration remain insufficiently theorised. This conceptual article asks whether grief can retain a self-determined rhythm within digital environments organised by notifications, automated resurfacing, metrics, and circulation. It brings grief theory, digital mourning research, algorithmic memory, Slow Living, and Slow Memory into dialogue. The article argues that grief has no universally correct speed: it is discontinuous, relational, and marked by oscillation between loss-oriented and restorative activity. The problem is therefore not digital speed alone, but the transfer of temporal agency from mourners to platforms. To address this problem, the article proposes “slow digital mourning” as an ethical framework centred on temporal autonomy, contextual remembrance, reversible consent, non-metricised commemoration, plural rhythms, and the right to silence or forgetting. It concludes with implications for platform design, digital cemetery governance, and future empirical research.

items.title: When AI Performs, What Remains? An Integrative Review of Generative AI and Cognitive Capital in Individuals and Organizations

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly entering knowledge work, and its short-term productivity benefits are increasingly documented. Less is known about what happens, over time, to the knowledge, skills, and judgment that remain in people and organizations. This integrative narrative review addresses that question through the construct of cognitive capital: the accumulated, renewable, and depletable stock of knowledge, cognitive, and metacognitive capabilities, and practices that enable an individual or an organization to learn, interpret information, exercise judgment, solve problems, and adapt. We distinguish individual and organizational cognitive capital from the capability of the human-AI system, so that gains in joint performance and losses in human capability can be observed at the same time. Drawing on experimental, field, and conceptual work, we propose four mechanisms through which interaction with AI affects cognitive capital: substitution of practice, scaffolding and feedback, metacognitive calibration, and organizational aggregation. Seven principles summarize the current evidence, including that assisted performance differs from retained competence, that the same technology can support or displace learning depending on design and use, and that individual gains can coexist with reduced collective diversity. For each mechanism, we derive testable propositions, and we discuss five design levers for organizations as proposals to be validated rather than established practice. We conclude that cognitive capital offers a multilevel frame for governing AI adoption and outline a research agenda centered on longitudinal, multilevel measurement.

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence is entering psychotherapy at almost every point of clinical work: therapist training, screening and detection, risk prediction, diagnostic support and treatment planning, patient education, chatbot-delivered session content, between-session tracking, supervision, and documentation. Discussion of the associated dangers to this process has so far been overwhelmingly patient directed. This narrative review addresses these questions from a futures-oriented perspective: what AI may do to psychotherapists as professionals. We first map current and emerging applications across the phases of therapy. We then distinguish four forms of competence loss reported in the wider clinical literature, namely deskilling, never-skilling, mis-skilling, and moral deskilling, and use them to structure a function-by-function analysis of nine clinical tasks. The risks we identify, most of which rest on extrapolation from medicine and education and are therefore best read as hypotheses, extend beyond technical skill. Algorithmic flags may redistribute clinical attention, and accountability may shift from the quality of judgement to adherence to procedure. Case formulation may close prematurely, and theoretical pluralism may narrow toward the traditions best represented in training data. Findings that chatbots are rated as more empathic than clinicians may threaten professional identity, while supervision may lose its relational and formative functions. We then set out four possible trajectories for the field: AI as a support to professional judgement, gradual dependency, standardized AI-mediated practice, and systems designed explicitly to preserve and cultivate expertise, together with the drivers that may lead toward each. Implications are drawn for training, clinical governance, and professional ethics.

items.abstract_text: Abstract The application of artificial intelligence technology in education is becoming increasingly widespread, but there is no consensus yet on its impact on learners’ critical thinking. To gain a deeper understanding of the complex relationship between the two, this study adopted the meta-analysis structural equation modeling method and systematically integrated data from 31 empirical studies worldwide in this field. The results show that the use of artificial intelligence is not directly associated with the improvement or decline of critical thinking, but rather appears to operate through two different psychological mechanisms. On the one hand, frequent use of artificial intelligence can easily lead to technological dependence, and this tendency of dependence can harm the development of critical thinking. On the other hand, the proper use of artificial intelligence tools can stimulate learning motivation, thereby promoting the cultivation of critical thinking skills. These two opposite indirect effects coexist and nearly offset each other; the net indirect effect was not statistically significant, whereas the direct association of AI use with critical thinking remained positive and significant. Further analysis suggests that this dual effect may vary across groups: the motivational pathway appeared especially pronounced among college students, whereas the group difference in the inhibition pathway was not statistically significant. This study, from a theoretical perspective, reveals the dual paths through which artificial intelligence influences critical thinking, providing an important reference for how to effectively utilize artificial intelligence tools in educational practice and also offering new directions for future related research. However, causal interpretations are limited by the predominantly cross-sectional nature of the included studies.

items.title: Navigating the Sea of Reviews: Unveiling the Effects of Introducing AI-Generated Summaries in E-Commerce

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: AI-generated review summaries are reshaping how consumers access product information, but their influence also extends to consumers who write reviews. Examining Amazon’s rollout of AI-generated review summaries, we find that these summaries encourage more review contributions and richer content. Consumers discuss product attributes absent from the summaries and elaborate on topics already covered. A controlled experiment suggests that summaries strengthen consumers’ belief that their contributions, together with others’, help future buyers make informed decisions. The increase in review contributions is stronger for products with many existing reviews or mixed ratings. Platform managers could prioritize summaries for products with mixed ratings, for which additional reviews can provide a more complete picture for future buyers. To build on richer review content, platforms could use writing prompts that highlight product attributes underrepresented in AI summaries. However, additional analyses suggest that AI summaries disproportionately benefit products that already sell well, potentially reinforcing sales concentration. Platforms could increase exposure for niche or new products, whereas policymakers could encourage fairness standards and periodic assessments of how AI-generated summaries affect product visibility and sales concentration. These findings highlight the potential of AI summaries to encourage consumer contributions, drawing attention to the risk of increased sales concentration.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education: Challenges and Managerial Risks

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has become a near-universal part of students’ academic practice, confronting universities with challenges that reach beyond technology to the core of teaching and assessment. This article is an integrative narrative review of peer-reviewed studies, preprints and policy documents published mainly between 2023 and 2026. It examines the crisis in the validity of knowledge assessment and the unreliability of AI detectors; cognitive dependence, metacognitive laziness and the erosion of critical thinking; digital inequality; the meta-analytic evidence on learning effects; and the regulatory framework set by UNESCO, the OECD and the EU Artificial Intelligence Act. The cross-cutting theme is the “performance–learning gap”: GenAI reliably improves task performance, but genuine learning gains depend on teacher support, pedagogical guardrails and the way students use the tool, and they often disappear when knowledge is assessed without AI. Particular attention is given to Georgia, where AI uptake is already high while the institutional response remains fragmented. The article proposes structural reform of assessment, a five-stage institutional pilot model for Georgian universities, a practical formula for students (“think first, ask AI, then evaluate critically”) and a research agenda of six priority directions.

items.title: Ideological framing in political communication: a comparative analysis of ChatGPT and DeepSeek

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Purpose This exploratory study examines how two conversation-based AI models, ChatGPT (USA) and DeepSeek (China), frame fundamental political concepts, “freedom, equality, democracy, social order” and the role of the state within political communication. It aims to compare the normative priorities and ideological assumptions in their responses and assess their possible relationship with the geopolitical contexts of their development. Design/methodology/approach The research used a structured comparative design and qualitative content analysis. The dataset comprises English responses to six core questions posed to GPT-4 and DeepSeek Chat in April 2024, followed by standardized follow-up questions for five items. Analysis focused on discursive framing, value priorities, and implicit assumptions. Findings Both models generally use similar democratic discourses when explaining freedom, equality, and democracy, but differ in value prioritization. ChatGPT foregrounds individual autonomy, personal rights, and democratic processes, whereas DeepSeek emphasizes collective welfare, social harmony, and the state's responsibility to maintain social order. Both refer to democracy, the rule of law, and human rights at a general level. These patterns are exploratory and not generalizable. Practical implications The study highlights the importance for policymakers, technology developers, and media professionals of understanding ideological asymmetries in AI-mediated political communication, and stresses transparency and critical awareness in conversational AI systems. Social implications The implicit normative assumptions of conversational AI can influence political information acquisition, democratic discourse, and cross-cultural understanding. Their spread in everyday information environments may shape how users interpret political concepts in unseen ways. Originality/value The study treats generative AI not merely as a technological tool but as systems situated in different geopolitical contexts that can participate in shaping social-political discourse. Comparing ChatGPT and DeepSeek offers an empirical framework for assessing ideological positioning and normative differences in conversational AI.
