items.venue: Proceedings of the Institution of Civil Engineers - Engineering Sustainability
items.abstract_text: Although artificial intelligence (AI)-driven digital twins (DTs) are increasingly promoted for sustainable built asset management, there is limited empirical evidence of their full lifecycle application – particularly in emerging economy contexts that combine technical, environmental, and human-centric performance indicators. This study examines the integration of an AI-enabled DT system across the design, construction, and operational stages of ‘Nirmitee Tower’, a green-certified commercial complex developed by a mid-sized construction firm in Central India. Adopting a mixed-methods case study approach, the research collected triangulated evidence from system analytics, environmental performance metrics, semi-structured interviews, and post-occupancy surveys. Operational definitions were applied for key measures such as material waste, comfort score, and heating, ventilation, and air conditioning energy use, with baselines drawn from comparable pre-DT projects. Key findings include: a 21% reduction in project delivery time, a 35.9% decrease in material waste, a 28.3% reduction in annual energy use, a 21.1% reduction in water consumption, and a 32% improvement in occupant comfort scores. This study contributes by providing a validated, multi-dimensional assessment framework for AI–DT performance, by demonstrating a rare emerging market case of full lifecycle DT integration in a small- and medium-scale enterprise context, and by aligning technical results with UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs 3, 8, 9, 11, 12, and 13).

items.title: AI-Based Diagnosis of Alzheimer’s Disease Using Brain MRI: Can Artificial Intelligence Improve Early Detection and Diagnostic Accuracy?

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Background/Objectives: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a neurological disorder that adversely affects cognition, memory, and overall quality of life. Identifying AD in its initial phase is especially challenging when patients display cognitive impairments. Conventional methods rely on physicians to manually examine patients and analyze images, which is time-consuming and prone to errors. This review examines the use of artificial intelligence (AI) techniques for diagnosing AD using CT scans and MRI brain imaging. Methods: Research papers published from 2018 to 2026 were sourced from Google Scholar, IEEE Xplore, and Semantic Scholar. The techniques that were investigated in this study include Convolutional Neural Networks, 3D Convolutional Neural Networks, transfer learning, Vision Transformers, ensemble models, and multimodal approaches. Five research questions were posed to analyse the practicality of using AI-driven techniques in clinical settings, their novelty, scalability, robustness, and accuracy. Results: This study found that AI models can autonomously extract information from brain images and yield highly accurate results, with numerous researches demonstrating over 90% accuracy. Deep learning applied to MRI imaging is effective, while CT-based techniques can detect brain alterations when MRI is inaccessible. Different data types, including imaging, age, medical history, and vocal characteristics, can provide valuable insights into AD. However, issues remain, such as dataset discrepancies, variations among scanners and individuals, and insufficient testing of complex models on diverse populations. Conclusions: Future efforts should focus on accurate and transparent AI, integration of multiple data types, rapid and secure models, and testing on large datasets from multiple hospitals. AI should be developed to assist physicians in accurately diagnosing AD rather than replacing them.

items.title: An Explainable Attention-Gated CNN–Transformer Framework for Automated Microplastic Recognition in Freshwater Microscopy Images

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Microplastic pollution requires rapid and reproducible monitoring methods that can complement labor-intensive visual and spectroscopic analyses. This study develops a morphology-aware artificial-intelligence framework for automated classification of field-collected microplastic particles and diatom algae in optical microscopy images. A public freshwater dataset containing 1,140 images from four classes (algae, filament, fragment, and pellet) was analyzed. After image-quality auditing, 1,137 unique images were retained for morphology–texture analysis, while deep-learning experiments used the original image collection under a fixed train/validation/test protocol. Handcrafted morphology and texture descriptors were evaluated with Random Forest, Extra Trees, radial-basis-function Support Vector Machine, and Histogram Gradient Boosting. Histogram Gradient Boosting achieved a cross-validation macro-F1 of 0.9341 ± 0.0255 and a held-out test accuracy of 0.9342. Deep-learning experiments compared ResNet50, Swin Transformer, and a CNN–Transformer fusion model combining ResNet50 and Swin representations. The fusion model achieved an accuracy of 0.9240, macro-F1 of 0.9222, and macro-AUC of 0.9954 on the 171-image test subset. Class-wise AUCs were 1.0000, 0.9950, 0.9886, and 0.9982 for algae, filament, fragment, and pellet, respectively. The results show that morphology-aware machine learning and complementary CNN–Transformer representations can support automated freshwater microplastic screening and provide a reproducible basis for environmental monitoring workflows.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Health systems are adding verifiers, AI models that check another AI’s drafted care plans, to reduce errors and omissions. We tested a verifier in two ways. First, three AI models drafted care plans for 447 retrospective test cases; a verifier caught 5 of 17 errors checkable against the patient’s record when counting flags for wrong recommendations, and 10 of 17 when also including flags for missing care. Second, in a prospective trial (NCT07718893), we randomized 240 patients in complex primary care management programs in four states to unassisted physicians, physicians with a guardrailed AI assistant, or physicians with the guardrailed assistant plus a verifier. The verifier raised 11 alerts across 77 encounters; physician adjudicators judged 9 correct, but clinicians in the trial acted on only 1. Safety events were similar across arms. Effective verification may therefore require alerts that clinicians must resolve, despite the risk of alert fatigue.

items.title: Perceived impact of generative artificial intelligence on clinical learning and decision-making among internal medicine residents in Ethiopia: a mixed- methods study

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in medical training, but evidence from African residency programs is scarce. We assessed how internal medicine residents in Ethiopia use GenAI and how they perceive its impact on clinical learning and clinical decision-making. Methods We conducted an explanatory sequential mixed-methods study consisting of a national cross-sectional online survey of internal medicine residents (June to August 2026), followed by two focus group discussions (FGDs) with 10 residents at two universities (September 2026) to explain the survey findings. Perceived impact was measured with five-point Likert items and two composite scores (learning, five items; decision-making, eight items). Associations with frequency of use were tested with chi-square or Fisher's exact tests. FGD data were organized deductively into categories based on the survey topics. Results Of 252 respondents from 18 institutions, 98.8% had used GenAI and 75.4% used it daily; ChatGPT was used by 91.6% of users. The mean composite score for perceived impact on clinical learning was 3.83 out of 5 (70.7% high) and for clinical decision-making 3.86 out of 5 (67.7% high). Agreement was highest for improved differential diagnosis (90.8%), learning efficiency (81.9%) and support for self-directed learning (79.5%), and lowest for ward-round performance (64.3%) and confidence in complex cases (71.4%). Daily use was more frequent among residents with more than three hours of daily internet use (82.3% versus 66.7% to 67.4%; p = 0.024) and was not associated with age, sex, marital status, year of residency, device access or formal training. In the FGDs, residents described GenAI as a fast, supportive tool for learning and clinical work, as an aid to reasoning and not a replacement for physician judgment, and as a possible threat to independent learning. Conclusions Residents perceive GenAI as helpful for self-directed learning and diagnostic reasoning while keeping final responsibility for clinical decisions. These findings reflect perceptions and not measured outcomes, so objective evaluation of its effects on learning and clinical performance is needed.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract AI-supported agricultural advice raises questions about useful information, the responsibilities of providers and the accessibility of legal-rights information. This study examines stated preferences about these issues in 385 adult, AI-aware survey records from Bangladesh. The mixed sample consists of law students, graduates, legal professionals and other respondents; the workbook does not identify farmers, agricultural AI users or actual knowledge of farmers’ legal rights. The analysis therefore examines questionnaire responses about rights information and safeguards rather than claiming to measure farmers’ rights awareness or the effects of an AI service. Individual items are reported using descriptive distributions, paired comparisons and exploratory rank correlations with Holm adjustment. Of 385 respondents, 338 (87.8%) endorsed including legal-rights information in responsible digital agricultural services, 330 (85.7%) endorsed identifying responsibility for important advice, 325 (84.4%) endorsed communicating uncertainty and limitations, and 247 (64.2%) endorsed human assistance when AI advice is inadequate. The rights-information item exceeded the usefulness item by 24.4 percentage points; 215 respondents endorsed both. The statements differ in content, and their paired comparison does not identify the effects of a service or rank the value of its features. Exploratory correlations with the rights-information item were small and did not provide clear evidence of association after adjustment for four tests. The article distinguishes information about rights from demonstrated legal knowledge and recommends evaluation with identified agricultural users, specific legal scenarios and observable referral pathways.

items.title: AI Skin Analysis in Real-World Practice: A Multi-Source Evidence Assessment

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly utilized to support the early assessment of skin lesions. While numerous studies report high diagnostic accuracy under controlled experimental conditions, considerably fewer integrate technical validation, independent clinical stress-testing, and large-scale real-world evidence (RWE) within a single transparent framework. Objective: To evaluate the capabilities, clinical utility, and operational limitations of a mobile AI-assisted skin analysis system by synthesizing three complementary streams of evidence. Methods: This study integrates: (1) an analysis of longitudinal technical performance metrics and big-data usage patterns from over 6.57 million real-world smartphone assessments; (2) an independent clinical evaluation ((n = 160) analyzed cases) conducted at a specialized tertiary referral dermatology center comparing AI predictions and triage routing against histopathological, cytological, or expert clinical reference standards; and (3) a comparative synthesis with contemporary peer-reviewed literature, including external validation on skin of color. Results: Longitudinal technical validation demonstrated consistent, balanced improvements across sensitivity (97.4%), specificity (93.1%), and overall accuracy (94.2%) by 2026. In real-world consumer usage, common inflammatory conditions (e.g., acne/rosacea, (n = 708,356)) accounted for the largest share of assessments, while preventable image-acquisition errors (poor lighting: 42.0%; poor focus: 28.0%; motion blur: 18.0%) represented the primary modifiable determinants of failure. In the independent tertiary referral cohort - heavily enriched with malignant and diagnostically challenging lesions - exact Top-1 and Top-3 diagnostic agreements were 54.4% and 70.6%, respectively. However, combining Top-3 agreement, correct broader disease-group assignment, and appropriate risk-based routing yielded a clinically useful triage outcome in 80.0% of cases. Conclusions: AI-assisted skin analysis provides clinically meaningful support for early risk stratification and patient referral when deployed as a clinical decision-support tool rather than an autonomous diagnostic system. Comprehensive evaluation of medical AI requires pairing conventional accuracy metrics with triage-oriented clinical endpoints and transparent RWE reporting.

items.title: Cross-Attention or Concatenation? A Multi-Seed Empirical Study of Code-Comment Fusion for Pull Request Outcome Prediction

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Predicting whether a pull request (PR) will be merged, rejected, or left unre solved is a recurring problem in empirical software engineering, yet it remains unclear how much explicit fusion of code changes and reviewer comments adds over simpler designs, and conclusions drawn from a single training run can be misleading. We report a multi-seed comparison of encoder-based fusion strategies on a retrospective dataset of 33,955 PRs from 155 projects, three platforms, and 12 programming languages. A CodeBERT–RoBERTa hybrid with bidirectional cross-modal attention is compared with concatenation and late-fusion variants, four alternative code encoders (GraphCodeBERT, UniXcoder, CodeT5, CodeReviewer), unimodal baselines, and two re-implemented prior systems, using five random seeds per model. The cross-attention hybrid reaches 88.11% mean accuracy (sample SD 0.39 percentage points, pp) and outperforms its code-only counterpart in every seed (+1.85 pp; Holm-adjusted paired p = 0.008). How-ever, the seven best models lie within a 0.42 pp band, and cross-attention exceeds concatenation by only 0.34 pp on average across five encoders (positive for four of five, not significant for any single encoder); at one seed (42) the ordering of the two reversed. Review comments alone are about as informative as code alone, and combining them adds roughly 1.6–1.9 pp. Project identity is strongly associated with the outcome (Cram´er’s V = 0.60), so the random split used here probably overstates generalisation. All analyses are retrospective, use features that become available only after review, and exclude LLM-based baselines.

items.abstract_text: Abstract Background Home-based exercise programs for congenital muscular torticollis (CMT) depend heavily on caregivers, yet adherence is often hindered by cognitive and emotional burdens. Objective This study conducted a formative usability evaluation of an AI-based CMT rehabilitation system comprising a clinician web interface and a caregiver mobile app to identify usability-related issues and preliminary design requirements during early development. Methods A formative usability evaluation was conducted with 8 clinical experts (rehabilitation physicians, nurses, and physical therapists). Participants engaged in focus group interviews (FGIs) following a demonstration of the system and completed the System Usability Scale (SUS) for the overall system, including a proxy evaluation of the caregiver mobile app. Qualitative data were analyzed using thematic analysis, and SUS scores were analyzed descriptively as a supplementary quantitative measure of perceived usability. Results The thematic analysis identified 2 core themes, “Usability Barriers of the CMT Rehabilitation System” and “Improvement Requirements,” encompassing 10 subthemes and 21 concepts. Key findings highlighted concerns regarding the reliability and interpretability of AI-generated feedback and the need to simplify data visualization to reduce the potential cognitive burden on caregivers. The mean SUS score for the overall system was 73.44 (SD 18.01). This result was interpreted descriptively and considered supplementary to the qualitative findings. Conclusions The formative evaluation identified preliminary usability strengths and areas for improvement from clinicians’ perspectives, with particular concerns regarding the reliability and interpretability of AI-generated feedback. The experts emphasized that the AI-based CMT rehabilitation system should function as a therapeutic bridge between clinicians and caregivers. As actual caregivers were not included in this evaluation, the findings represent preliminary formative design inputs based on clinicians’ proxy perspectives rather than evidence of usability for caregivers. Future iterations should incorporate the identified improvements and undergo evaluation with actual caregivers in home environments, along with separate technical verification of the accuracy of the AI feedback algorithm.

items.title: Recoverability-Centered Trajectory Governance for Long-Horizon Clinical AI Agents

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Unlabelled: Clinical AI is moving from systems that generate discrete predictions and recommendations toward agents capable of pursuing clinical objectives through repeated tool use, communication, planning, and state-changing actions. Emerging systems support multistep electronic health record workflows, and increasingly envision longitudinal care across repeated encounters. This transition expands safety assessment beyond discrete outputs and actions. Through its actions, an agent can help create the clinical state on which its subsequent decisions depend. Consequently, individually defensible actions may compose into an unsafe trajectory, even when no single action is clearly erroneous. We propose recoverability-centered trajectory governance as a clinical synthesis of established safety approaches, linking patient-specific corrective capacity to the continuing justification for delegated authority. Its central objective is clinical recoverability: preserving the opportunity for the human-AI care system to redirect care before clinically acceptable corrective pathways are exhausted. We define recovery margin as the remaining opportunity for such correction, and reauthorization boundaries as conditions requiring delegated authority to end or narrow pending renewed human judgment. This framing distinguishes reversibility, primarily a property of an action, from recoverability, a property of an evolving clinical trajectory. The operational framework combines persistent obligation tracking, independent monitoring, explicit reauthorization, authority contraction, graceful degradation, independent escalation, and verified human takeover. Oversight should concentrate at consequential trajectory junctions. Evaluation should combine trajectory stress testing, component-specific recovery-margin indicators, interruption-and-takeover testing, and population-level surveillance. Trajectory governance complements product lifecycle oversight by examining whether continued patient-specific delegation remains justified as care evolves. Because corrective capacity depends partly on access to timely monitoring and human rescue, recoverability is also an equity issue. The defining safety question is therefore not only whether an action is acceptable but whether continued delegation remains justified. The proposed indicators and governance mechanisms require domain-specific operationalization and empirical validation, including comparison with established safeguards.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming multiple sectors, including public health. Recent years have witnessed a substantial increase in research on integrating AI into public health systems, reflecting a growing interest in its potential to improve surveillance, diagnostics, policy development, and health outcomes. Objective This study aims to identify how AI has been applied in public health, examine its impact on the field, and determine future research directions at the intersection of AI and public health. Methods A systematic literature review was conducted to analyze existing scholarly research on AI applications in public health. Relevant studies were collected, screened, and categorized to identify dominant research themes and gaps in the literature. Results The analysis revealed five primary thematic clusters within the literature: (1) AI model development and performance, (2) public health threats and outbreak management, (3) systematic reviews and evidence synthesis, (4) social and ethical issues in public health, and (5) governance, policy, and innovation. The review also identified underexplored areas and inconsistencies across studies, highlighting significant research gaps. Conclusions AI has demonstrated substantial potential to enhance public health practice and research. However, further investigation is needed to address ethical, governance, and implementation challenges. Future research should focus on strengthening policy frameworks, improving transparency and accountability in AI systems, and promoting interdisciplinary collaboration to ensure the responsible and equitable integration of AI into public health.

items.title: Explainable Machine Learning Models for Predicting Significant Fibrosis in Steatotic Liver Disease: Model Development Study

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: Online Journal of Public Health Informatics
items.abstract_text: Abstract Background Steatotic liver disease (SLD) is highly prevalent, and noninvasive identification of patients with significant fibrosis remains a clinical challenge. Objective We conducted an exploratory evaluation of explainable machine learning models for predicting significant fibrosis in a US-based cohort of adults with SLD, with particular attention to sensitivity, false-negative risk, and the limitations of using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) alone to assess screening suitability. Methods We evaluated explainable machine learning models for predicting significant fibrosis in a US population–based dataset. A total of 43 routinely available clinical, demographic, anthropometric, laboratory, and lifestyle variables were included. After preprocessing and imputation, data were split into training (80%) and testing (20%) sets. The synthetic minority oversampling technique (SMOTE) was used to address class imbalance in the training set. Logistic regression, random forest, support vector machine, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), k-nearest neighbors, naive Bayes, an artificial neural network, and a stacked ensemble were trained and evaluated. Performance metrics included accuracy, precision, recall, F 1 -score, Cohen κ, and the AUROC. Because the intended use case was screening or triage, sensitivity was given particular interpretive importance. In addition to overall discrimination, a primary analytical objective was to examine sensitivity trade-offs, false-negative classifications, and the implications of model performance for screening suitability. Global and local model interpretability were assessed using feature importance, Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) values, individual conditional expectation (ICE) plots, and individualized explanations. Results Among 7056 participants, 716 (10.1%) had significant fibrosis. XGBoost achieved the highest discrimination (AUROC 0.79), followed by random forest (AUROC 0.78) and logistic regression (AUROC 0.77); however, XGBoost had low sensitivity (0.17), indicating limited utility for screening at the evaluated threshold. Logistic regression and naive Bayes demonstrated the highest sensitivity (0.65 and 0.55, respectively), suggesting that models with slightly lower discrimination may be more appropriate for triage-oriented use. Across models, waist circumference, BMI, cardiovascular comorbidity, sex, hemoglobin A 1c (HbA 1c ), and liver enzymes were the most influential predictors. Conclusions In this exploratory model development study, moderate discrimination did not necessarily translate into clinically meaningful screening performance. The model with the highest AUROC showed poor sensitivity, indicating a substantial risk of false-negative classifications and limiting its usefulness for screening in its current form. Because imputation was performed before the train-test split, the reported performance estimates may be optimistic and should not be interpreted as definitive evidence of clinical readiness. Leakage-free preprocessing, threshold optimization, calibration assessment, decision curve analysis, external validation, and prospective evaluation are needed before clinical application.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Background Skin cancer incidence is rising globally, increasing pressure on dermatology services and making efficient triage increasingly important. AI-driven skin cancer mobile health apps may help address this need, but their usefulness depends on whether users trust the advice and intend to follow it. Teledermatologist supervision has been proposed to combine AI efficiency with human clinical oversight, but dermatologist shortages make it critical to understand whether such supervision improves patient trust and adherence at the population level, or whether AI-only advice suffices for most users. Objective This study tests whether teledermatologist supervision in an AI-driven skin cancer app affects patient trust and adherence intentions, compared with AI-only advice, and whether these effects differ by motivational context and risk assessment level. Methods The randomized controlled, online vignette experiment with repeated measures was conducted from May to June 2025 as a single-center study among Dutch adults via an academic hospital-based patient panel. Eligible participants were adult members of the Erasmus MC Digital Patient Panel invited by email; those not completing all 4 vignette trials were excluded from the analysis. Participants completed 4 simulated mobile app scenarios varying in advice source (AI-only vs hybrid teledermatologist and AI) and risk assessment level (high vs low). The primary outcomes were trust in the advice (0‐100 scale) and adherence intention (recoded 3-level ordinal scale). Mixed-effects models were used to analyze the data. Results Of the 2707 patient panel members, 879 participated (response rate: 32.5%). Participants were aged 18 to 93 (mean 62.5, SD 12.64) years; 50.4% (n=443) were female, and 21.4% (n=188) had a history of skin cancer. Participants were randomly allocated to motivation conditions (concern: n=438 vs curiosity: n=441). Trust was higher for hybrid advice than AI-only advice (mean 76.9, SE 0.73 vs mean 65.7, SE 0.73; estimated difference 11.98; partial η ²=0.22; P <.001). The odds of adherence were 1.7 times greater with hybrid vs AI-only (odds ratio 1/0.59=1.7, 95% CI 1.28-2.22; P <.001). High-risk assessments increased adherence (odds ratio 2.9, 95% CI 2.2-3.8; P <.001), with a moderated effect by motivation ( P =.03), showing stronger adherence with concern vs curiosity. The effect of advice source on adherence was fully mediated by trust. Conclusions Teledermatologist supervision of AI-based advice robustly increased patient trust and adherence intentions, particularly for high-risk assessments and concerned users. Our experiment is innovative in testing teledermatologist supervision in a population-level AI skin cancer app and in examining how motivational context shapes responses to advice. Unlike studies focused on postreferral teledermatology or chatbot-based advice, this study isolates the effect of hybrid AI-human advice in a store-and-forward screening context. These findings suggest that developers and health care implementers may consider integrating teledermatologist supervision to maximize patient trust of and adherence to advice, potentially improving triaging efficiency and safety.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Background: Predictive AI models, such as AI-generated early warning systems for detecting critical conditions, are being praised as promising applications in neonatology. Despite technological advancements in predictive AI, the integration of AI at the bedside remains challenging, and few AI technologies are currently integrated into routine neonatal care. A better understanding of the wishes and barriers of patients and, in the case of neonatal patients, their parents, is essential to bridge this gap. Yet, parental perspectives on the use of AI remain underexplored. Objective: This study explored the perspectives of parents whose child had previously been admitted to a neonatal intensive care unit about the development and use of predictive AI in neonatal clinical settings. Methods: We conducted 3 focus groups with 18 Dutch parents of children admitted to a neonatal intensive care unit to explore their views on AI in neonatal care. Participants were purposively recruited via a neonatology parent and patient organization. Discussions focused on predictive AI in acute settings and on AI to predict neurodevelopmental outcomes in later life. A reflexive thematic analysis of the focus group data was performed. Results: Parents generally welcomed predictive AI as a supportive tool for the medical team, anticipating improvements in patient outcomes. AI for short-term predictions was especially appreciated, whereas longer-term predictions were received with some reservations. Overarching concerns regarding predictive AI systems included AI undermining parental intuition, overreliance on AI in decision-making, and undesirable ethical and psychological implications of long-term health predictions. Interestingly, in addition to predictive AI systems that support medical judgment, parents also hoped that other AI tools could be developed to better involve parental input in the decision-making process. Specifically, they envisioned applications that extend beyond clinical decision support to provide parents with information, emotional support, and tailored guidance on the right course of action. Conclusions: Parental perspectives highlight both opportunities and challenges for predictive AI integration in neonatal care. Engaging parents in the design and implementation of AI informs the development of family-centered, ethically responsible AI solutions and may identify opportunities for developing parent-centered AI tools alongside systems designed to support clinicians.

items.title: AI-Based Social Connection Interventions of Emerging Categories of Support for Older Adults: Scoping Review

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Background Social connection is a critical determinant of well-being in later life. However, older adults often experience social isolation and increased loneliness, which are associated with mental and physical health challenges. AI-based interventions have emerged as scalable approaches to support social connection. A growing body of research has examined the effects of individual AI technologies on improving social connection across diverse devices and care settings. Despite growing evidence of their effects, little attention has been paid to the common pathways through which these interventions support social connection. Objective This scoping review aimed to develop a typology of common categories of support across AI-based interventions and to map how these categories are configured in different intervention contexts. Methods Five databases (PubMed, MEDLINE, CINAHL, PsycINFO, and Web of Science) were searched for studies published from 2016 through 2025. Studies were included if they examined AI-based interventions designed to support social connection among older adults, conceptualized as a multidimensional construct encompassing loneliness reduction, social interaction, and behavioral engagement. Results A total of 1110 articles were retrieved, of which 47 met the inclusion criteria. Qualitative and mixed methods studies were the most prevalent (n=32, 68%), with quantitative studies accounting for the remainder (n=15, 32%). Four common support categories were identified: relational interaction (forming ties), emotional support (enhancing interaction quality), functional support (sustaining engagement), and risk detection (reducing constraints). Relational interaction and emotional support were present across all studies. Functional support and risk detection were observed in 70% (n=33) and 17% (n=8) of studies, respectively. The most prevalent configuration combined relational interaction, emotional support, and functional support, forming a companionship-plus-routine pathway that sustained engagement in everyday contexts. Functional support was associated with sustained participation in daily routines and activities, which may have contributed to opportunities for ongoing social interaction. Risk detection, while less prevalent, functioned as a constraint-reducing condition that supported continuity of engagement. Conclusions This review proposes a conceptual framework that shifts attention from specific technologies to the interactional configurations that enable AI to support social connection across care settings. This framework may inform the design and tailoring of AI-based interventions to address the multidimensional nature of social connection among older adults.

items.title: AI-ASSISTED ACOUSTIC ANALYSIS OF LEGAL DISCOURSE PROSODY: OPPORTUNITIES AND LIMITATIONS

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: The article examines the methodological potential of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted acoustic analysis for investigating prosody in legal discourse. Prosody is viewed as an essential component of spoken legal communication, shaping the expression of epistemic stance, interpersonal relations, discourse organisation, and persuasive strategies through variations in pitch, intensity, rhythm, pausing, speech rate, and voice quality. The study addresses the limited attention paid to the acoustic dimension of legal discourse and evaluates the opportunities and challenges of integrating AI technologies into prosodic research. The object of the study is the prosodic organisation of spoken legal discourse; the subject is the methodological potential and limitations of AI-assisted acoustic analysis of legal speech. The aim of the study is to provide a criteria-based evaluation of AI-assisted acoustic analysis as a methodological framework for research on legal prosody. The research is theoretical and methodological, drawing on studies in acoustic phonetics, computational paralinguistics, forensic phonetics, legal linguistics, and speech processing. Descriptive, comparative, and criticalevaluative methods are applied to assess AI-assisted acoustic analysis according to six methodological criteria: validity, reliability, scalability, interpretability, ecological validity, and legal and ethical admissibility. The findings demonstrate that AI significantly improves the efficiency, reproducibility, and scalability of acoustic analysis by automating speech preprocessing, feature extraction, and computational modelling, enabling large-scale investigation of authentic legal speech. At the same time, important limitations remain, including reduced ecological validity, limited model transparency, algorithmic bias, risks of overinterpreting acoustic evidence, and legal and ethical concerns. The study argues that AI should complement rather than replace expert phonetic interpretation. It concludes that a human-in-the-loop approach integrating computational technologies with linguistic expertise provides the most reliable framework for future research on legal prosody while ensuring methodological transparency, scientific validity, and legal accountability.

items.abstract_text: Humanware represents an emerging paradigm in human cognitive enhancement, extending the AI frontier through integration of human-centered technological interfaces with cognitive learning, metacognition, and adaptive behavioral engagement. Humanware 4.0 advances a human–technology partnership in which intelligent systems function as responsive cognitive scaffolds, facilitating learning, self-regulation, and the progressive development of intellectual capacity. This paper demonstrates the evolution from technology-as-tool (Tech 1.0–3.0) to technology-as-partner (Humanware 4.0), introducing Mirrored Intelligence through a unique case study of the Responsive MQ Mirror which is an innovation developed and implemented at the Oral Roberts University. Integrating artificial intelligence, machine learning, virtual digital assistance, e-learning, and 5G connectivity, the MQ Mirror exemplifies an interactive neurocognitive interface designed to place humans at the centre of technological engagement instead of the device. MQ Mirrors multimodal capabilities comprise personalized coaching, instructional guidance, physical fitness, auditory stimulation, motivational reinforcement, and spiritually oriented reflection. Such an interface supports cognitive engagement, verbal reasoning, spatial processing, attentional regulation, digital literacy, and metacognitive awareness particularly in young adults. On the other hand, technology-centric gadgets or devices risk promoting addictive design, over-dependency, psychological withdrawals, sleep deprivation, disrupted socialization, sedentary lifestyles with ripple effects of anxiety and depression especially in adolescents. This case-study depicts how independent active learning, cognitive autonomy, holistic wellness and individual development across intellectual, physical, and psychosocial domains is orchestrated through Humanware. This original research proposes that Mirrored Intelligence could establish complementary neural networks facilitating human cognitive enhancement with significant implications for cognitive neuroscience, neuropsychology, and educational technology in future.

items.title: Bridging the intention–practice gap in higher education faculty’s use of generative AI: A systematic literature review

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence has rapidly entered higher education teaching. A growing body of empirical research examines faculty attitudes and intention to adopt tools such as ChatGPT. However, emerging evidence suggests that intention does not consistently translate into sustained pedagogical integration. Unlike previous syntheses of AI in higher education, which have focused on applications, perceptions, or acceptance, this study addresses this discrepancy through a systematic review of empirical research published between 2023 and 2026. Following the PRISMA protocol, the review identified 150 methodologically adequate studies indexed in Scopus and Web of Science. A focused explanatory synthesis was conducted on 33 core investigations that included both intention-related constructs and indicators of pedagogical use. The analysis mapped publication trends, research designs, theoretical orientations, and predictors of behavioral intention, and examined mechanisms underlying the intention–practice gap. The findings indicate that technology acceptance models dominate the literature and consistently explain intention formation through perceived usefulness, performance expectancy, effort expectancy, and social influence. Nevertheless, only one-third of the core studies explicitly identified a discrepancy between intention and enacted pedagogical practice, whereas the majority did not directly examine or report this relationship. The evidence suggests that pedagogical capability, particularly TPACK-related competence and instructional design knowledge, mediates the translation of intention into structured classroom integration. Institutional support, governance clarity, professional development, and identity-related factors moderate the strength of this process. The review proposes a conditional intention–practice translation model integrating UTAUT and TPACK. The findings suggest that the central challenge in higher education lies not in faculty willingness, but in developing pedagogical capability within supportive institutional environments that enable sustained instructional transformation.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in higher education in Pakistan has created both opportunities and concerns for educators, researchers, and policymakers. ChatGPT, a generative AI tool developed by OpenAI, can support teaching, learning, assessment, research, and academic work. This study examined how experienced academicians view its benefits, limitations, and ethical implications in Pakistani higher education. A qualitative exploratory design was used in this study. Twelve experienced academicians from different higher education institutions in Pakistan were selected purposively and interviewed through a semi-structured guide. The interviews were transcribed and analysed through familiarization, coding, development and review of themes. ChatGPT was used only to help organize provisional codes; the researchers checked its suggestions against the transcripts and made the final analytical decisions. Five themes were identified: teaching, learning, assessment, research, and ethics. Participants reported that ChatGPT supported lesson planning, content preparation, student engagement, idea generation, academic writing, and research productivity. They also noted that it enables students to understand difficult topics, improve their writing skills, and obtain immediate academic support. Main concerns were identified as plagiarism, over-reliance on AI-generated content, weaker critical thinking, and the absence of clear institutional policies. The findings show that ChatGPT may be useful in higher education when its use is guided by academic judgment and clear rules. Universities should redesign assessment, prepare ethical guidelines, train faculty, and strengthen AI literacy. The study offers practical information for teachers, administrators, and policymakers planning the responsible use of generative AI in Pakistan.

items.venue: Scientific notes of Taurida National V I Vernadsky University Series Juridical Sciences

items.abstract_text: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) and robotic process automation (RPA) is transforming the technological environment in which legal relations arise and are implemented. Unlike traditional automation based primarily on predetermined rules, AI systems can analyse large volumes of data, identify patterns, generate predictions, adapt their behaviour and select among alternative outputs. This creates new challenges concerning legal attribution, liability, contractual relations and intellectual property. The article examines the relationship between AI and RPA from legal, technological and inter- disciplinary perspectives, with particular attention to the relationship between technological auton- omy and legal personality. It argues that technological autonomy cannot, by itself, constitute grounds for granting an AI system legal personality, since legal personality is a normative construct estab- lished by law. The relevant question is whether a special legal status would provide an effective response to specific regulatory problems. The study distinguishes conventional automated information systems, AI systems that assist human decision-making, and highly autonomous AI systems. While traditional legal mechanisms may generally be sufficient for conventional automation, AI-assisted and highly autonomous sys- tems require additional safeguards concerning transparency, traceability, human oversight and accountability. The article also examines the informational structure of AI and the need to distin- guish hardware, software, algorithms, models and data in relation to property rights, intellectual property and liability. The concept of electronic personality is analysed in the context of the contemporary European approach, particularly Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), which establishes a risk-based framework focused on safety, fundamental rights, transparency and human oversight. For Ukraine, the article proposes a gradual regulatory model based on coherent terminology, risk- based classification, transparency, traceability, human oversight and clear liability rules. Further regulation should address automated contractual activity, AI-generated results and risk insurance. A special electronic legal status should be considered only after sufficient technological, legislative and judicial practice has demonstrated that existing legal mechanisms are inadequate.

items.title: The Emotion Economy: Algorithmic amplification, cognitive fluency, and cultural schemas in Instapoetry

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: The contemporary literary landscape has been fundamentally reshaped by the rise of Instapoetry: short, visual, and emotionally direct verse disseminated primarily through Instagram, a platform whose image-first architecture and recommender systems privilege affectively engaging content. This article argues that the dominance of this poetic form represents not a superficial cultural trend but an adaptive response to a digitally mediated attention economy. It advances an integrative theoretical framework explaining Instapoetry through the convergence of three dimensions: algorithmic, psychological, and cultural. First, algorithmic amplification on Instagram leverages patterns of repetition and social proof to promote specific formal styles. Second, the cognitive state of the platform’s users—marked by social media fatigue and elevated cognitive load—produces a preference for content high in processing fluency. Third, the cultural motifs that dominate Instapoetry function as accessible affective schemas, enabling readers to engage in self-expression, identity construction, and emotional validation. Drawing on research in media studies, cognitive science, and feminist literary criticism—and referencing the influential work of early Instapoets such as Rupi Kaur and Amanda Lovelace—this paper proposes a multidisciplinary account of how digital infrastructures and human psychology jointly shape contemporary poetic production and reception.

items.title: Artificial intelligence for poultry disease and health monitoring: a narrative review of computer vision, multimodal sensing, edge AI, and generative AI

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Poultry diseases and welfare issues can lead to significant production losses, compromise food safety, and create a need for ongoing farm monitoring. This narrative review summarises 81 peer-reviewed research papers published between 2016 and 2026 focusing on the use of artificial intelligence (AI) for monitoring poultry diseases and health. The papers were grouped into the following categories, namely disease diagnosis, health and welfare monitoring, mortality and biosecurity surveillance, and post-harvest food safety, and are summarised in a study-level appendix by modality, technique and reported data details. Conventional machine learning, convolutional neural networks, transfer learning, YOLO-based object detection, transformer models, explainable AI, multimodal fusion, IoT, edge AI, federated learning, generative AI, and vision-language models are the focus of the reviewed literature. The most common methods are image and faecal-image analysis, complemented by audio, thermal, video, behavioural, and environmental sensing. The trend in recent work is to use lightweight models on local devices and to integrate multiple modalities. Some limitations to direct comparison of reported results include small sample sizes and the nature of the datasets in some studies, differences in class definitions, unbalanced classes, inconsistent validation protocols, and limited cross-farm testing. Cross-farm generalisation, standardised benchmarking, explainability, prospective veterinary validation, privacy-preserving collaboration features, and cost-effective edge deployment are highlighted as key priorities. Future work should involve creating multi-country and multi-breed benchmark datasets, developing commercially validated decision-support tools and poultry-specific foundation models, and implementing continual-learning systems and multimodal fusion frameworks. The review suggests that AI has the potential to enhance precision poultry production, but successful long-term implementation of AI in the field requires not only high accuracy but also robustness, interpretability, and affordability.

items.abstract_text: Debates concerning generative artificial intelligence increasingly address not only what these systems can produce, but also who receives credit, who is compensated, and whose professional authority is safeguarded. This study examines how news and industry publications in the United States and Mexico represented AI and creative labor between 2023 and 2026. It draws on a comparative, cross-sectional quantitative content analysis of a purposively stratified corpus of 120 articles, focusing on represented harms, worker agency, institutional responsibility, proposed responses, and dominant frames. Coverage in both countries addressed displacement, compensation, authorship, and unauthorized reproduction, but differed in how it interpreted these concerns. Labor rights and collective action constituted the dominant frame in 50.0% of United States articles and 6.7% of Mexican articles, whereas legal and intellectual property concerns predominated in 50.0% of Mexican articles and 8.3% of United States articles. Regulation or legislation appeared in 86.7% of Mexican coverage and 36.7% of United States coverage, while collective bargaining or labor action appeared more frequently in the United States sample. The regulatory contrast remained evident across analyses restricted by publication period and publication category. From a Media Ecology perspective, these patterns suggest that coverage helps define which harms, actors, and remedies become publicly visible. The study therefore identifies differences in the institutional meaning assigned to AI-related disruption without making claims about audience-level effects.

items.abstract_text: Introduction This study aims to analyse university students' perceptions of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in their academic education, exploring how they construct meaning around its use and how these representations influence notions of learning, authorship and critical literacy in higher education. Methods The sample comprised 20 students from Argentina, Chile, Mexico and Peru. The Zaltman Metaphor Elicitation Technique (ZMET) was employed as a qualitative elicitation approach using images and metaphorical narratives, applied via a two-phase protocol: a) a pre-task involving the independent selection of seven images; and b) a guided elicitation phase, based on questions that explore the participant's perception through analogies, sensory contrasts and emotional narratives. Results Within this corpus, participants articulated ambivalent representations of GenAI through several distinct metaphorical configurations, including an “other” to which participants attribute agency (a silent companion or tutor) and a pragmatic cognitive extension valued for its efficiency. On an emotional level, some accounts represented GenAI as an emotional buffer, offering relief from academic overload; however, this relief coexists with ethical vigilance and unease about “crossing a line” in academic honesty, reflecting processes of negotiation over intellectual responsibility and the legitimate use of generative systems in educational contexts. Discussion Regarding institutional adaptation, metaphors of misalignment and accounts of GenAI bridging gaps in academic support point to perceived gaps in institutional guidance and to the importance of pedagogical mediation, including clearer approaches to teaching and assessment in a context where GenAI is already part of university life. Taken together, the accounts show how participants interpret GenAI as a context-specific form of academic support and guidance. These representations link the negotiation of trust and authorship to the perceived accessibility of university support, offering insights into critical literacy and institutional mediation.

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) can transform teaching, learning, assessment and research in higher education. In Ecuador, the adoption of ChatGPT, Gemini and other language models is driving academic interest, yet little is known about the scientific production that addresses it. This systematic mapping review, reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement, maps the scientific production on generative artificial intelligence that explicitly refers to Ecuador, indexed in Scopus and the Web of Science Core Collection between 2024 and 2026, in order to establish the weight that higher education holds within it. No disciplinary filter was applied to the query, so that this weight could be measured rather than assumed. The search, executed on 4 July 2026, retrieved 57 records (all 16 Web of Science records were also in Scopus, so the corpus comes in practice from Scopus; regional databases were not searched); after removing 16 duplicates and excluding 9 records, 32 documents were mapped with bibliometric indicators (Bibliometrix, VOSviewer), and the 18 higher education studies with primary data were subjected to a focused synthesis that included the appraisal of their methodological quality with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Higher education accounts for 20 of the 32 documents (63%); the other 12 are spread over political communication and journalism, legal and technical applications and four smaller domains. A sensitivity search with synonyms, Spanish terms and the year 2023, run on 15 October 2026, gave a similar share (44 of 73 documents, 60%). Within the higher education corpus, perceptions and acceptance of GAI are the most frequent outcome domain (16 of 18 studies); learning outcomes appear in six, but only two measure them directly. Eight studies use descriptive or cross-sectional designs, and none is randomised or longitudinal. ChatGPT is the most frequently examined tool (11 of 18). Sample representativeness and control of confounding were the most frequent methodological weaknesses. The findings highlight the need for experimental and longitudinal research evaluating the impact of GAI on Ecuadorian higher education.

items.abstract_text: Background Emergency medicine is characterized by urgency, criticality, severity, and diversity, which places high demands on undergraduate medical education. Traditional lecture-based teaching has limitations in developing students' advanced clinical competence and clinical transfer ability. Although virtual simulation and case-based learning (CBL) have demonstrated benefits in medical education, their combined application in emergency medicine teaching has not been systematically evaluated, especially based on artificial intelligence (AI). This study primarily aimed to investigate whether the integrated AI-powered virtual simulation combined with CBL could improve students' higher-order clinical competencies and clinical transfer ability, and secondarily to obtain empirical evidence to support the optimization of undergraduate emergency medicine teaching. Methods Third-year undergraduate students majoring in clinical medicine were selected as the research subjects and randomly divided into the control group and the experimental group. The control group adopted the traditional teaching method, while the experimental group adopted the AI-enabled virtual simulation combined with real emergency case teaching method. The learning situation of the virtual simulation platform was automatically recorded by the platform, and the teaching effect was evaluated through theoretical scores, objective structured clinical examination (OSCE) scores, clinical practice tracking evaluation (including advanced clinical ability and clinical transfer effect evaluation), comprehensive evaluation of learning psychology, and teaching satisfaction questionnaire. Results Compared with the control group, the students in the experimental group demonstrated significant advantages in all assessment dimensions, including theoretical test, various practical skills in OSCE, disease assessment, emergency management, clinical decision-making, as well as learning confidence, autonomous learning ability and teaching satisfaction ( P &lt; 0.001). Further analysis indicated that within the experimental group, greater investment in study time was significantly associated with better clinical performance and diagnostic accuracy. Crucially, Cox regression analysis confirmed that diagnostic accuracy was an independent protective factor for the weakness of clinical transfer ability (HR = 0.6469, P &lt; 0.00001), meaning that students with higher diagnostic accuracy had a significantly superior clinical competence. Conclusions In conclusion, this study demonstrates that the teaching model combining AI-powered virtual simulation with real cases can comprehensively and significantly enhance the comprehensive clinical skills and learning experience of medical students. The teaching effect can effectively transfer to the real clinical environment, and the diagnostic accuracy cultivated during the teaching process has important predictive value for the long-term clinical prognosis. This provides empirical evidence for the reform of emergency medicine education and emphasizes the importance of linking educational process evaluation with clinical outcomes.

items.title: Beyond access: the evolution of Portugal’s pharmacy-based vaccination strategy and the future role of AI-driven outreach

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Vaccination programmes increasingly face a paradox: expanding access does not necessarily translate into coverage at policy targets. Portugal provides an instructive example. The integration of community pharmacies into seasonal influenza and COVID-19 vaccination created more than 3,500 vaccination points and approximately 70% of influenza doses were administered in pharmacies in 2023–2024. The pharmacy share then fell to under 46% by 2025–2026, while total influenza doses remained broadly stable (2.41 to 2.56 million per season). This indicates a redistribution of doses across settings rather than a loss of vaccination activity; changes in age eligibility, high-dose vaccination for adults aged ≥85 years in SNS units, and invitation and recall activity may all have contributed. Influenza coverage among adults aged ≥65 years remained below the World Health Organization target of 75%, at 70.5% in 2024–2025 and 73.0% in 2025–2026. This suggests that, residual under-vaccination reflects barriers beyond physical access. The authors use “activation gap” descriptively for potentially addressable interruptions between eligibility and vaccination. Portugal already uses registry-based invitations and reminders, the open question is what a conversational layer, scripted or based on generative AI, could add. Evidence is relatively strong for reminders, growing for scripted conversational interventions and preliminary for generative AI. The authors therefore propose a registry-based randomised comparison of existing recall, existing recall plus a scripted conversational intervention, and existing recall plus a generative-AI conversational intervention, with incremental vaccination, safety, equity, trust and cost per additional vaccinated person as outcomes.

items.title: Nurse–patient communication when patients introduce AI-generated health information: a qualitative study of clinical nurses’ experiences and responses

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Background As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) increasingly becomes a source of health information for patients, some patients and family members have already obtained relevant explanations or recommendations from AI and brought this information into clinical communication. This change may create new communication demands for nurses. This study aimed to explore clinical nurses’ communication experiences and response strategies when patients or family members introduced AI-generated health information into nurse–patient communication. Methods A qualitative descriptive design was adopted. Using purposive sampling combined with a maximum variation strategy, 18 clinical nurses with relevant communication experience were recruited from three tertiary hospitals in Sichuan Province and Shanghai, China. One-to-one semi-structured interviews were conducted between May and August 2026. The interviews focused on specific nurse–patient communication events personally experienced by the participants. Data were analyzed using inductive reflexive thematic analysis. Results Two themes and six subthemes were identified. The first theme, changes in nurse–patient communication in the context of AI, included seeking confirmation from or questioning nurses using AI-generated health information, increased explanatory work, and increased communication opportunities. The second theme, nurses’ responses to AI-generated health information, included identifying patients’ actual concerns, explaining information differences in relation to the patient’s specific situation, and maintaining communication while seeking professional support. Conclusion The introduction of AI-generated health information into nurse–patient communication may both increase nurses’ explanatory work and create new opportunities for communication. Nurses may need to consider patients’ existing understanding and actual concerns, explain discrepancies between AI-generated health information and clinical arrangements in relation to the patient’s specific situation, and seek professional support when necessary. These findings may inform efforts to support nurses’ communication skills, although their applicability across different clinical settings requires further exploration.

items.title: The limits of declarative authorship: the structural vulnerability of intellectual property in the age of generative AI

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Generative AI functions as a near zero cost execution engine, weakening the long standing reliance on human effort on which traditional intellectual property (IP) systems depend. The academic response has focused, so far, on studying productivity at the micro level, debating the doctrinal question of IP infringement through AI training at the macro level, or blunt denial of AI authorship. These responses miss the central problem: the human provenance at the heart of IP law is now cheap to falsify and hard to verify. In this paper I argue that AI output appropriation poses a significant threat to IP through an adverse selection dynamic. The threat comes from humans who use AI to appropriate its output and extract the value attached to human effort. Skill compression effects cutting across writing, coding, and consulting have begun to commoditize execution, compressing the quality distribution that once supported premium prices for IP protected output. This process is compounded by the difficulty of verifying declared human authorship or inventorship, which may reward deception and discourage honest effort. I therefore explore value migration from execution skill to concentrated complementary assets. Building on market evidence from platform economies, the paper considers an evolution of IP from a rights based asset model to a verification model, in which the human role shifts from creator to authenticator.

items.abstract_text: Practice-oriented cybersecurity education often requires novice learners to build target web systems by hand before security analysis begins, imposing extraneous cognitive load. An earlier study introduced a Red/Blue teaming model in which a large language model (LLM) agent builds the target systems (vibe coding) under Human-on-the-Loop (HOTL) control, so that learners audit, attack, and defend. This single-cohort study examines learner-level evidence from the 2026 cohort (n = 34) of a university web-security course, set against institutional Course-Quality-Improvement (CQI) satisfaction records for nine of the ten academic years 2017–2026. Logged total coding effort had a median of 3.8 h. In the final-course survey, 96% agreed implementation burden had decreased and 93% that deeper engagement in vulnerability analysis and defense design was possible (raw means 4.67 and 4.44 of 5; Wilcoxon p < 0.001). The 2026 CQI score (91.55) ranked second among the nine records (descriptive). In this single-institution context, delegating system construction to an LLM agent was associated with lower perceived implementation burden, greater reported security-analysis engagement, and high satisfaction; multi-site replication is required.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Post-stroke cognitive impairment (PSCI) is a common and disabling consequence of stroke, arising from the complex interplay of vascular injury, cerebral small vessel disease, network disruption, neuroinflammation, neurodegeneration, and individual susceptibility factors. Advances in neuroimaging have improved understanding of PSCI pathophysiology and enabled the identification of imaging biomarkers associated with cognitive outcomes. This narrative review provides a comprehensive overview of current neuroimaging markers relevant to PSCI, including conventional magnetic resonance imaging, diffusion tensor imaging, resting-state functional MRI, arterial spin labeling, positron emission tomography, and connectome-based approaches. Particular attention is devoted to radiomics and artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning, deep learning, explainable AI, multimodal AI, and foundation models, which are increasingly investigated approaches for biomarker discovery, biological phenotyping, and prediction of cognitive outcomes. The review further examines multimodal frameworks that integrate neuroimaging, radiomic features, blood-based biomarkers, digital biomarkers, and AI-driven analytics to support risk assessment and prognostic stratification. Despite considerable progress, important challenges remain, including methodological heterogeneity, limited standardization, insufficient external validation, concerns regarding model interpretability, and regulatory barriers to clinical implementation. Emerging technologies, such as federated learning, foundation models, digital twins, and large language models, may further contribute to the advancement of precision neurology. The convergence of multimodal biomarkers, advanced analytical approaches, and digital-health technologies may improve prognostic assessment, support individualized management strategies, and facilitate the translation of precision-medicine approaches into routine clinical care for individuals with PSCI.

items.title: How Can Artificial Intelligence Explain its Thinking? A Review of Explainable AI
items.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference on AI Research.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly shaping decision-making across industries such as healthcare, finance, e-commerce, education, and cybersecurity. Despite significant advances in machine learning and generative AI, many AI models continue to function as “black boxes,” producing outputs and recommendations without clearly communicating the reasoning behind them. This lack of transparency has raised growing concerns regarding trust, accountability, fairness, and ethical AI adoption. As organizations become more dependent on AI-driven systems, explainability has emerged as a critical factor influencing how users perceive, trust, and adopt artificial intelligence technologies. This literature review examines how Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) enables AI systems to communicate their reasoning in ways understandable to human users. The paper analyzes existing academic and industry research on explainability, transparency, and interpretability within AI systems, with a particular focus on how explanations influence human trust and organizational acceptance of AI technologies. The review evaluates major explainability approaches used in both traditional machine learning models and modern generative AI systems, including techniques such as Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME), SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), attention visualization, counterfactual explanations, and chain-of-thought reasoning methods used in large language models (LLMs). In addition, the paper examines the distinctions between transparency, interpretability, and explainability, and how these concepts contribute to building trustworthy AI systems. The review further analyzes explainability from a human-centered perspective, including perceived fairness, ethical AI design, user confidence, and organizational adoption challenges. The paper also discusses the growing importance of explainability within responsible AI governance frameworks, particularly as regulatory initiatives such as the European Union AI Act increasingly emphasize transparency and accountable AI decision-making. This study contributes to the growing body of literature on explainable AI by consolidating fragmented research on transparency, trust, and human-centered AI adoption. The review identifies current research gaps, limitations of existing explainability approaches, and future opportunities for designing AI systems that are not only accurate and efficient but also understandable, trustworthy, and ethically aligned with human values.

items.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference on AI Research.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: AI-driven beauty filters are now embedded in adolescents' everyday digital self-presentation, yet their ethical implications for marketing communication have received limited attention within management and consumer research. Existing studies largely rely on exposure-based quantitative designs that assess outcomes such as body dissatisfaction, offering limited insight into how young users actively interpret digitally altered imagery. This study contributes to this literature by examining how early adolescent girls aged 10–14 make sense of AI-filtered and unfiltered facial images and how their side-by-side visual contrast shapes evaluations of beauty and postability. The study employs a three-stage qualitative visual elicitation design that mirrors naturalistic social media engagement. In Stage 1, participants are presented with five variations of the same face, ranging from unfiltered to differently filtered versions, and select their preferred image for beauty and posting suitability, providing baseline judgements for the analysis. Stage 2 introduces paired filtered and unfiltered images presented side by side, creating visual contrast that renders digital modification perceptually salient and functions as a brief visual micro-intervention. Stage 3 reintroduces the same facial images presented in Stage 1 to examine whether participants’ evaluative judgements shift following the contrast exposure in Stage 2. Audio-recorded interviews capture participants’ verbal explanations, enabling analysis of how adolescents articulate, justify, and reason about digitally modified appearance cues. The study contributes methodologically by showing how sequential visual exposure can be used to examine adolescents’ interpretations rather than relying only on scale-based outcomes. Theoretically, it draws on Social Comparison Theory and Online Self-Presentation Theory because evaluating what is considered beautiful and deciding what is suitable to post represent related but distinct processes. Together, these theories explain how filtered and unfiltered appearances are evaluated and how these evaluations inform posting preferences. By foregrounding adolescents’ own interpretations, the research advances understanding of how beauty norms are cognitively constructed within digital marketing environments and highlights the ethical significance of representational authenticity in visual communication targeting young consumers.

items.abstract_text: Do you know what is in your beer? Increasingly, the answer depends not only on ingredients and fermentation, but on the integrity of the digital and physical systems that govern production. This paper examines commercial brewing as an underdeveloped cyberbiosecurity workforce problem intensified by AI. Brewing increasingly depends on digital networks, automated control, and connected supply chains. Yet the process remains a biologically active process shaped by human judgment, microbial control, and physical equipment. Although cyberbiosecurity research addresses biotechnology, biomanufacturing, food, and agriculture, commercial fermentation has received comparatively limited attention. Brewing is a useful case because cyber incidents can disrupt fermentation, sanitation, packaging, quality control, and operational decision-making even when finished beer remains inhospitable to many pathogens. Malicious use of AI to uplift novice actors, used in conjunction with generative phishing attacks, may further reduce informational barriers and support coordination across cyber, biological, and physical domains, although current evidence does not establish fully autonomous adversarial operations. Drawing on cyberbiosecurity, OT-security, workforce, and training frameworks, this paper identifies a socio-technical gap between brewing science and cybersecurity and proposes a competency model incorporating AI literacy, OT awareness, biological anomaly recognition, and scenario-based training. It argues that workforce preparedness should complement technical and governance controls in securing increasingly digitized brewing environments.

items.abstract_text: Human-centered artificial intelligence (HCAI) seeks to orient AI toward human values, autonomy, oversight, safety, and meaningful control. Yet the term “human-centered” leaves a prior question unresolved: what conception of the human is being centered? Much HCAI discourse approaches the human as user, decision-maker, rights-holder, stakeholder, or bearer of preferences and values. These conceptions are indispensable but incomplete. This article argues that HCAI must also recognize the human as an aesthetic subject: a being whose perception, attention, imagination, interpretation, and judgment are formed through experience. As recommendation, personalization, generative AI, and predictive systems increasingly organize the conditions under which people encounter and evaluate the world, AI can participate in forming rather than merely serving human preferences. The article develops the concept of aesthetic agency to describe the human capacity to participate meaningfully in the formation of one’s perceptual, imaginative, interpretive, and evaluative relation to the world. It distinguishes choice from judgment, preference from taste, generation from imagination, and optimization from experience. On this basis, it proposes an aesthetically expanded HCAI organized around openness, plurality, reflectivity, and transformability. To center the human is not only to preserve control over AI, but to preserve the capacity to perceive, imagine, judge, and become otherwise.

items.abstract_text: Generative AI can enable production without corresponding learning, yet wholesale exclusion from assessed work forgoes opportunities needed for workplace and lifelong learning. This article proposes learning-consequential assessment design. Students may use AI to produce assessed work, but success also depends on showing they possess the understanding their AI-supported work displays. Knowing this may encourage students to use AI for learning through explanation, comparison and challenge, rather than product optimisation alone.
