items.venue: EPRA International Journal of Multidisciplinary Research (IJMR)
items.abstract_text: This study examined how internal control systems and ethical oversight shape corporate governance effectiveness in AI-driven organisations, using listed deposit money banks in Nigeria as the focus. The increasing use of artificial intelligence in banking operations has introduced governance risks that traditional control systems may no longer fully address. Previous studies mostly considered internal controls, ethics, and governance as separate issues, with limited evidence on how they work together in emerging economies. The study therefore assessed the effects of Risk Assessment, Control Activities, Information and Communication, and Monitoring Activities on Tobin’s Q, and also examined the moderating role of Ethical Oversight. A correlational and panel data research design was adopted. Secondary data were sourced from the audited annual reports and accounts of 13 listed deposit money banks in Nigeria for the period 2015 to 2024. Descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, Hausman specification test, and random effects regression were used for the analysis. The findings showed that all the internal control variables had positive and significant effects on Tobin’s Q, while Information and Communication had the strongest influence. Ethical Oversight also showed a positive direct effect and significantly strengthened the relationship between internal control systems and firm value. The study concludes that effective internal controls, when supported by credible ethical governance, improve market performance and broaden the traditional view of corporate governance in technology-driven institutions. It therefore recommends that deposit money banks strengthen risk management systems, widen internal audits to cover AI systems, establish active ethics committees, invest in secure digital reporting platforms, and provide continuous governance training for directors and compliance officers.

items.venue: International Journal of Technology in Teaching and Learning

items.abstract_text: The dominant automation paradigm, which measures artificial intelligence by its capacity to act independently of humans, is increasingly inadequate for complex problem-solving. This article develops the concept of Hybrid Intelligence, defined as an adaptive, self-regulating system arising from the synergistic integration of human and artificial intelligence to enhance cognitive abilities. Revisiting the cognitive-tools tradition through an information-processing lens, it argues that generative AI dissolves the safeguard that once ensured tools amplified rather than supplanted human thinking. It then specifies a layered, multi-agentic architecture in which AI agents and agentic AI are embedded within contextual and collaborative human layers. It applies this architecture to the phases of complex problem-solving. The overriding argument is that sustainable Hybrid Intelligence requires enduring theoretical foundations that outlast individual model releases, ensuring that human–AI collaboration genuinely enhances, rather than inadvertently constrains, human cognitive agency.

items.abstract_text: Purpose: This study synthesizes research on Responsible AI in education to develop an Islamic ethical framework that supports human agency, cognitive autonomy, and academic integrity. Method: We conducted a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) using PRISMA 2020 and analyzed 50 articles published between 2022 and 2026 from Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, Dimensions, and Google Scholar. Findings: Research has shifted from technology acceptance toward ethics and governance, although it remains dominated by higher education and cross-sectional designs. Responsible AI principles include transparency, accountability, fairness, and human oversight. The Islamic perspective strengthens these principles through maqāṣid al-sharī‘ah and the values of amanah, 'adl, ihsan, sidq, and tabayyun. The relationship between AI and human agency, cognitive autonomy, and academic integrity is conditional: reflective and verified use tends to support these dimensions, whereas dependence may undermine them. Novelty: This review's findings point to a shift from governance-centered responsibility to moral-epistemic responsibility, with three propositions: tabayyun as an obligation of epistemic verification, hifẓ al-‘aql as an educational orientation, and integrating AI governance with moral-educational development. Contribution: This study provides a conceptual foundation for responsible AI use in Islamic education by placing human oversight, information verification, independent thinking, and academic integrity at its core. Future Research: Future studies should test these propositions through longitudinal and experimental designs and develop instruments that integrate Islamic ethical values, human agency, cognitive autonomy, and academic integrity. Hubungan AI dengan agensi manusia, otonomi kognitif, dan integritas akademik bersifat kondisional: penggunaan reflektif dan terverifikasi cenderung mendukung, sedangkan ketergantungan berisiko melemahkan. publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: International Journal of Innovative Science and Research Technology
items.abstract_text: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have become useful tools for analysing medical images because they can learn visual patterns associated with normal and abnormal tissue. In cancer screening and diagnosis, however, a high classification score alone is not sufficient: clinicians also need to understand which image regions influenced a model’s output. This paper proposes an explainable deep-learning framework that combines CNN-based image classification with Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods to support early cancer detection from histopathological images. The proposed workflow includes image collection, quality assessment, preprocessing, augmentation, CNN training, prediction, and explanation generation. Grad-CAM is used to produce class-specific heatmaps, while LIME and SHAP are considered for local image-region and feature-contribution explanations. The explanations are intended to help users inspect whether the model focuses on tissue regions that are relevant to the predicted class rather than irrelevant background patterns. Model performance can be assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, specificity, and area under the ROC curve. Explanation quality should additionally be examined through localization agreement, stability, and review by qualified domain experts. The framework is presented as a research proposal; its diagnostic performance and clinical usefulness must be established through controlled experiments and external validation. It is designed as a decision-support approach and is not intended to replace professional diagnosis.

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly transformed gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy, with most early applications focusing on computer-aided detection and diagnosis of lesions from endoscopic images. However, real-world endoscopic practice extends beyond image interpretation. Endoscopists must integrate real-time video, anatomical location, lesion morphology, procedural context, histopathological findings, clinical history, and standardized terminology to make diagnostic decisions and generate clinically meaningful reports. Recent advances in multimodal AI and large language models (LLMs) provide an opportunity to move beyond isolated endoscopic image analysis toward more comprehensive endoscopic workflow support. By integrating visual, textual, temporal, and clinical information, these models can support lesion characterization, anatomical navigation, procedure quality assessment, structured documentation, report generation, and patient-centered communication. Nevertheless, clinical translation remains limited by scarce high-quality multimodal datasets, heterogeneous reporting standards, insufficient external validation, hallucination risk, limited interpretability, real-time integration challenges, privacy concerns, and evolving regulation. This review summarizes current applications of AI in GI endoscopy, with particular emphasis on the emerging role of multimodal learning and LLMs in bridging lesion detection, context-aware interpretation, and automated report generation. Furthermore, the article analyzes future challenges and the methodological, clinical, ethical, and regulatory requirements for the reliable integration of these systems into clinical endoscopic practice.

items.title: Coping with sustainability information overload:  The role of generative artificial intelligence literacy

items.venue: Ho Chi Minh City Open University Journal of Science - Economics and Business Administration
items.abstract_text: Consumers can use sustainability information to consume responsibly; however, excessive and complex sustainability claims might confuse consumers and hinder proper evaluations. Based on cognitive appraisal theory, this study empirically investigates the impacts of sustainability information overload (SIO) on green information avoidance (GIA) and green information verification behavior (GIVB) and examines the moderating role of generative AI literacy (GAIL) and the associations of GIA and GIVB with green purchase decision confidence (GPDC). Data from an online cross-sectional survey of 468 adult consumers in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. Findings revealed that SIO positively influenced GIA, and GIA negatively influenced GPDC. However, SIO did not negatively influence GIVB on average. GAIL significantly moderated the SIO-GIVB relationship: SIO was negatively associated with GIVB at low GAIL but not significantly at mean or high GAIL.GIVB positively influenced GPDC. An indirect effect of SIO on GPDC through GIA is significant, but the indirect effect through GIVB is not significant unconditionally. These results suggest that sustainability information overload is associated with distinct coping responses. From a practical perspective, sustainability portals and shopping applications involving GenAI should emphasize evaluability and verifiability rather than enhancing disclosures. Through defining GAIL as a digitally mediated capability from the consumer’s perspective which can serve as a coping tool, this paper builds on cognitive appraisal theory in the context of AI-mediated sustainable consumption and explains the critical engagement of consumers with sustainability information amid overload situations.

items.abstract_text: In this study, we adopted a holistic approach by integrating bibliometric analysis and systematic review methods to thoroughly evaluate the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in mathematics education and its research trends. The study aims to understand the current state of the field and provide strategic direction for future research by assessing general trends, intellectual contributions, and application potential in AI-focused mathematics education research from a multidimensional perspective. In the first phase, we conducted a content analysis of 363 articles published in high-quality journals indexed in the Web of Science (WoS) database, focusing on dimensions such as publishers, method types, research designs, study groups, theoretical or conceptual frameworks, data collection techniques, preferred technologies, purposes of use, and roles. Subsequently, we conducted a comprehensive and systematic evaluation of scientific productivity, citation performance, collaboration networks, conceptual structures, thematic maps, and intellectual transformations. During this process, we followed the guidelines outlined in the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA). The findings indicate that AI technologies have been increasingly utilized in mathematics education, with significant growth observed since 2015. AI-focused mathematics education research has been predominantly concentrated in countries like the USA, China, and Germany, delving into areas such as personalized learning, assessment, feedback, and pedagogical innovations. Most studies have employed quantitative and mixed methods, with middle school and undergraduate students being the primary target groups. Bibliometric analyses reveal a rapid expansion in scientific productivity and collaboration networks, while thematic trends primarily focus on personalized learning and the integration of digital tools.

items.abstract_text: Having been studied for centuries, mathematical modelling is an important perspective in mathematics education; however, teachers often face difficulties in accessing appropriate and high-quality modelling activities for classroom use. This study investigates the capacity of ChatGPT and its customised version, the Mathematical Modelling Problem Generator (MMPG), to produce mathematically and pedagogically meaningful modelling problems. Four AI-generated model-eliciting activities were comparatively analysed: three produced in independent ChatGPT-4 sessions and one produced by MMPG, all focusing on ratios and proportions. The problem scenarios were evaluated using five characteristics from established frameworks, focusing on context (non-routine and real-life relevance) and complexity (multiple steps, uncertain solution paths, and multiple solutions). The results show that ChatGPT failed to produce MEAs that met key modelling characteristics, whereas MMPG successfully generated non-routine, multi-step MEAs with unclear solution paths and multiple valid solutions. Therefore, MMPG can be considered an effective tool for supporting pedagogical practice by improving teachers’ access to and design of content-aligned, high-quality modelling activities.

items.venue: Journal of Economics, Finance And Management Studies
items.abstract_text: This study investigates how generative AI enabled financial forecasting capability and business analytics capability shape strategic financial decision quality in emerging market SMEs, with particular attention to the moderating role of AI governance maturity. Grounded in organizational information processing theory and dynamic capabilities theory, the study argues that better financial decisions depend not simply on access to advanced technologies, but on how effectively firms turn AI generated forecasts and analytical information into useful financial judgment. AI governance maturity is expected to strengthen this process by providing appropriate oversight, accountability, validation, and control over the use of AI generated financial information. A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted with 385 respondents who possessed relevant knowledge of SME financial management, business analytics, AI applications, or organizational decision making. Data were collected using a five-point Likert scale questionnaire and analyzed with IBM SPSS version 26. Reliability analysis, exploratory factor analysis, and multiple linear regression were performed, while Hayes’ Process Macro Model 1 was used to test the moderating effect. The results show that generative AI enabled financial forecasting capability (β = 0.613) and business analytics capability (β = 0.487) both have significant positive effects on strategic financial decision quality. AI governance maturity also strengthens the relationship between generative AI enabled financial forecasting capability and strategic financial decision quality, with an interaction coefficient of 0.518. These findings suggest that emerging market SMEs gain greater value from generative AI when forecasting tools are supported by sound analytical capabilities and governance practices. Effective financial decision making therefore requires not only better technology, but also the organizational capacity to interpret, review, and responsibly use AI generated financial insights.

items.abstract_text: In a global information environment characterised by strong propaganda pressures and a lack of transparency, the demand for independent, high-quality sources is constantly growing. A significant gap is thus emerging between the growing complexity of information flows and users' ability to critically evaluate information. Currently, neither information professionals nor engaged citizens are able to accurately verify every single piece of news, nor do they have access to online platforms capable of selecting, verifying, and aggregating thematic content based on shared quality criteria. The lack of human and technical resources severely hinders the creation of information ecosystems resilient to disinformation. To address this challenge, recent efforts have focused on integrated platforms that combine human expertise with advanced automated analysis tools. Technologies such as machine learning, semantic analysis, and generative artificial intelligence offer innovative solutions for processing large volumes of data and supporting automated fact-checking. Nonetheless, the evolution of these technologies introduces new complexities, reshaping content production and distribution. Algorithms often amplify information polarisation. Traditional media increasingly align with partisan political and economic interests, losing credibility. As a result, citizens align themselves with different news sources in an attempt to reconstruct the truth within a fragmented digital landscape. By bringing together the analysis of manipulative strategies, the evolution of verification methods, hybrid human–AI workflows, and the requirements of explainability within a single survey, the article aims to offer researchers and practitioners a more integrated reference point for the design of effective and accountable verification systems.

items.abstract_text: This qualitative case study examined how ten secondary school ESL students in Malaysia used ChatGPT when revising their writing. The study did not focus on writing scores. Instead, it looked at students’ writing behaviours, the decisions they made when using ChatGPT, and the changes that appeared between their first and revised drafts. The students first wrote an essay on “Having a Balanced Diet” without using ChatGPT. After a short introduction to the tool, students revised the same essay with the help of ChatGPT. The interview data were analysed using thematic analysis, while the comparison between the first and the second drafts was conducted using document analysis. From the findings, it is clear that the students made use of ChatGPT to go through grammar, vocabulary, sentence structure, and content of their essays. Many improvements had been made in the revised drafts. Most of the students managed to fix grammar errors and use more suitable vocabulary, along with presenting new ideas in their work. Nonetheless, there are some flaws in the second drafts such as incorrect expressions, informal language and some incorrect ideas. The interviews also showed that the students did not accept the suggestions directly. The students chose those suggestions which were clear to them, appropriate to the task and related to their original meaning. Overall, the study shows that ChatGPT may be used to support ESL writing revision but students still need teacher guidance and their own judgement to use it critically and responsibly.

items.abstract_text: Chronic liver disease, particularly cirrhosis, produces a fragile, rebalanced hemostatic state. Patients may develop bleeding or thrombosis. The international normalized ratio and platelet count incompletely reflect concurrent procoagulant and anticoagulant changes and poorly predict procedural bleeding. Viscoelastic testing and thrombin-generation assays assess hemostasis more broadly. Randomized trials support viscoelastic testing-guided reductions in blood product use, but these trials do not establish prediction of later bleeding or thrombosis. Machine-learning models address gastrointestinal bleeding outcomes, variceal hemorrhage, portal vein thrombosis (PVT), and transfusion requirements using clinical records, imaging, or elastography. Most cirrhosis models address one outcome, omit direct hemostatic measurements, and have limited external validation. Within the English-language eligibility criteria and focused queries of a PubMed update on July 29, 2026, no adult model jointly estimating future bleeding and PVT in cirrhosis was identified. This structured narrative minireview evaluates the evidence for both outcomes and specifies research requirements for paired-risk models and a possible digital twin of the coagulation-portal axis. Treatment-specific predictions would require additional causal validation.

items.abstract_text: Conversational artificial intelligence now belongs to ordinary adolescent life, but the psychological research that should guide its design spreads over fields which seldom cite each other. Research on adolescent development, on misinformation susceptibility, on trust in automation, on chatbot-supported learning and on companion-chatbot overreliance has grown up separately, and each of these areas answers only part of the question of how a general-purpose chatbot should talk to a teenager. This paper brings together twenty-one sources from developmental psychology, human factors, human-computer interaction and educational technology, in order to show what is now known about adolescent chatbot interaction and what this means for conversational design. Three results appear repeatedly in this research. First, adolescence is a design context of its own, not a smaller version of adulthood, since reward sensitivity, social influence and emotional regulation are still developing, while exposure to persuasive conversational systems has already reached almost everyone. Second, trust in a chatbot changes behavior in ways that can be measured; thus, the proper design target is calibrated trust rather than maximal trust. Third, the failure modes that matter most for adolescent users, that is, hallucination, sycophancy and unwarranted confidence, originate in the model; the user is not their source. From these results this paper consolidates ten conversational design principles into four clusters, namely epistemic calibration, metacognitive scaffolding, bounded emotional support and autonomy preservation. The framework here is a conceptual synthesis and puts forward testable predictions, but it has not been empirically validated.

items.venue: Lecture Notes in Education Psychology and Public Media

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: As large language models (LLMs) increasingly generate human-like text, it is becoming an increasingly pressing empirical and societal question: how can AI-generated text be distinguished from human-written text? Through two studies, this paper explored whether and how people judge AI authorship. In Study 1, participants (n = 101) judged the written responses to an inside joke prompt (the prompt chosen based on LLMs' response) and assessed each response on a 7-point scale of −3, definitely AI-written, to +3, definitely human-written, followed by self-reports of justifications. People's classifications were near chance accuracy (51.1%), but their continuous ratings did separate the human-written from the AI-written responses. Multivariate logistic regression showed that accuracy was best predicted by attention to surface-level errors and structural features rather than by deeper experiential cues (for example, interpretations of humor and personal schema matches). In Study 2, a new sample (n = 100) evaluated AI responses deliberately modified with spelling and grammatical errors. Accuracy dropped steeply in participants below chance (39.2%), validating the conclusion of Study 1. Together, the results of these two studies reveal that people's capacity to detect human expression rests less on detecting genuine lived experience than on superficial linguistic cues that are easy to manipulate.

items.title: Retrospective analysis of nursing interventions using artificial intelligence multimodal emotion recognition for perioperative depression in head and neck tumors

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: BACKGROUND Perioperative depression is prevalent among head and neck tumor patients, while traditional emotional assessment methods lag and fail to meet clinical nursing needs. AIM To investigate artificial intelligence (AI) multimodal emotion recognition's effects on enhancing individualized nursing care for depression patients during perioperative head and neck tumor surgeries, focusing on emotional fluctuations, nursing response efficiency, and postoperative recovery outcomes. METHODS Sixty patients with perioperative depression associated with head and neck tumors admitted to our hospital between January 2023 and December 2025 were selected and divided into two groups: The conventional care group (27 patients.) and the AI individualized care group (33 patients). We compared the baseline data, perioperative emotional indicators, postoperative outcomes, emotional recognition, and nursing responses between the two groups while simultaneously evaluating the recognition performance of the multimodal model. RESULTS There were no significant baseline differences between the groups. During observation, the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAMD) score, emotional score, Emotional Mood Index (EMI), and proportion of positive emotions showed dynamic changes with significant group-time interaction. The AI-individualized care group demonstrated lower HAMD and EMI scores, higher comprehensive emotional scores, and a greater proportion of positive emotions, postoperatively. Additionally, hospital stay length was reduced, complications decreased, and Physical Component Summary, Mental Component Summary, and Emotional Recovery Score improved significantly. The AI group outperformed the conventional nursing group in recognizing negative emotions, intervention matching, and emotional improvement within 24 hours. The time for initial recognition and nursing responses was much shorter. The area under the curve, sensitivity, and specificity of the multimodal fusion model were 0.894, 86.364%, and 83.871%, respectively, indicating its superiority over the single-modal model. CONCLUSION AI-informed individualized nursing can facilitate earlier identification of abnormal emotions in patients with head and neck tumors perioperatively, enhance nursing efficiency, and positively influence perioperative emotions and recovery.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: BACKGROUND High rates of psychological distress among university students, together with persistently low use of professional mental health services, have become a notable public health issue. AIM To examine how help-seeking attitudes, stigma and individual psychological characteristics jointly shape university students’ preferences for different counseling formats. METHODS A cross-sectional survey was conducted which included 313 university students. Latent profile analysis was applied to identify distinct subgroups based on help-seeking attitudes and perceived stigma. Differences in psychological symptoms and preferences for artificial intelligence (AI) counseling were then compared across these subgroups. RESULTS The following three subgroups were identified: “Low willingness-high stigma” (36.4%), “moderate willingness-moderate stigma” (43.8%), and “high willingness-low stigma” (19.8%). Interestingly, the “low willingness-high stigma” group showed the most severe depression and anxiety symptoms, and reported the highest prior use of AI-based support and the strongest preference for AI counseling. CONCLUSION AI and human counselors play complementary roles: AI offers advantages in accessibility and anonymity, while human counselors remain irreplaceable in terms of empathy, complex problem-solving, and long-term therapeutic relationships.

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming traditional productivity and task management systems by enabling intelligent assistance for task planning, prioritization, scheduling, collaboration, and decision-making. This paper presents a survey of AI-driven personal and collaborative productivity systems, focusing on intelligent task management, scheduling, meeting management, large language models (LLMs), AI agents, multi-agent systems, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Existing research is reviewed and classified according to the AI techniques employed, application areas, system capabilities, and limitations. The survey examines how these technologies support individual productivity as well as collaborative workflows involving tasks, calendars, meetings, communication, and shared knowledge. A comparative analysis is presented to identify the strengths and limitations of existing approaches. The study further highlights key research gaps, including fragmented productivity tools, limited contextual awareness and personalization, challenges in autonomous task execution and multi-agent coordination, and concerns related to privacy, security, reliability, and human oversight. Finally, emerging trends and future research directions are discussed toward developing more integrated, adaptive, trustworthy, and context-aware AI-driven productivity systems. This survey provides a structured understanding of the current research landscape and identifies opportunities for advancing intelligent productivity and task management systems. Keywords— Artificial Intelligence, Productivity Management, Task Management, Intelligent Scheduling, Large Language Models, AI Agents, Multi-Agent Systems, Human-AI Collaboration, Retrieval-Augmented Generation.

items.venue: International Scientific Journal of Engineering and Management
items.abstract_text: The increasing use of automation and advanced machinery in modern industries has made equipment reliability and operational efficiency important factors in industrial production. Unexpected machine failures can interrupt production activities, increase maintenance expenses, and affect overall productivity. Traditional maintenance approaches, such as reactive and preventive maintenance, are often unable to identify early signs of equipment failure or accurately determine when maintenance is actually required. To overcome these limitations, this paper explores the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Digital Twin technology for predictive maintenance in industrial environments. A Digital Twin is a virtual representation of a physical machine or industrial system that is continuously updated using data collected from sensors installed on the actual equipment. By combining this technology with Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning algorithms, it becomes possible to monitor equipment conditions, analyse operational patterns, detect abnormal behaviour, and predict potential failures before they cause major interruptions. The proposed approach integrates Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, real-time data acquisition, data preprocessing, virtual equipment modelling, and AI-based predictive analysis into a unified maintenance framework. Machine learning techniques such as Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks can be applied for fault detection, condition monitoring, and Remaining Useful Life (RUL) estimation. This paper presents a case-study-based investigation of AI-enabled Digital Twins for industrial equipment monitoring, with particular emphasis on understanding how real-time data and predictive analytics can improve maintenance planning. It also examines the system architecture, working methodology, potential advantages, implementation challenges, and limitations of the proposed approach. The study highlights the potential of integrating AI with Digital Twin technology to transform conventional maintenance practices into more intelligent, data-driven, and condition-based systems, thereby supporting improved equipment reliability, reduced unplanned downtime, and more efficient industrial operations. Keywords— Artificial Intelligence, Digital Twin, Predictive Maintenance, Machine Learning, Internet of Things (IoT), Industry 4.0, Fault Detection, Condition Monitoring, Remaining Useful Life (RUL).

items.abstract_text: In this paper, the authors argue that Uganda’s efforts to integrate Artificial Intelligence (AI) in key development sectors such as agriculture, climate services, health, and digital governance are bedeviled by the lack of a human-centred AI path that supports resilience, livelihoods, and inclusive development. Although the national government agencies, universities, innovation hubs, and non-profit technology organisations have all contributed to an emerging national AI ecosystem characterised by experimentation, partnerships, and gradual institutionalisation to address the challenges of climate change and youth underemployment in Uganda, this paper interrogates the question of how the lack of a relevant policy framework is affecting the coordination of implementation efforts and the overall effect of such initiatives. Drawing on a narrative, problem-driven literature review process, we focus on the effect of the policy lacuna on the adoption of AI technology in sectoral applications, climate-smart agriculture, predictive analytics for health and environmental management, youth-centred skills and entrepreneurship, and Natural Language Processing (NLP) for local languages. We recommend the institutionalisation of responsible AI use by enacting a foundational governance framework that defines how AI technologies are ethically, securely, and legally developed and utilised. The government, we further recommend, should treat NLP databases and models as digital public goods to create pathways to integrate apprenticeships for youth experiencing underemployment.

items.title: Cross-Modal Attention Fusion for Clinical Risk Prediction: Integrating EHR Data with Dual-Attribution Explain ability

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MEDICAL EVALUATION AND PHYSICAL REPORT
items.abstract_text: Abstract Clinical prediction models have historically relied on structured electronic health record data, leaving the rich prognostic signal embedded in free-text clinical documentation systematically underutilized. The proposed Clinical Multimodal Adaptive Clinical Prediction (CMACP) architecture — a dual-pathway prediction system integrating structured EHR features through gradient-boosted tree processing with unstructured clinical note embeddings through Clinical BERT encoding, unified by a cross-modal attention mechanism that weighs each modality's contribution by predictive confidence. The architecture is designed for geriatric acute care settings where clinical notes capture disease severity, symptom trajectory, and functional context unavailable from structured data alone. A federated fine-tuning protocol enables privacypreserving multi-institutional model development across health systems with different EHR platforms and patient populations. An attribution framework combining SHAP-based structured feature importance with Integrated Gradients note concept attribution provides role-differentiated clinical explanations, with a concordance quality badge signalling modality alignment. A governance framework specifies deployment standards, post-market performance monitoring, and equity evaluation protocols calibrated to multi-site clinical NLP systems. The CMACP framework addresses the technical and governance requirements for safe deployment of multimodal clinical AI in settings where older adult patients are most vulnerable to prediction errors. External validation across multiple health system types, equity stratification by race and documentation quality environment, and prospective evaluation of attribution quality are identified as priority research requirements.

items.venue: Interdisciplinary Journal of Research and Development

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly integrated into modern justice systems, influencing decision-making in criminal justice, hiring, surveillance, healthcare, and public administration. Although AI promises efficiency and consistency, a growing body of research documents risks of algorithmic bias and unequal performance across demographic groups. This paper examines the relationship between artificial intelligence, gender bias, and human rights within contemporary justice systems through a qualitative, interdisciplinary analysis combining a narrative review of scholarly literature with doctrinal analysis of relevant international and European legal and ethical frameworks. It considers how biased datasets, discriminatory or uneven algorithmic outcomes, and unequal technological representation may affect fairness, equality, privacy, due process, and access to justice. Particular attention is given to documented evidence on facial-analysis systems and automated recruitment, while broader claims concerning institutional legitimacy and human-centered justice are treated as normative implications rather than empirical findings. The paper also evaluates regulatory responses, including Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (the EU Artificial Intelligence Act) and UNESCO’s Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence. It concludes by identifying transparency, accountability, representative data, independent evaluation, and meaningful human oversight as central safeguards for rights-respecting AI governance. items.title: Generative AI adoption in organizations: A conceptual model of job crafting, employee productivity, creativity and work engagement

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: International Journal of Business and Management (IJBM)
items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly reshaping organizational work, yet its behavioural consequences for employees remain unevenly understood. Existing research on productivity, creativity and engagement is fragmented and rarely examined within a single theoretical framework. Drawing on Job Demands Resources theory, Conservation of Resources theory and Self Determination Theory, this conceptual paper develops an integrative model of how organizational GenAI adoption affects employee productivity, creativity and work engagement. Job crafting is proposed as the central behavioural mechanism. The model treats GenAI as both a job resource and a job demand. It therefore recognizes a double edged pathway in which technology insecurity and passive over reliance can offset the benefits of adoption. AI literacy, ethical use clarity and organizational readiness are identified as boundary conditions that determine which pathway prevails. Four hypotheses are developed, covering the mediating role of job crafting for productivity and engagement, its moderating role for creativity, and the conditioning effect of AI literacy and ethical guidance. A time lagged, multi source survey design, supplemented by supervisor ratings and an optional field experiment, is proposed for future empirical testing. The paper offers a resource based account of human and AI collaboration. It also provides managerial guidance for organizations that want GenAI adoption to deliver sustainable gains in performance and well being rather than short lived efficiency gains that erode over time.

items.abstract_text: Aim: This study examines persistent memory architectures for large language models (LLMs) and AI agents, develops a functional taxonomy of memory systems, evaluates emerging approaches to context-management limitations, and assesses how cloud-native services can support agent memory implementation. Methods: The study synthesizes literature on persistent agent memory, attention-efficient architectures, in-context learning, and inference-time adaptation. The study uses a thematic framework to compare the mechanisms, computational implications, and implementation requirements of different memory approaches. The study also presents a case study of Google Cloud’s memory ecosystem, examining Memorystore, AlloyDB with pgvector, Vertex AI Vector Search, and the conceptual Agent Engine. Results: The synthesis indicates that efficient attention mechanisms, inference-time adaptation, and persistent external memory address different aspects of the agent-memory problem and should not be treated as interchangeable solutions. The Google Cloud case study illustrates how cloud-native services can provide complementary capabilities for implementing persistent agent memory. Conclusion: The study concludes that effective agent memory requires a coordinated approach to memory representation, retrieval, updating, consolidation, and evaluation. Increasing context-window capacity alone does not adequately address the architectural limitations associated with persistent memory in LLM-based agents. Recommendation: The study recommends developing reproducible benchmarks and cost-aware evaluation frameworks to compare memory architectures under realistic agent workloads.

However, excessive dependency on AI raises concerns of technostress, fatigue, and anxiety among students that can negatively impact relationships with learning. Additionally, decreases in peer connection have led to a lack of social learning. However, upon conducting a digital study at Davis Senior High, the 101 sophomores surveyed routinely scored higher on trust for peers over their trust for AI on three of four metrics of trust: personalization, intent, and objectivity. Given the geographical cluster sample, more research is needed to expand on the differences in trust between AI and peers.

items.abstract_text: This study aimed to determine the influence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools on learners’ critical thinking and academic performance as a basis for developing an AI-Driven Instructional Toolkit for San Carlos Elementary School, Caba, La Union. Specifically, it examined learners’ awareness and experiences in using AI tools, their level of critical thinking, academic performance in Mathematics, Science, and English, and the relationship among these variables. The study employed a quantitative research design involving twenty-six (26) learner-respondents who answered a validated and reliable survey questionnaire. The findings revealed that learners had a high level of awareness of AI tools, including ChatGPT, Grammarly, QuillBot, and Jenni AI, while their learning and collaborative experiences were very high. Their overall level of critical thinking was high, with a median of 4.17, particularly in reasoning, problem-solving, and collaborative skills. Likewise, their academic performance in Mathematics, Science, and English was very high, with grades ranging from 91 to 95. Statistical analysis further revealed a significant but weak positive correlation between awareness of AI tools and critical thinking (r = .300), as well as a significant positive correlation with academic performance in Mathematics (r = .343). These findings suggest that AI tools can support learners’ critical thinking and academic performance when integrated meaningfully and responsibly into instruction. The developed AI-Driven Instructional Toolkit obtained a very high level of validity, indicating its suitability for instructional use. The study recommends the guided integration of AI tools to promote responsible technology use, independent thinking, collaborative learning, and improved academic outcomes.

items.abstract_text: This study examined the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot use as a learning aid and the perceived learning comprehension of first-year to third-year Bachelor of Secondary Education (BSED) Science students at Central Bicol State University of Agriculture–Pasacao Campus during Academic Year 2025–2026. It assessed AI chatbot use (concept explanation, problem-solving support, and review and reinforcement), perceived learning comprehension (understanding, retention, and application of scientific concepts), and their statistical relationship to inform instructional recommendations. Using a quantitative descriptive-correlational design with open-ended qualitative inquiry, data were gathered from 158 students selected via proportionate stratified random sampling from 260 students (N=260) through a validated 30-item Likert questionnaire on Google Forms (Cronbach’s α=.951). Data were analyzed using weighted mean, ranking, Pearson’s r, t-test, coefficient of determination (r^2), and semantic thematic analysis. Overall AI chatbot use was High (M=4.04), led by concept explanation (M=4.22, Very High), problem-solving support (M=4.04, High), and review and reinforcement (M=3.85, High). Perceived learning comprehension was also High (M=3.83) across understanding (M=3.84), application (M=3.83), and retention (M=3.82). Correlation analysis revealed a significant, moderate positive relationship between AI chatbot use and perceived learning comprehension, r(156)=.470, t=6.651, p<.001, r^2=.221, explaining 22.1% of comprehension variance. Thematic analysis corroborated these findings while highlighting output accuracy and overdependence concerns, concluding that AI chatbots serve as effective scaffolds when paired with source verification, independent reasoning, and faculty guidance.

items.abstract_text: This research seeks to analyze the connection between perceived AI menace, fear of unemployment, and mental well-being of employees through a quantitative correlational approach. The emergence of artificial intelligence in the working environment raises worries in regard to job security and the threat of unemployment. Thus, there may be a rise in employment worries and a decrease in employees' mental well-being. The methodology to collect data on employees levels of perceived AI menace, fear of unemployment, and mental well-being is based on surveying them using conventional self-reported questionnaires. Descriptive statistics will be used to analyze the levels of these factors in terms of their means (M) and standard deviations (SD). The reliability analysis is going to be done for checking internal reliability of a research tool using Cronbach's alpha. To measure the relationships between these three variables, a Pearson product-moment correlation will be used. Additionally, a simple linear regression will be run in order to see if perceived threat from AI can predict unemployment anxiety and psychological well-being and if unemployment anxiety can predict psychological well-being. The measurement of psychological well-being is going to be based on the six dimensions introduced by Ryff: autonomy, environmental mastery, personal growth, positive relations with others, purpose in life, and self-acceptance. The results of this study will allow understanding how the way employees view AI being a threat to their jobs relates to worries about unemployment and psychological well-being. All in all, the results of this research can be helpful for realizing the significance of recognizing employees’ concerns in the course of technological changes and encourage businesses to provide adequate support to employees for mitigating job-related uncertainty and reaching psychological well-being.

items.abstract_text: Purpose: This review synthesizes evidence from recent studies of human–AI collaboration in service and digital ecosystems to build and test a multi-level conceptual framework. Design/methodology/approach: Thirteen studies (Tier A) from 2024 to 2026 were analyzed in full text and compared with 25 qualitative and mixed-methods studies (Tier B). In total, 38 service and digital ecosystem studies were analyzed within this review. Service-Dominant (S-D) Logic and the Affect–Behavior–Cognition (ABC) model was used as the underlying theoretical framework. Narrative and thematic analysis were employed to synthesize the results from the included studies. Findings: Transparency, process control and outcome control have significant effects on employees in terms of cognitive and behavioral effects, while system-initiated engagement has little effect. Human–AI interaction does not, on average, perform better than the best human in each task (g = ?0.23, p < .001), but does perform better than a single human in a variety of tasks (g = 0.64). Value is created through the integration of systems and not through technology itself. User experience, digital maturity, interoperable IT, and AI-induced technostress condition value realization. Originality/value: The study provides a three-stage framework, seven testable hypotheses, seven gaps in current research and an operational measurement for value creation at the employee level and for firm- and network-level value co-creation.

items.abstract_text: The rapid emergence of autonomous artificial intelligence agents, predictive supply chain orchestration, and real-time cross-border regulatory analytics is fundamentally transforming how multinational enterprises (MNEs) govern global value chains (GVCs) and enter foreign markets. Yet International Business (IB) higher education remains largely tethered to twentieth-century pedagogical paradigms—relying on static international trade models, retrospective written case studies, and essentialist cultural heuristics that fail to prepare graduates for algorithmically mediated global commerce. Moving beyond surface-level classroom adoption of generative chatbots, this study develops a comprehensive theoretical and operational framework for re-engineering International Business education through the lenses of Global Value Chain Governance Theory, Activity Theory, and Metacognitive Scaffolding. We argue that the defining competency for next-generation IB professionals is Algorithmic Value-Chain Orchestration—the ability to align predictive and generative AI systems with cross-jurisdictional institutional realities, geopolitical risks, and culturally grounded human judgment. To operationalize this capability, the paper introduces a Three-Horizon Curricular Transformation Architecture alongside a Synthetic Global Commerce Laboratory that immerses students in dynamic multi-tier supply chain disruptions, automated customs and rules-of-origin auditing, and cross-cultural digital platform governance. Drawing upon longitudinal pedagogical implementations across undergraduate and postgraduate IB cohorts, we demonstrate significant gains in students' systemic risk reasoning, critical verification of algorithmic outputs, and cross-border strategic adaptability. Finally, the study examines structural challenges—including cognitive atrophy, Western-centric training data biases, and cross-border data compliance—and establishes an institutional governance charter for sustainable business school transformation.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Digital Marketing Strategies for Enhancing Sales Conversion in E-Commerce: An Empirical and Analytical Investigation

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: The rapid expansion of global e-commerce has intensified competition for consumer attention, rendering traditional demographic-segmented and rule-based marketing increasingly ineffective. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative paradigm in digital marketing, enabling firms to process high-velocity behavioral datasets and deliver hyper-personalized customer journeys in real time. While industry adoption of AI marketing tools is widespread, a substantial maturity gap persists between experimental deployment and fully scaled conversion optimization. This paper integrates a multi-stage analytical research design—combining psychometric Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) of consumer survey data ($N = 420$), econometric before-and-after funnel cohort modeling across retail deployments, and regression-based moderation analysis—to quantify how AI-enabled digital marketing drives sales conversion. Specifically, the study examines four core strategic pillars: neural recommendation engines, predictive programmatic acquisition, dynamic pricing optimization, and generative conversational AI. Analytical results demonstrate that Perceived Personalization significantly enhances Customer Experience Quality ($\beta = 0.499, p < 0.001$) and Digital Marketing Effectiveness ($\beta = 0.488, p < 0.001$), which jointly mediate downstream Purchase Intention and actual checkout conversion ($R^2 = 0.412$). Econometric cohort tracking further reveals a 23.4% to 31.0% relative lift in session-to-purchase conversion rates, a 27% reduction in bounce rates, and up to a 50% increase in Average Order Value (AOV) via real-time affinity bundling. However, moderation analysis confirms that perceived algorithmic opacity and privacy intrusion negatively attenuate conversion gains ($\beta = -0.214, p < 0.01$). The study concludes with an actionable governance and MLOps framework for balancing algorithmic conversion efficiency with consumer trust.

items.title: Large language model generation of plausible semantic distractors for data science Parsons problems

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Parsons problems have been widely recognised to support novice learners by reducing the cognitive demands of writing code from scratch through rearrangement of provided code blocks. A common variation includes distractors – erroneous blocks of code which do not belong to the correct solution. While Parsons problems have been widely studied for introductory programming, they remain underexplored in various domains including in data science education, where students may possess statistical knowledge but limited programming experience. Developing distractors is also time-consuming for educators. This study investigated the feasibility of using a large language model (LLM) to generate semantic distractors for data science Parsons problems. A set of distractors was generated for 315 Python-based data science Parsons problems and was evaluated for pedagogical plausibility, compilability, and output divergence. Validated distractors were then incorporated as exemplars in a refined prompt to generate a second set of distractors, which were evaluated using the same criteria. The findings demonstrate that LLMs can be used to develop semantic distractors for data science Parsons problems and refining the prompts using validated exemplars further improved the quality. This study contributes to the limited literature on data science Parsons problems, distractor design and LLM-supported development of these problems.

items.abstract_text: Generative AI is increasingly used in learning environments, yet sustained interaction does not necessarily indicate cognitively engaged learning. This exploratory study examined how conversation openings related to cognitive engagement levels and the support orientations reflected in student messages during student-AI interactions. Cognitive engagement was classified by an adapted ICAP framework, openings were organised into a descriptive typology, and semantic thematic analysis was conducted on student messages. Openings oriented towards strategy guidance, conceptual explanation, error understanding, and resource review feedback were more often associated with moderate or deep engagement, whereas resource-evaluation openings were often associated with longer interactions despite limited cognitive depth. Semantic patterns revealed overlapping orientations towards questioning, improvement, examples, feedback, and concepts, spanning clarification, answer checking, revision, application, and task-focused support. These findings distinguish interaction persistence from cognitive engagement and suggest that conversation design should support students to articulate their reasoning and co-construct knowledge with AI, rather than prioritising continued interaction alone.

items.abstract_text: In spite of the fact that there is widespread agreement regarding the ethical principles that need to guide artificial intelligence, there is still a significant gap between these normative objectives and the operational realities of technical implementation. An investigation into how to operationalize a proactive, iterative AI governance paradigm is the focus of this study. The investigation is conducted via the prism of private law liabilities and constant technical verification. Both corporate compliance theater and opportunistic ethics shopping are the driving forces behind our inquiry. Both of these shortcomings in practice have occurred repeatedly. During the course of the study, a multi-layered methodological framework is utilized. This framework triangulates a comparative assessment of growing international regulatory frameworks and a "cross-sectoral typological mapping of auditing procedures from banking, data privacy, and environmental law." The findings reveal a systemic disconnect: corporate ethical commitments continue to be largely detached from operational audit systems, leaving data scientists frustrated by guidelines that are too abstract to act on. Furthermore, existing environmental, social, and governance standards do not provide any AI-specific tools for quantifying the hidden socio-technical harms that are embedded in global supply chains. rules that are abstract, whereas the existing ESG standards do not provide the AI-specific guidance that is required to assess the hidden socio-technical damages that are present throughout global supply chains.The purpose of this article is to offer a solution to this problem by advocating for the transition from voluntary soft law to an enforceable, longitudinal regulatory framework. We propose that corporate governance frameworks be merged with automated auditing pipelines, value-based engineering (also known as ethics-by-design), and independent third-party oversight. This would result in the transformation of abstract ethical concepts into private law duties that can be verified.

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is rapidly entering higher education, yet its implications for learner autonomy remain unsettled, particularly in resource-constrained contexts. This explanatory sequential mixed-methods study examined how pedagogical GAI use relates to self-regulated learning, cognitive engagement, augmented cognitive autonomy (ACA), and deep learning in six Cameroonian higher education institutions. Quantitative data from 812 students and faculty members were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling, followed by 24 semi-structured interviews. GAI use was positively associated with self-regulation, while self-regulation and cognitive engagement sequentially mediated its relationship with ACA. ACA was strongly associated with deep learning. AI literacy and institutional governance strengthened the relationship between GAI use and ACA. Qualitative findings revealed both reflective, dialogic uses and cognitive delegation. The findings support an emerging Augmented Cognitive Autonomy framework in which GAI amplifies learning conditionally, depending on users' regulatory capacities and institutional support, with implications for equity and human capability development.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Financial Crime Detection: Economic Efficiency, Accountability, and Legal Responsibility
items.venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence Machine Learning and Data Analytics

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being applied to financial crime detection, offering potential efficiency gains over traditional rule-based systems while raising important questions concerning algorithmic accountability and criminal liability. This review examines 25 scholarly and institutional sources across law, criminology, computer science, and regulatory policy. It focuses on three areas: (1) the economic efficiency of AI in anti-money laundering (AML) and fraud detection; (2) criminal liability issues associated with false negatives, algorithmic opacity, and the due diligence responsibilities of system deployers; and (3) governance challenges relating to explainability, human oversight, and cross-jurisdictional regulatory harmonization. The review indicates that machine learning approaches offer potential advantages in identifying complex financial crime patterns and reducing false-positive alerts. However, the available evidence on overall cost-effectiveness and measurable crime reduction remains limited. False negatives represent a particularly significant challenge because undetected suspicious transactions may create regulatory, reputational, and legal risks. The analysis further highlights fragmented liability frameworks and the importance of due diligence in determining responsibility for AI-related failures. The review concludes that effective AI-based financial crime detection requires a human-machine collaborative governance approach supported by explainability, systematic false-negative monitoring, appropriate human oversight, and stronger international regulatory coordination.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: International Journal of Sports Science and Human Performance
items.abstract_text: Background: Children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) show frequent motor difficulties, lower physical activity (PA) and fewer opportunities for sport participation than their peers. Individualized programs are therefore needed. Artificial intelligence (AI), wearable sensors and the Internet of Things (IoT) could support such personalization, but the evidence base has not been examined from a sport-science perspective. Objective: To synthesize evidence on PA interventions and AI- and IoT-enabled technologies relevant to children with ASD and to propose a framework for personalized, AI-supported sport and PA programs. Methods: A narrative review, guided by the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA), combined a previously completed thematic synthesis of 49 studies of AI- and IoT-enabled assistive systems for children with disabilities (16 ASD-related) with targeted searches of PubMed/MEDLINE and publisher databases up to November 2026. Results: Meta-analyses indicate moderate benefits of PA interventions for motor skills, skill-related fitness and social functioning (e.g., Hedges' g = 0.62), although study quality is generally low. ASD-focused AI research mainly addresses gesture recognition, emotion analysis and socially assistive robotics in small samples (about 10–24 children), and none has tested fitness outcomes. The proposed artificial intelligence of things (AIoT)-CARE framework (Capability, Applicability, Robustness, and Ethics and Safety) links five stages: co-designed profiling, an accessible activity catalog, consent-based sensing, explainable recommendations with human override, and family-involved review. Conclusion: AI-supported personalization is a promising design direction, not a proven intervention. Phased evaluation using participant-level validation, real-world testing and AI-specific reporting guidelines is required.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Background: Children with disabilities are less physically active than their peers and face personal, social and environmental barriers to sport. Their needs differ across and within diagnostic groups, so uniform activity programs often fit poorly. Artificial intelligence (AI) and the Internet of Things (IoT) could support individualized activity recommendations, but their readiness for this purpose is uncertain. Objective: To synthesize evidence on physical activity (PA) and AI- and IoT-enabled technologies across disability groups and to propose a cross-disability framework for personalized sports recommendation. Methods: This narrative review combined a previously completed thematic synthesis of 49 studies (2015–2025) with a targeted PubMed/MEDLINE search (January 2000 to November 2026) using predefined terms and inclusion criteria, plus checks of IEEE Xplore and publisher records. Results: PA interventions show small-to-moderate benefits that vary by disability and outcome; for example, aerobic exercise improved attention in attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD; standardized mean difference = 0.84), whereas exercise trials in cerebral palsy were at high risk of bias. Technologies follow disability-specific patterns: gesture sensing in autism, activity monitoring in ADHD, gait sensing in cerebral palsy, seizure-detection wearables in epilepsy and sign-language recognition in hearing impairment. Small samples, laboratory validation and weak privacy reporting are common. The proposed framework links six modules: individual profiling, a structured activity catalog, hard safety filtering, transparent ranking, feedback and human governance. Conclusion: AI-supported recommendation may help organize accessible choices, but no health benefit has yet been shown. Staged evaluation is required.

items.title: AI Marketing Transparency and Brand Trust: How AI Literacy and Perceived Manipulative Intent Shape Consumer Responses in Pakistan

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: With AI’s increasing role in digital marketing, a brand’s transparency about its use of AI could act as an informational signal of accountability. However, the interpretation consumers make of such transparency might vary with their knowledge of AI and their perception of persuasive intent. This study examines the relationship between perceived AI marketing transparency, brand trust, and purchase intention and the role of perceived manipulative intent as a mechanism and AI literacy as a boundary condition. We surveyed 387 matched Pakistani consumers, in two waves. AI literacy was operationalised with the core 18-item AI literacy dimensions of the MAILS instrument (use and apply AI, know and understand AI, detect AI, and AI ethics), whereas the remaining MAILS dimensions were treated as separate constructs. We tested the hypotheses using regression-based simple mediation (PROCESS Model 4) and first-stage moderated mediation (PROCESS Model 7). Perceived AI marketing transparency was positively associated with brand trust (β = 0.24, p < 0.001). Brand trust carried a significant indirect association between perceived AI marketing transparency and purchase intention (indirect effect = 0.06, 95% CI [0.02, 0.11]); the direct association was not statistically significant (c′ = 0.10, p = 0.081). Perceived manipulative intent was negatively associated with brand trust (b = −0.25, p < 0.001). AI literacy positively moderated the association between perceived AI marketing transparency and perceived manipulative intent (B = 0.13, p = 0.031), such that this association was positive and significant only at high AI literacy (B = 0.25, p < 0.001). The conditional indirect association was statistically distinguishable from zero only at high AI literacy (effect = −0.06, 95% CI [−0.13, −0.01]). The index of moderated mediation was statistically significant at the 5% level (index = −0.03, 95% CI [−0.07, −0.001]) but the CI was close to the null value. The results are consistent with both theoretically opposite mechanisms suggested: an accountability-related association between perceived transparency and brand trust, and a conditional suspicion-related indirect association via perceived manipulative intent, which were analysed under the umbrella of two different empirical models. The interaction was small and the moderated-mediation evidence was statistically weak and should be considered a preliminary rather than a general finding of the negative effects on transparency. One of the contributions of the study is distinguishing perceived transparency from its interpretation, and examining core AI literacy competencies in addition to a focused measure of persuasion knowledge activation in the context of AI marketing and signaling research. Finally, practical implications highlight the importance of AI disclosure being credible and context-specific, not necessarily a strategy that builds trust.

items.title: Does Generative AI Reduce Mental Effort at The Expense of Deep Thinking? An Experimental Investigation of Cognitive Load and Knowledge Retention
items.venue: Kashmir Journal of Academic Research and Development

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: The rapid integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into higher education has transformed learning practices, raising critical concerns regarding its influence on cognitive engagement, analytical reasoning, and knowledge retention. This study experimentally examines whether GenAI-assisted learning reduces cognitive load at the expense of deep thinking and sustained knowledge acquisition. A randomized controlled experimental design was employed involving 120 undergraduate students, randomly assigned to an experimental group utilizing ChatGPT (n = 60) and a control group completing equivalent learning activities without AI assistance (n = 60). Participants undertook analytical reading, conceptual problem-solving, and critical reasoning tasks under standardized experimental conditions. Cognitive load was measured using a mental effort rating scale, deep thinking was assessed through rubric-based analytical reasoning evaluations, and knowledge retention was examined using immediate and delayed post-tests administered two weeks apart. Results revealed significantly lower perceived cognitive load among AI-assisted learners (M = 3.42, SD = 1.11) compared with the control group (M = 5.76, SD = 1.24), t(118) = 10.88, p < .001. Conversely, students learning without AI demonstrated superior deep-thinking performance (M = 78.40, SD = 9.65) relative to AI-assisted participants (M = 70.25, SD = 10.82), p < .001. Immediate knowledge retention scores showed comparatively modest differences between the experimental and control groups (82.30% versus 80.10%, respectively). However, delayed retention assessments revealed a substantial performance advantage for the control group (74.60%) over AI-assisted learners (65.20%), indicating greater knowledge deterioration following AI-supported learning. These findings suggest that although GenAI effectively reduces perceived mental effort during academic tasks, such efficiency gains may coincide with diminished analytical engagement and weaker long-term knowledge retention. The study extends cognitive load theory and cognitive offloading perspectives by identifying a potential trade-off between immediate learning efficiency and sustained cognitive development. The findings underscore the importance of pedagogically structured GenAI integration that encourages independent reasoning, active knowledge construction, and meaningful cognitive engagement rather than passive dependence on AI-generated responses. Implications for instructional design, assessment practices, and responsible AI adoption in higher education are discussed.

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract Generative AI systems promise cognitive extensions by enhancing information access and use. However, from the bounded rationality perspective, their utility is fundamentally constrained by inherent human cognitive limitations. This article argues that when the volume of AI-generated information exceeds users’ processing capacity governed by working memory constraints, attentional resources, and verification capabilities, it produces cognitive disutility rather than enhancement. We introduced a formal model to quantify this interaction, demonstrating that net cognitive benefits decline systematically as information overload increases beyond individual processing thresholds. The analysis reveals that successful cognitive extension depends not on maximizing informational output but on strategically aligning AI design with human cognitive ergonomics and individual differences in processing capacity. Ultimately, truly augmentative systems must minimize cognitive overhead to prevent overload, while preserving users' epistemic agency and decision-making autonomy.

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract Sustained cognitive engagement, short and mistimed sleep, chronic stress and reduced recovery co-occur in AI-intensive environments, yet how this profile acts on brain energy metabolism is unknown. We built a neuron–astrocyte genome-scale model of human grey matter from Human-GEM v2.1.1, contextualised each cell with human single-nucleus expression, made transport, sodium-pumping and glutathione-recycling costs explicit, and calibrated one parameter to measured cerebral glucose use. Without further fitting the model reproduced the astrocytic share of oxidative metabolism measured by ¹³C spectroscopy (15.7% vs 14%), both the oxidative and the glycolytic regimes of human brain activation, and an independent reconstruction; deletion of genes causing inherited brain-energy disorders compromised its energetic margin far more often than deletion of other genes (odds ratio 79, p = 6 × 10⁻²⁰). Translating the five stressors into constraints, sleep loss and cognitive load each exhausted the margin within the protocol range, at a 25% loss of mitochondrial capacity and a 39% rise in signalling demand, whereas circadian misalignment, chronic stress and reduced recovery acted on arms with reserve. Combined, the stressors exhausted the margin at 0.72 times the moderate profile; across 400 parameter draws demand was met in 99.2% at low and 28.5% at moderate exposure. Substrate oxidation, not substrate supply, set the margin: restoring sleep or reducing load restored it, whereas ketone bodies, lactate or fibre-derived acetate helped only when glucose delivery itself was limiting. Results held across thresholds, releases, solvers and enzyme-capacity limits, and the thresholds are testable with ³¹P and ¹³C spectroscopy.

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract Background and Objective. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) solves school math problems on demand. Higher scores during live tool access do not prove retained mathematical competence once that support disappears. Earlier meta-analyses pooled assisted task completion together with unmonitored and closed-book posttests, which obscured whether pupils actually learned to work alone. This PRISMA 2020 systematic review and stratified meta-analysis evaluates K–12 mathematics outcomes by separating test-time resource rules from instructional design. Methods. Two-stream searches across ERIC, APA PsycNet, OpenAlex, Crossref, Semantic Scholar, arXiv, EuropePMC, and bidirectional citation chasing (1 January 2022–8 November 2026) returned 11,061 raw entries and 6,530 unique records. Every sought report was retrieved in full (372 / 372; 0 unretrieved). Eligibility verification and mathematical consistency checks retained 49 K–12 school-mathematics reports across 46 independent cohorts and supplied 36 quantitative contrasts across 20 controlled study families (21 controlled quantitative reports, plus 1 factorial within-AI modality trial synthesized narratively) alongside 28 qualitative, single-arm, observational, and boundary-comparator reports. Conclusions AI dependence and procrastination do not covary uniformly: a substantial subgroup exhibits elevated functional and cognitive reliance on AI without severe procrastination, while a smaller subgroup shows co-occurring dependence and procrastination together with the lowest adaptive resources. quarantine.abstract_text: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) makes it harder to infer a student’s own capability from a submitted product, so assessment increasingly needs evidence of how students reason and regulate their learning. This study examined four questions. Which assessment practices do higher education educators publicly report, and how do they describe their implementation? Which cognitive-engagement and self-regulated learning (SRL) processes are these practices intended to elicit? How does a framework derived from these reports fare against separately sampled external documents? Methods Public posts and comments were collected with TinyFish from Reddit (the principal source), Hacker News, Stack Exchange, Lemmy and Mastodon, covering December 2022 to October 2026. Of 29,355 unique records, 13,903 were eligible, and 5,091 reported or discussed at least one of 11 assessment practices (75.2% from Reddit; 3,741 in educator voice; 1,336 threads). Records were coded with transparent dictionaries, which were validated against an independent model-based coder on a hold-out sample (any practice: κ = 0.49; implemented vs. proposed: κ = 0.69). A seven-component framework built from the corpus was then appraised against 40 external documents not used in its construction. Results Detection and sanction (43.2%) and supervised in-class tasks (28.5%) dominated discussion. Detection’s share fell from 56.4% in 2023 to 37.6% in 2026, while oral, process-based and stakes-related practices roughly doubled. Reasoning was the intended process described most often, yet only 2.2% of records mentioned planning, monitoring and reflection or revision together. Several practice–mechanism associations were largely lexical: reflection vocabulary accompanying reflective tasks fell from 94.2% to 5.5% when shared words were masked. Learning-oriented records described monitoring, application and reasoning more often than detection-only records. The framework described all 40 external documents (13 implemented cases, 13 institutional guidance documents, 14 commentaries; mean fit 3.9/5). However, those documents emphasised authentic task design and reflection rather than secured checkpoints, and they prompted an eighth component, student co-design and transparency. Discussion Public discussion favours securing assessment over making learning visible, and no single practice is described as eliciting both cognitive engagement and a connected SRL cycle. This supports combining complementary forms of evidence. The study documents patterns in public reporting and offers a provisional design framework; it does not measure students’ cognition or learning outcomes.
