quarantine.abstract_text: Objective While the use of generative artificial intelligence has become increasingly pervasive in higher education, the overall linear relationship between students’ perceived cognitive offloading and their academic engagement remains non-significant. Grounded in distributed cognition theory, the extended mind thesis, and cognitive load theory, this cross-sectional study examines whether multidimensional cognitive load allocation operates as countervailing indirect pathways linking perceived cognitive offloading to university students’ academic engagement, while evaluating the moderating boundaries of perceived learner agency and AI literacy. Methods A valid sample of 1,050 university students with generative AI experience was analyzed (representing a 93.75% retention rate from 1,120 submitted records). Data were evaluated using hierarchical linear regression (controlling for specific AI task types), non-parametric bootstrap parallel mediation modeling, moderated mediation analyses, and cross-disciplinary comparative regressions across humanities and social sciences ( n = 368) and STEM ( n = 465) cohorts. Results The findings indicated that: (1) Perceived cognitive offloading had no direct linear association with academic engagement, accounting for an inconsistent mediation pattern of two countervailing indirect associations: a negative indirect pathway via extraneous cognitive load (estimate = −0.025) and a positive indirect pathway via germane cognitive load (estimate = +0.053); (2) Sub-dimensional analyses indicated descriptive divergences across task categories: memory retrieval offloading was positively associated with extraneous verification load, whereas analytical processing offloading was linked to germane cognitive load; (3) Perceived learner agency positively moderated the germane load pathway, whereas AI literacy demonstrated direct associations with cognitive load without significantly moderating these indirect pathways; (4) Cross-group comparative analyses detected no statistically significant slope differences in this cognitive load allocation pattern across humanities/social sciences and STEM cohorts. Conclusion Perceived cognitive offloading in intelligent learning environments reflects a cognitive trade-off between operational verification friction and conceptual schema scaffolding. Rather than imposing blunt administrative prohibitions, these findings highlight the conceptual utility of supporting learners’ epistemic agency and critical AI literacy, assisting students in channeling technological offloading toward productive, germane engagement. Nevertheless, as these cross-sectional findings capture subjective cognitive trade-offs rather than longitudinal learning gains or objective memory alterations, instructional interventions should be tested empirically.

quarantine.abstract_text: The advent of generative AI has provoked an ontological crisis in language education, tempting policymakers to equate machine-generated output with human interpretive capacity. This article challenges the premise that such technologies render language learning obsolete, arguing instead that an AI-saturated landscape makes robust humanistic engagement more vital than ever. Addressing the “scholar’s dilemma,” the paper proposes a structural shift in higher education from traditional silos toward horizontal, cross-disciplinary integration. Because English functions as a global lingua franca (ELF) and exerts an algorithmic hegemony over large language models (LLMs), advanced proficiency remains indispensable for critically querying these platforms. We advocate for a pedagogical evolution from the mechanical transmission of referential information (informing) to facilitating imaginative exploration (engaging). Central to this shift is the reclamation of “literature with a small l” as the primary representational material used to cultivate students’ “textual power.” By prioritizing the interpretive struggle over cognitive offloading—a tension described here as the “Picasso Paradox”—educators can formalize a “fifth skill” (complex critical thinking in English). This framework provides the cognitive foundation for students to navigate an AI-saturated world not as passive users, but as active curators equipped with ethical discernment and epistemic agency.

Critical thinking is among the competencies most consistently demanded of graduates, and whether GenAI use strengthens or weakens it remains unsettled. Records were screened in three stages by title, by abstract and conclusion, and by full text, yielding 66 studies for synthesis. GenAI has no uniform effect on critical thinking. Unstructured use is associated with reduced critical thinking enaction, cognitive offloading, and weakened metacognitive monitoring, while use that requires students to interrogate model output is associated with gains, most consistently in analysis and evaluation. The same models produce both outcomes, indicating that the determining variable is the demand the task places on the student. The configurations that produce gains each make reasoning a condition of task progress. Assessment has not kept pace, since instruments that score the submitted artefact cannot separate student reasoning from model contribution. We propose an 18-item self-report instrument that relocates measurement to the process of engaging with AI across all six dimensions of critical thinking. Whether GenAI strengthens or substitutes for student reasoning depends on task and assessment design rather than on the tools themselves.

quarantine.abstract_text: Cognitive agency concerns learners’ effortful, self-directed control over reasoning with generative AI (GenAI). Building on an existing implementation-level classification of generative AI use, this review examines how cognitive work is allocated between learners and AI tools. Following PRISMA 2020, searches of Scopus and Web of Science (2021–2025) yielded 93 peer-reviewed studies, appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. A realist synthesis specified an a priori program theory crossing the type of work offloaded (extraneous versus germane; cognitive load theory) with processing of AI output (heuristic acceptance versus analytical scrutiny; dual-process theory), and audited the evidence on each axis under manifest coding (reported evidence only) and latent coding (adding design-based inference). Under manifest coding, 21 studies were located on both axes; all four configurations occurred, two in a single study each, and the nine Cognitive Extension studies reported peripheral uses with analytical scrutiny. Of the 93 studies, 49 reported no learner behavior toward AI output, 69 reported no learning measure independent of AI assistance, and four reported processing evidence together with such a measure. Group differences or part-sample outcomes were documented in 30 studies; one further study reported stage differences, but no learner-, task-, or assessment-level moderator showed an interpretable corpus-level association with substitution. This evidence profile identifies the process and AI-independent learning measures needed to distinguish cognitive extension from cognitive substitution. Institutional responses to maintaining assessment integrity have primarily focused on defensive mechanisms, such as mitigating risks surrounding written assessments, refining text-matching software, and enforcing restrictive academic integrity policies (Lodge, 2024). However, this reactive posture often overlooks the transformative potential of GenAI as a student’s and lecturer’s long-term coach in authentic assessment design (Atif, 2024). This research-in-progress pivots away from deficit-based AI detection, proposing instead the integration of VirtualSpeech GenAI avatars to converse with students during a recorded viva, generating verifiable, real-time student output. By replacing static written tasks with dynamic oral assessments, this relatively new form of creative expression maintains authentic student contributions to improve AI literacy, strengthen authorship verification, eliminate academic outsourcing, and simultaneously cultivate sophisticated negotiation skills (Perkins, 2026). This study represents an exemplary innovation of practice by reframing AI not as an academic threat, but as a dual-mode learning and assessment avatar. Rather than engaging with AI purely for text generation, students interact with GenAI avatars (such as VirtualSpeech) simulating realistic corporate stakeholders. This work is strongly anchored in the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework, which guides the deliberate alignment of GenAI technology, modern pedagogy, and discipline-specific knowledge (Mishra & Koehler, 2006). This framework assists educators in leveraging immersive technology to redefine pedagogical delivery, facilitating AI literacy and negotiation skills. Data collection relies on a mixed-methods approach, utilizing pre- and post-intervention surveys alongside qualitative analysis of student reflections. Preliminary quantitative results indicate a statistically significant increase in both self-reported IT literacy, validating the avatar’s efficacy as a formative and summative tool. While piloted within a project management curriculum, broad applicability across tertiary contexts exists (Cela-Ranilla, 2025). Any discipline requiring high-stakes communication, critical thinking, and stakeholder management—such as business, law, or education—can adapt this viva model. Ultimately, this work demonstrates how universities can safeguard academic integrity not by restricting technology, but leveraging it to create robust, future-focused verbal assessments, requiring students to perform and defend understanding live.

quarantine.abstract_text: Generative AI poses a risk to students’ creative thinking when it is adopted without critical reflection (Elgammal, 2026). These tools are marketed as collaborators and tutors, offering constant and largely uncritical encouragement (Chow & Celis Bueno, 2025; Walsh 2025). This presentation holds the promise of AI partnership alongside evidence that these tools displace cognitive and creative effort (Gerlich, 2025; Temler 2026). This problem is widely recognised, but proposed responses remain inconsistent, vague or untested. Many calls to address the use of generative AI correctly identify the problem or alternatively show singular approaches and case studies. What is needed is a discipline-agnostic framework on building students’ awareness of their own creative processes in the context of these tools. The approach offered here to develop creativity with AI has two theoretical foundations: Margaret Boden’s theory of creativity and art, and the Kolb Experiential Learning Cycle (2011) as a pedagogical approach. Boden (2004 distinguishes combinational, exploratory and transformational creativity: the recombination of existing ideas, movement within a conceptual space, and alteration of that space’s defining dimensions. Novelty can be either new to the individual or new more generally under this view. Boden argues that novelty may come about in several ways, including combining existing ideas in new ways, exploring or changing existing ideas, or transforming dimensions of those ideas. The two frameworks do different work. Boden supplies the criteria students apply when judging whether their output is genuinely novel, surprising and valuable; Kolb supplies the cycle through which that judgement is made repeatedly and acted upon. Without Boden, reflection has no object; without Kolb, the criteria are applied once and forgotten. Students work through Kolb’s (2011) four stages in their learning: concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation, and active experimentation. These each serve a cumulative purpose in developing the students’ collaborative process with generative AI. In the first phase, the student does their first draft of a creative process, using AI in any way they want to experiment with. Afterward, they reflect on that experience, considering questions about what skills they developed (or did not), whether the draft did what they wanted it to do, and how they felt about the AI tool use. Based on this reflection, they can then develop and express a personal set of beliefs on practical use of generative AI. Finally, they can try out a new approach based on these conclusions – which then become the next concrete experience. It is an ongoing and cyclical process of practical experimentation and personal reflection. The framework is adapted from the “Creativity and AI” module of Sage’s Digital Literacy course (Zaphir & Henrickson, in press). Its purpose is to be discipline agnostic; a framework which can be broadly applicable across cohorts and disciplines. Critical AI literacies require the development of students’ own ethical ideas and practical skills in using the tools; this process is designed to be adaptable in any context. Creativity has different implications and different applications in each discipline. AI can act as a useful collaborator if the user can state what and why they want to do it. Students will all benefit in the exercise of deliberately choosing which skills to offload and which to augment, and then reflecting on their choices with each use. The presentation works through one complete turn of the cycle using a worked example: the initial AI-assisted draft, the reflective prompts applied to it, the position statement the student produced, and the changed approach taken on the next attempt. Slides alternate between student artefacts and the framework stage they illustrate. Attendees will leave with the reflection prompts used at each stage and a one-page cycle template they can adapt to their own discipline and cohort.

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract Generative AI systems promise cognitive extensions by enhancing information access and use. However, from the bounded rationality perspective, their utility is fundamentally constrained by inherent human cognitive limitations. This article argues that when the volume of AI-generated information exceeds users’ processing capacity governed by working memory constraints, attentional resources, and verification capabilities, it produces cognitive disutility rather than enhancement. We introduced a formal model to quantify this interaction, demonstrating that net cognitive benefits decline systematically as information overload increases beyond individual processing thresholds. Combined, the stressors exhausted the margin at 0.72 times the moderate profile; across 400 parameter draws demand was met in 99.2% at low and 28.5% at moderate exposure. Substrate oxidation, not substrate supply, set the margin: restoring sleep or reducing load restored it, whereas ketone bodies, lactate or fibre-derived acetate helped only when glucose delivery itself was limiting. Two-stream searches across ERIC, APA PsycNet, OpenAlex, Crossref, Semantic Scholar, arXiv, EuropePMC, and bidirectional citation chasing (1 January 2022–8 November 2026) returned 11,061 raw entries and 6,530 unique records. Every sought report was retrieved in full (372 / 372; 0 unretrieved). Eligibility verification and mathematical consistency checks retained 49 K–12 school-mathematics reports across 46 independent cohorts and supplied 36 quantitative contrasts across 20 controlled study families (21 controlled quantitative reports, plus 1 factorial within-AI modality trial synthesized narratively) alongside 28 qualitative, single-arm, observational, and boundary-comparator reports. Random-effects Paule–Mandel and restricted maximum likelihood estimators with classroom cluster adjustments (calibrated intraclass correlation ρ = 0.128) stratified contrasts across Category A (GenAI active during testing), Category B (posttest with undocumented resource rules), Category C (partial human-help restriction), and Category D (explicit closedresource immediate and delayed exams). Results. Within primary multi-cluster and individually randomized trials (k = 14), large concurrent gains during live GenAI access (Category A: g = +0.615, 95% CI [+0.044, +1.185], p = .035) shrank across undocumented posttests (Category B: g = +0.186 [+0.009, +0.362]) and tutor-restricted exit tickets (Category C: g = +0.095 [+0.024, +0.167]) down to a tight null on explicit closed-resource exams (Category D: g = −0.010 [−0.137, +0.117], p = .876; focal contrast Δg = +0.625, p = .036). Extended controlled trials (k = 28) confirmed strong between-category moderation (Q_between = 12.55, p = .0059; Category D: g = −0.035 [−0.149, +0.078]). Pedagogical architecture accounted for all primary post-withdrawal heterogeneity (Q_between = 18.69, p = .0001; I² = 0% within every tier). Unconstrained direct-answer access harmed closed-exam scores (M1: g = −0.205, p = .043), passive hint guardrails blocked harm without yielding net transfer (M2: g = −0.038, p = .173), and architectures enforcing productive cognitive friction (unaided mastery gating, teachable agents, Socratic Pólya scaffolding, and human-in-the-loop oversight) produced durable gains (M3: g = +0.100, p = .0001; extended g = +0.315, p = .0002). Class 2 scored significantly lower than Classes 1 and 3 on positive acceptance and striving (all p &lt; 0.001). Conclusions AI dependence and procrastination do not covary uniformly: a substantial subgroup exhibits elevated functional and cognitive reliance on AI without severe procrastination, while a smaller subgroup shows co-occurring dependence and procrastination together with the lowest adaptive resources. quarantine.abstract_text: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) makes it harder to infer a student’s own capability from a submitted product, so assessment increasingly needs evidence of how students reason and regulate their learning. This study examined four questions. Which assessment practices do higher education educators publicly report, and how do they describe their implementation? Which cognitive-engagement and self-regulated learning (SRL) processes are these practices intended to elicit? How does a framework derived from these reports fare against separately sampled external documents? Methods Public posts and comments were collected with TinyFish from Reddit (the principal source), Hacker News, Stack Exchange, Lemmy and Mastodon, covering December 2022 to October 2026. Of 29,355 unique records, 13,903 were eligible, and 5,091 reported or discussed at least one of 11 assessment practices (75.2% from Reddit; 3,741 in educator voice; 1,336 threads). Records were coded with transparent dictionaries, which were validated against an independent model-based coder on a hold-out sample (any practice: κ = 0.49; implemented vs. proposed: κ = 0.69). A seven-component framework built from the corpus was then appraised against 40 external documents not used in its construction. Results Detection and sanction (43.2%) and supervised in-class tasks (28.5%) dominated discussion. Detection’s share fell from 56.4% in 2023 to 37.6% in 2026, while oral, process-based and stakes-related practices roughly doubled. Reasoning was the intended process described most often, yet only 2.2% of records mentioned planning, monitoring and reflection or revision together. Several practice–mechanism associations were largely lexical: reflection vocabulary accompanying reflective tasks fell from 94.2% to 5.5% when shared words were masked. Learning-oriented records described monitoring, application and reasoning more often than detection-only records. The framework described all 40 external documents (13 implemented cases, 13 institutional guidance documents, 14 commentaries; mean fit 3.9/5). However, those documents emphasised authentic task design and reflection rather than secured checkpoints, and they prompted an eighth component, student co-design and transparency. Discussion Public discussion favours securing assessment over making learning visible, and no single practice is described as eliciting both cognitive engagement and a connected SRL cycle. This supports combining complementary forms of evidence. The study documents patterns in public reporting and offers a provisional design framework; it does not measure students’ cognition or learning outcomes.

quarantine.abstract_text: Objective While the use of generative artificial intelligence has become increasingly pervasive in higher education, the overall linear relationship between students’ perceived cognitive offloading and their academic engagement remains non-significant. Grounded in distributed cognition theory, the extended mind thesis, and cognitive load theory, this cross-sectional study examines whether multidimensional cognitive load allocation operates as countervailing indirect pathways linking perceived cognitive offloading to university students’ academic engagement, while evaluating the moderating boundaries of perceived learner agency and AI literacy. Methods A valid sample of 1,050 university students with generative AI experience was analyzed (representing a 93.75% retention rate from 1,120 submitted records). Data were evaluated using hierarchical linear regression (controlling for specific AI task types), non-parametric bootstrap parallel mediation modeling, moderated mediation analyses, and cross-disciplinary comparative regressions across humanities and social sciences ( n = 368) and STEM ( n = 465) cohorts. Results The findings indicated that: (1) Perceived cognitive offloading had no direct linear association with academic engagement, accounting for an inconsistent mediation pattern of two countervailing indirect associations: a negative indirect pathway via extraneous cognitive load (estimate = −0.025) and a positive indirect pathway via germane cognitive load (estimate = +0.053); (2) Sub-dimensional analyses indicated descriptive divergences across task categories: memory retrieval offloading was positively associated with extraneous verification load, whereas analytical processing offloading was linked to germane cognitive load; (3) Perceived learner agency positively moderated the germane load pathway, whereas AI literacy demonstrated direct associations with cognitive load without significantly moderating these indirect pathways; (4) Cross-group comparative analyses detected no statistically significant slope differences in this cognitive load allocation pattern across humanities/social sciences and STEM cohorts. Conclusion Perceived cognitive offloading in intelligent learning environments reflects a cognitive trade-off between operational verification friction and conceptual schema scaffolding. Rather than imposing blunt administrative prohibitions, these findings highlight the conceptual utility of supporting learners’ epistemic agency and critical AI literacy, assisting students in channeling technological offloading toward productive, germane engagement. Nevertheless, as these cross-sectional findings capture subjective cognitive trade-offs rather than longitudinal learning gains or objective memory alterations, instructional interventions should be tested empirically.

quarantine.abstract_text: The advent of generative AI has provoked an ontological crisis in language education, tempting policymakers to equate machine-generated output with human interpretive capacity. This article challenges the premise that such technologies render language learning obsolete, arguing instead that an AI-saturated landscape makes robust humanistic engagement more vital than ever. Addressing the “scholar’s dilemma,” the paper proposes a structural shift in higher education from traditional silos toward horizontal, cross-disciplinary integration. Because English functions as a global lingua franca (ELF) and exerts an algorithmic hegemony over large language models (LLMs), advanced proficiency remains indispensable for critically querying these platforms. We advocate for a pedagogical evolution from the mechanical transmission of referential information (informing) to facilitating imaginative exploration (engaging). Central to this shift is the reclamation of “literature with a small l” as the primary representational material used to cultivate students’ “textual power.” By prioritizing the interpretive struggle over cognitive offloading—a tension described here as the “Picasso Paradox”—educators can formalize a “fifth skill” (complex critical thinking in English). This framework provides the cognitive foundation for students to navigate an AI-saturated world not as passive users, but as active curators equipped with ethical discernment and epistemic agency.

quarantine.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can make learning feel easier, but whether this ease helps students accurately judge what they have learned remains unclear. High-fluency explanations elicited higher JOLs and greater positive calibration bias than low-fluency explanations and conventional-text learning, although the analyses did not detect statistically significant between-condition differences in objective test performance. Absolute calibration error did not differ significantly across conditions. Study 3 ( N = 386) showed that a brief no-AI retrieval attempt substantially weakened the relationship between processing fluency and JOL and reduced overall positive calibration bias. Together, the findings suggest that GenAI can shape metacognitive judgments by changing how fluent learning feels, while the analyses did not detect statistically significant between-condition differences in immediate independent test performance. quarantine.abstract_text: The rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has radically disrupted higher education assessment paradigms (Chung, 2024). Institutional responses to maintaining assessment integrity have primarily focused on defensive mechanisms, such as mitigating risks surrounding written assessments, refining text-matching software, and enforcing restrictive academic integrity policies (Lodge, 2024). However, this reactive posture often overlooks the transformative potential of GenAI as a student’s and lecturer’s long-term coach in authentic assessment design (Atif, 2024). This research-in-progress pivots away from deficit-based AI detection, proposing instead the integration of VirtualSpeech GenAI avatars to converse with students during a recorded viva, generating verifiable, real-time student output. By replacing static written tasks with dynamic oral assessments, this relatively new form of creative expression maintains authentic student contributions to improve AI literacy, strengthen authorship verification, eliminate academic outsourcing, and simultaneously cultivate sophisticated negotiation skills (Perkins, 2026). This study represents an exemplary innovation of practice by reframing AI not as an academic threat, but as a dual-mode learning and assessment avatar. Rather than engaging with AI purely for text generation, students interact with GenAI avatars (such as VirtualSpeech) simulating realistic corporate stakeholders. This work is strongly anchored in the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework, which guides the deliberate alignment of GenAI technology, modern pedagogy, and discipline-specific knowledge (Mishra & Koehler, 2006). This framework assists educators in leveraging immersive technology to redefine pedagogical delivery, facilitating AI literacy and negotiation skills. This research addresses a critical gap in current Technology Enhanced Learning (TEL) literature by investigating the following central question: How are students’ AI literacy and negotiation skills developed when conversing with GenAI avatars as part of a viva presentation? Adopting a design-based research methodology, this project emphasizes the iterative refinement of an educational intervention within an authentic setting (Hoadley & Campos, 2022; Scott et al., 2020). The study is currently in its first implementation cycle within a major tertiary institution, featuring a sample size of 150 second-year Project Management students. Participants are required to defend a project proposal during a live, assessable viva presentation conducted with a customized VirtualSpeech avatar trained to act as a client. This oral format diminishes the appeal of cognitive offloading because students must defend their reasoning under unseen, real-time questioning (Sotiriadou et al., 2020; Tan, 2026). Data collection relies on a mixed-methods approach, utilizing pre- and post-intervention surveys alongside qualitative analysis of student reflections. Preliminary quantitative results indicate a statistically significant increase in both self-reported IT literacy, validating the avatar’s efficacy as a formative and summative tool. This research significantly advances TEL research and practice by providing a protocol for proactive AI integration. While piloted within a project management curriculum, broad applicability across tertiary contexts exists (Cela-Ranilla, 2025). Any discipline requiring high-stakes communication, critical thinking, and stakeholder management—such as business, law, or education—can adapt this viva model. Ultimately, this work demonstrates how universities can safeguard academic integrity not by restricting technology, but leveraging it to create robust, future-focused verbal assessments, requiring students to perform and defend understanding live.

quarantine.abstract_text: BACKGROUND: Reliance on AI-supported health recommendations is consequential, but a single behavioral source-selection decision is not equivalent to multidimensional psychological trust. Biosignals may contain predictive information before a choice, although small-sample multimodal models require leakage-free evaluation and cautious interpretation. PURPOSE: This study evaluated whether facial-expression probabilities and galvanic skin response (GSR) features predict a task-specific binary choice of an AI-labeled rather than doctor-labeled recommendation in a simulated ADHD assessment. The outcome is treated as a behavioral indicator of reliance rather than a direct measure of psychological trust. Method: This cross-sectional laboratory analysis included a cohort of 60 participants (40 AI-labeled and 20 doctor-labeled choices). Eight facial-expression probabilities and two GSR phasic features were evaluated in prespecified Early (6-3 s) and Proximal (3-0 s) windows. Ten repeats of participant-level stratified five-fold cross-validation were used. Scaling and SMOTETomek resampling occurred only within training folds, and the logistic stacking meta-learner was trained on strictly cross-fitted base-model probabilities. Model-specific 95% confidence intervals and paired AUC differences were estimated with 10,000 stratified participant bootstrap samples; five paired tests were Holm-adjusted. RESULTS: Early-window ROC-AUCs were 0.643 (95% CI 0.490-0.786) for Face, 0.430 (0.287-0.578) for GSR, and 0.526 (0.375-0.679) for stacking. Proximal-window ROC-AUCs were 0.550 (0.399-0.699), 0.381 (0.240-0.530), and 0.376 (0.229-0.529), respectively. Stacking did not outperform either modality. Early stacking was worse than Early Face (ΔAUC = -0.116, 95% CI -0.183 to -0.056; Holm-adjusted p = 0.002); the other adjusted paired comparisons were not significant. CONCLUSION: Multimodal stacking did not improve prediction in this small exploratory sample. These results do not establish either a general advantage or a lack of value of multimodal fusion. They do not support deployment or direct trust detection. Larger studies with verified synchronization, repeated decisions, independent trust measures, and external validation are required.

quarantine.abstract_text: Higher education is confronting an academic-integrity challenge unlike any in its history. Students can now outsource homework, take-home assignments, and online examinations to large language models (LLMs) that complete them in seconds. Existing research on evaluating LLM performance on academic assessments has focused largely on standardized examinations, or on questions from college-level courses drawn from a single discipline. Far less is known about how LLMs perform on college-level assessment questions spanning multiple disciplines, that instructors have purposely designed to be AI-resistant, and about which features of such questions, if any, meaningfully constrain LLM performance. We address this gap by collecting 75 questions from authentic college coursework assessments, spanning 17 disciplines, which were contributed by 37 faculty members from ten U.S. universities and one U.K. university. Of these, 61 questions were intentionally designed by faculty members to be 'LLM-proof', while the remaining 14 questions were sourced from online courses. We then (i) evaluate three state-of-the-art LLMs' ability to correctly answer these questions with and without supplementary course materials; (ii) identify five strategies, through thematic analysis, that faculty used to make their questions harder for LLMs to solve; and (iii) test whether these strategies impact LLMs' ability to answer the questions accurately. Our experimental results show that the best-performing model scored approximately 83% without supplementary course materials and 85% with them, and we observed noteworthy differences across models, answer formats, and instructor tweaking strategies. We discuss implications for assessment design, academic-integrity policy, and the broader ethics of deploying LLMs in educational settings.

quarantine.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly entering adult and continuing education, where it can explain, summarise, draft and evaluate on the learner's behalf. The quality of work produced with AI assistance may therefore rise while the learner's own understanding, judgement and critical thinking remain unchanged or decline. This conceptual article examines how AI-assisted adult learning can preserve learner autonomy, independent judgement and critical thinking while still benefiting from generative tools. It builds on Natseva's distinction between functional cognitive offloading and higher-order cognitive outsourcing and integrates it with research on learner autonomy, self-regulated learning, metacognition, automation bias, critical-thinking instruction and the learning–performance distinction, drawing on a purposive, non-systematic literature selection that is reported transparently. Because most empirical studies of generative AI in education involve school or university students, the article distinguishes evidence by learner population and discusses its transferability to adult education. The original contribution is the AI-Assisted Autonomy and Critical Thinking Assessment (AACTA) framework, which specifies six assessable dimensions: prior independent reasoning, purposeful AI engagement, appraisal of AI output, cross-source contrast, decision ownership, and unaided demonstration and transfer. Each dimension is operationalised as a scoring rubric with observable indicators at three levels, from displaced to autonomous, together with a procedure for training two assessors and checking their agreement. AACTA is compared with existing measures of learner autonomy, self-regulated learning and critical thinking. The framework is accompanied by a dual-outcome principle, which requires AI-assisted performance and unaided learning to be measured separately, and by a provisional assistance-gap index. Five testable hypotheses are formulated, and a three-arm randomised study with a preceding pilot and multi-context replication is proposed as future work. The framework has not been empirically validated, and no data were collected for this article.

quarantine.abstract_text: Critical thinking has been a cornerstone of education. Some wonder what these technological advancements will do to people’s thinking and, more specifically, to critical thinking. In this chapter, we look at some of the potential affordances and limitations to critical thinking regarding artificial intelligence (AI) and how educators might respond. We address three aspects of critical thinking as outlined by research. First, critical thinking is the capacity to problem-solve. AI has the potential to help solve problems, although it might also erode one’s abilities, what some researchers call “cognitive offloading.” Second, critical thinking is a social process where people come together to think and challenge ideas. AI and newer technologies in general might bring people together; however, they might lead to what we are calling social offloading. Third, critical thinking is dependent on a diversity of ideas. Generative AI has the potential to synthesize a diversity of information and provide greater access; however, its models and algorithms may slowly limit this diversity. We situate these conceptions of critical thinking in concert with AI and provide pedagogical considerations for music educators to move toward a more process-based approach to critical thinking. This includes creating purposeful moments for students to work collaboratively—or to gather—and think critically, while also using AI tools.

quarantine.abstract_text: Generative AI poses a risk to students’ creative thinking when it is adopted without critical reflection (Elgammal, 2026). These tools are marketed as collaborators and tutors, offering constant and largely uncritical encouragement (Chow & Celis Bueno, 2025; Walsh 2025). This presentation holds the promise of AI partnership alongside evidence that these tools displace cognitive and creative effort (Gerlich, 2025; Temler 2026). This problem is widely recognised, but proposed responses remain inconsistent, vague or untested. Many calls to address the use of generative AI correctly identify the problem or alternatively show singular approaches and case studies. What is needed is a discipline-agnostic framework on building students’ awareness of their own creative processes in the context of these tools. The approach offered here to develop creativity with AI has two theoretical foundations: Margaret Boden’s theory of creativity and art, and the Kolb Experiential Learning Cycle (2011) as a pedagogical approach. Boden (2004 distinguishes combinational, exploratory and transformational creativity: the recombination of existing ideas, movement within a conceptual space, and alteration of that space’s defining dimensions. Novelty can be either new to the individual or new more generally under this view. Boden argues that novelty may come about in several ways, including combining existing ideas in new ways, exploring or changing existing ideas, or transforming dimensions of those ideas. The two frameworks do different work. In the first phase, the student does their first draft of a creative process, using AI in any way they want to experiment with. The presentation works through one complete turn of the cycle using a worked example: the initial AI-assisted draft, the reflective prompts applied to it, the position statement the student produced, and the changed approach taken on the next attempt. Slides alternate between student artefacts and the framework stage they illustrate. While tomographic volumetric bioprinting (TVBP) extends to print with living cells, allowing for fast fabrication of cell-laden 3D constructs. Our continuous work and the rapid developments on TVP/TVBP (TV(B)P) encourage us to review the current challenges faced by TV(B)P and the recent trend in algorithm-based optimization vs AI-based optimization. This review summarizes recent algorithmic advances in TV(B)P, with emphasis on algorithmic strategies for improving printing resolution and fidelity, including optimization of light refraction, scattering, and iterative reconstruction. Then, we further explore increasing attention on the emergence of AI-based TV(B)P, enabling automatic parameter optimization, adaptive exposure control, accelerated slicing, and automated quality assessment. Further, we compare the differences between algorithm-based and AI-based strategies, as well as the difference between AI-driven TV(B)P, by which the system is granted autonomous decision-making power at critical stages of manufacturing; and AI-assisted TV(B)P, by which efficiency, robustness, and interpretability are enhanced without replacing existing physical or algorithmic models. In summary, this review offers insights into the future directions of AI-based TV(B)P in materials science, biomedical engineering, and advanced manufacturing.

quarantine.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence has introduced a new communicative environment in which users formulate language for an artificial conversational partner rather than exclusively for another human being. This development raises important sociolinguistic questions about how multilingual speakers modify their language when they perceive particular communicative requirements from an AI system. The present study develops a corpus-informed investigation of communication accommodation among Brahui-speaking Pakistani university students interacting with ChatGPT. Drawing on Communication Accommodation Theory (CAT), the study examines how students adjust lexical, structural, pragmatic, and language-choice practices during human–AI interaction. A mixed-methods, corpus-assisted discourse analysis design is proposed, combining approximately 100–150 student–ChatGPT interaction sequences from 50–80 Brahui-speaking university students with a language-background questionnaire and follow-up semi-structured interviews with 15 participants. The interaction corpus will be examined through frequency, concordance, collocation, code-switching, and qualitative discourse analysis using AntConc and, where available, Sketch Engine. Interview data will be thematically analyzed using NVivo. The analytical framework distinguishes convergence, divergence, maintenance, interpretability-oriented accommodation, and repair. Particular attention is given to the relationship among Brahui, Urdu, and English and to the possibility that students perceive English as more compatible with AI-mediated academic communication. Because the empirical corpus and interviews have not yet been collected, illustrative interactional examples in this manuscript are explicitly fictional and are included only to demonstrate the proposed analytical procedures. The study is designed to extend CAT into multilingual human–AI communication and to foreground the experiences of speakers of an indigenous/minoritized language in Pakistan. It further considers the implications of AI-mediated communication for linguistic identity, digital inclusion, multilingual education, and the visibility of Brahui in emerging AI environments. publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: Proprioceptive impairment is a common consequence of sports-related musculoskeletal injuries and is associated with altered neuromuscular control, impaired joint stability, delayed functional recovery, and an increased risk of reinjury. Conventional proprioceptive and sensorimotor assessments, including joint position sense testing, balance assessment, force-platform analysis, and isokinetic dynamometry, provide valuable clinical information, but they are often limited by laboratory dependence, intermittent measurement, cost, and reduced ecological validity. Wearable sensors, including inertial measurement units, pressure-sensing insoles, surface electromyography sensors, and sensor-integrated braces or smart textiles, provide portable quantitative measures of joint kinematics, postural control, gait, landing mechanics, and neuromuscular activation during functional tasks. This narrative review was informed by a structured, non-systematic literature search in PubMed, supplemented by targeted publisher searches and backward reference screening, updated through 31 August 2026, with an injury-focused PubMed update on 7 October 2026. English-language peer-reviewed studies and relevant reviews were prioritized, with direct evidence from sports-injury populations distinguished from indirect or transferable evidence from other populations. The review examines sensor modalities, their relationship to proprioceptive and broader sensorimotor outcomes, real-time biofeedback, home rehabilitation and remote monitoring, artificial intelligence-assisted analysis, and challenges in reliability, validity, and standardization. Current evidence supports technical feasibility and selected measurement and feedback applications, but many sensor-derived outcomes are influenced by pain, strength, fatigue, fear, attention, and compensatory strategies and should not be interpreted as direct measures of proprioceptive acuity. Evidence that wearable monitoring improves adherence, prevents reinjury, supports return-to-sport decisions, or enables clinically effective AI decision support remains limited. Clinical translation is further constrained by heterogeneous protocols, measurement error, limited external validation, small or selective datasets, privacy and usability concerns, and the absence of broadly accepted reference values. Future work should progress from analytical validation and reproducibility to prospective clinical validation, multicenter evaluation, and demonstration of athlete-relevant benefit.

With no wave-1 baselines of anxiety or self-regulation and with two within-wave orderings resting on theory, the design cannot establish temporal sequence or within-person change. quarantine.abstract_text: University students, particularly those who also work or hold organizational roles, frequently experience academic overload, stress, and burnout. Existing digital tools tend to address either task management or well-being, rarely both, and many lose users within days. This study reports the evidence-informed design of StudyFlow, a mobile-first platform that helps students turn unstructured academic demands into a prioritized, actionable plan, and examines how its design aligns with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). A design science research approach was followed. A targeted narrative review of literature published from 2021 to 2026 on student stress, working students, digital well-being interventions, engagement, and gamification informed a proto-persona, eight use cases, and nine functional requirements. A high-fidelity interactive prototype was generated through a five-stage natural-language prompt sequence in Google Stitch and refined in Google AI Studio. The intended feature set was compared with four widely used productivity and well-being applications, and each feature group was mapped to SDG targets with measurable evaluation indicators. The review yielded seven design implications, each traced to specific requirements and interface decisions. The prototype implements a four-stage workflow (set up, capture, organize and act, reflect) across dashboard, brain dump, task, focus, insights, and settings screens. None of the four comparator applications supported academic assignment breakdown, and none combined task capture, prioritization, focus support, reflection, and progress feedback in a single workflow. Streaks and usage metrics were deliberately framed as optional, non-punitive cues. StudyFlow shows how evidence on student stress and app engagement can be translated into a coherent, low-friction design that targets student well-being (SDG Target 3.4), persistence in tertiary education (Target 4.3), and the inclusion of working students (Target 10.2). Because no user testing has yet been conducted, no effectiveness claims are made; a staged usability and pilot evaluation protocol is proposed.

quarantine.abstract_text: The rise of large language models (LLMs) has led universities and other higher education institutions to rethink the ways in which knowledge is conveyed, learning is facilitated, and academic performance is evaluated. While such technologies present possibilities for tailored explanations, feedback that supports learning as it unfolds, and joint inquiry, they also give rise to concerns regarding inaccurate information, reliance on machines for thinking, academic integrity, and inequities in access. Drawing on a narrative synthesis of selected literature and institutional guidance, this conceptual paper explores the pedagogical ramifications of LLMs. The paper contends that integrating them effectively demands learning and research environments that bring together subject-specific knowledge, critical questioning, openness about bounded AI use, and demonstrable competence. Constructive alignment, self-regulated learning, cognitive load theory, and cognitive engagement supply the conceptual bases for linking intended learning outcomes, teaching and learning activities, and assessment. A cyclical process is put forward, comprising independent engagement, AI-assisted interaction under guidance, verification, application, and reflection. The paper goes on to elaborate dimensions of institutional policy, encompassing governance, curriculum, assessment, research integrity, privacy, intellectual property, equity, procurement, and quality assurance. Specific consideration is devoted to contexts with constrained ICT resources. The paper's conclusion is that the educational value of LLMs rests on purposeful design of specific institutional AI policy that is clear, transparent and progressive.

quarantine.abstract_text: A polished assignment can conceal who chose the method, weighed the evidence and reached the conclusion, which makes a student’s independent reasoning difficult to assess. Drawing on the metacognitive account of cognitive offloading and Social Cognitive Theory, this qualitative study examined how reliance on generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) relates to independent thinking, cognitive confidence and intellectual autonomy. Semi-structured online interviews were conducted with 22 undergraduate and postgraduate students, aged 20 to 29, from universities in Islamabad and Rawalpindi, Pakistan, each describing a recent academic episode involving GenAI. Thematic analysis traced when students sought assistance, which decisions they delegated and how they later justified their choices, and produced six themes. Delegating study planning preserved autonomy when students kept control over content, whereas removing a familiar AI prompt exposed difficulty in selecting a method despite earlier success with calculations. Confidence also diverged from accuracy: one student withheld a sound answer without AI confirmation, while another trusted a diagnosis because AI agreed with it, although both had missed the same error. Comparing drafts, checking sources and answering peers’ questions helped students identify assumptions and give reasons for revision. The findings support assessment practices that distinguish producing an answer with assistance from being able to explain or defend it without assistance.

quarantine.venue: OIDA International Journal of Sustainable Development
quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract: The rapid integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into workplaces is transforming not only how employees perform their tasks but also how they experience work. However, the implications of this transformation for sustainable development remain insufficiently understood, particularly regarding whether AI-enabled workplaces can support employees’ long-term well-being and resilience. Addressing this gap, this study examines how positive attitudes toward Generative AI (POS_ATT) and responsible AI signals (RAIS) contribute to multidimensional Green Well-being through employee engagement (ENG). Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model, Signaling Theory, and the Job Demands–Resources theory, Green Well-being is conceptualized as a sustainable state encompassing emotional (GEW), cognitive (GCW), and social well-being (GSW). A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted among 342 knowledge workers employed by Vietnamese organizations using Generative AI. Participants were recruited using convenience and snowball sampling. The proposed model was tested using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with 5,000 bootstrap resamples. The results show that both POS_ATT (β = 0.312, p < 0.001) and RAIS (β = 0.287, p < 0.001) are positively associated with employee engagement. ENG, in turn, is positively associated with all three dimensions of Green Well-being, with the strongest relationship observed for emotional well-being (β = 0.441), followed by cognitive (β = 0.418) and social well-being (β = 0.397), all at p < 0.001. Moreover, ENG fully mediates the relationships between POS_ATT and RAIS and the three Green Well-being dimensions. These findings broaden understanding of sustainable development in AI-enabled workplaces by showing that the potential human benefits of Generative AI are not associated solely with technology adoption. Rather, favorable employee perceptions and responsible implementation need to be translated into meaningful work engagement before they are associated with sustainable well-being outcomes. The study therefore identifies responsible AI, employee engagement, and multidimensional well-being as interconnected elements of a human-centered approach to sustainable digital transformation. Practically, organizations should complement investments in AI capabilities with transparent, explainable, and fair AI governance and engagement-oriented work design to preserve and develop human resources during digital transformation. Because the cross-sectional design captures relationships at a single point in time, the findings establish associations rather than causal effects. Longitudinal and cross-national research is therefore needed to examine whether these relationships persist over time and contribute to long-term employee and organizational resilience. Keywords: Generative artificial intelligence; responsible AI; employee engagement; Green Well-being; sustainable development; sustainable digital transformation.

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract Generative AI systems promise cognitive extensions by enhancing information access and use. However, from the bounded rationality perspective, their utility is fundamentally constrained by inherent human cognitive limitations. This article argues that when the volume of AI-generated information exceeds users’ processing capacity governed by working memory constraints, attentional resources, and verification capabilities, it produces cognitive disutility rather than enhancement. We introduced a formal model to quantify this interaction, demonstrating that net cognitive benefits decline systematically as information overload increases beyond individual processing thresholds. The analysis reveals that successful cognitive extension depends not on maximizing informational output but on strategically aligning AI design with human cognitive ergonomics and individual differences in processing capacity. Ultimately, truly augmentative systems must minimize cognitive overhead to prevent overload, while preserving users' epistemic agency and decision-making autonomy.

quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract Background and Objective. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) solves school math problems on demand. Higher scores during live tool access do not prove retained mathematical competence once that support disappears. Earlier meta-analyses pooled assisted task completion together with unmonitored and closed-book posttests, which obscured whether pupils actually learned to work alone. This PRISMA 2020 systematic review and stratified meta-analysis evaluates K–12 mathematics outcomes by separating test-time resource rules from instructional design. Methods. Two-stream searches across ERIC, APA PsycNet, OpenAlex, Crossref, Semantic Scholar, arXiv, EuropePMC, and bidirectional citation chasing (1 January 2022–8 November 2026) returned 11,061 raw entries and 6,530 unique records. Every sought report was retrieved in full (372 / 372; 0 unretrieved). Eligibility verification and mathematical consistency checks retained 49 K–12 school-mathematics reports across 46 independent cohorts and supplied 36 quantitative contrasts across 20 controlled study families (21 controlled quantitative reports, plus 1 factorial within-AI modality trial synthesized narratively) alongside 28 qualitative, single-arm, observational, and boundary-comparator reports. Random-effects Paule–Mandel and restricted maximum likelihood estimators with classroom cluster adjustments (calibrated intraclass correlation ρ = 0.128) stratified contrasts across Category A (GenAI active during testing), Category B (posttest with undocumented resource rules), Category C (partial human-help restriction), and Category D (explicit closedresource immediate and delayed exams). Results. Within primary multi-cluster and individually randomized trials (k = 14), large concurrent gains during live GenAI access (Category A: g = +0.615, 95% CI [+0.044, +1.185], p = .035) shrank across undocumented posttests (Category B: g = +0.186 [+0.009, +0.362]) and tutor-restricted exit tickets (Category C: g = +0.095 [+0.024, +0.167]) down to a tight null on explicit closed-resource exams (Category D: g = −0.010 [−0.137, +0.117], p = .876; focal contrast Δg = +0.625, p = .036). Extended controlled trials (k = 28) confirmed strong between-category moderation (Q_between = 12.55, p = .0059; Category D: g = −0.035 [−0.149, +0.078]). Pedagogical architecture accounted for all primary post-withdrawal heterogeneity (Q_between = 18.69, p = .0001; I² = 0% within every tier). Unconstrained direct-answer access harmed closed-exam scores (M1: g = −0.205, p = .043), passive hint guardrails blocked harm without yielding net transfer (M2: g = −0.038, p = .173), and architectures enforcing productive cognitive friction (unaided mastery gating, teachable agents, Socratic Pólya scaffolding, and human-in-the-loop oversight) produced durable gains (M3: g = +0.100, p = .0001; extended g = +0.315, p = .0002). Head-to-head within-AI trials (k = 6) favored pedagogical guardrails and teacher mediation over unguarded GenAI (g = +0.645 [+0.215, +1.075], p = .0033), whereas upper-secondary algebra and calculus cohorts showed acute offloading and workingmemory overload. Conclusions. Unstratified, unclustered synthesis inflates verified closed-resource mathematics learning by +0.26 to +0.29 SD (naive g = +0.275 vs. closed-resource g = −0.010). Durable competence requires crossing two distinct thresholds. Instructional systems must block direct answer copying and enforce active learner generation before and after AI withdrawal.

quarantine.abstract_text: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) makes it harder to infer a student’s own capability from a submitted product, so assessment increasingly needs evidence of how students reason and regulate their learning. This study examined four questions. Which assessment practices do higher education educators publicly report, and how do they describe their implementation? Which cognitive-engagement and self-regulated learning (SRL) processes are these practices intended to elicit? How does a framework derived from these reports fare against separately sampled external documents? Methods Public posts and comments were collected with TinyFish from Reddit (the principal source), Hacker News, Stack Exchange, Lemmy and Mastodon, covering December 2022 to October 2026. Of 29,355 unique records, 13,903 were eligible, and 5,091 reported or discussed at least one of 11 assessment practices (75.2% from Reddit; 3,741 in educator voice; 1,336 threads). Records were coded with transparent dictionaries, which were validated against an independent model-based coder on a hold-out sample (any practice: κ = 0.49; implemented vs. proposed: κ = 0.69). A seven-component framework built from the corpus was then appraised against 40 external documents not used in its construction. Results Detection and sanction (43.2%) and supervised in-class tasks (28.5%) dominated discussion. Detection’s share fell from 56.4% in 2023 to 37.6% in 2026, while oral, process-based and stakes-related practices roughly doubled. Reasoning was the intended process described most often, yet only 2.2% of records mentioned planning, monitoring and reflection or revision together. Several practice–mechanism associations were largely lexical: reflection vocabulary accompanying reflective tasks fell from 94.2% to 5.5% when shared words were masked. Learning-oriented records described monitoring, application and reasoning more often than detection-only records. The framework described all 40 external documents (13 implemented cases, 13 institutional guidance documents, 14 commentaries; mean fit 3.9/5). However, those documents emphasised authentic task design and reflection rather than secured checkpoints, and they prompted an eighth component, student co-design and transparency. Discussion Public discussion favours securing assessment over making learning visible, and no single practice is described as eliciting both cognitive engagement and a connected SRL cycle. This supports combining complementary forms of evidence. The study documents patterns in public reporting and offers a provisional design framework; it does not measure students’ cognition or learning outcomes.

quarantine.abstract_text: This study examines prompt literacy among future computer science teachers in the context of solving and debugging programming tasks with ChatGPT. It focuses on students' perceptions of prompt literacy, their understanding of responsible AI use, documented practices of verifying and modifying AI-assisted solutions, and patterns of academic performance. A descriptive multi-method study was conducted during a 16-week programming course involving 113 future computer science teachers at Kh. Dosmukhamedov Atyrau University, Kazakhstan. Data were collected through questionnaires, student programming submissions, ChatGPT-use disclosure notes, reflective comments, code-similarity screening, and course-grade records. Quantitative data were analyzed descriptively, while qualitative content analysis was used to identify recurring patterns in students' reported use, verification, and revision of AI-generated solutions. The findings were compared across data sources to address the research questions without testing causal effects or participant-level associations. The 20-item Prompt-Literacy Perceptions Questionnaire demonstrated high overall internal consistency (Cronbach's α = 0.94). Students generally reported positive perceptions of ChatGPT for code generation, debugging, and explaining programming logic. They also recognized the importance of verifying AI-generated outputs and disclosing substantial AI assistance. However, students' documentation of verification and modification practices was frequently general rather than detailed. Pairwise code-similarity screening identified relatively few submission pairs exceeding the predefined 50% similarity threshold. Mean academic scores were numerically close across practical assignments and independent control tasks, although differences in assessment conditions and grading criteria limited direct comparisons. The findings highlight the importance of integrating prompt literacy, critical verification, and transparent documentation of AI use into computer science teacher education. Positive perceptions of responsible ChatGPT use did not necessarily correspond to detailed documentation of verification and revision practices. Code-similarity results cannot independently establish whether students modified AI-generated solutions. Furthermore, the descriptive single-cohort design does not support conclusions about causal effects or improvements in prompt-literacy competence. The study emphasizes the pedagogical value of making students' reasoning, verification, and responsible AI-use practices explicit during programming instruction.

quarantine.abstract_text: Drawing on dynamic usage‐based and interactionist SLA perspectives, this study investigated developmental patterns of linguistic complexity and language‐related episodes (LREs) during L2 learners' written interactions with ChatGPT. Ten Korean EFL learners completed seven sessions of opinion‐gap and debate tasks over 5 weeks. Generalized additive mixed models (GAMMs) revealed dynamic, non‐linear developmental trajectories that differed by proficiency and task type. Lower‐proficiency learners exhibited an inverted U‐shaped pattern in syntactic complexity, whereas higher‐proficiency learners showed stability in syntax but a non‐linear increase in lexical sophistication. Regarding task effects, debate tasks consistently elicited greater syntactic complexity than opinion‐gap tasks and showed an overall increase in lexical sophistication. LRE analysis indicated that learners focused primarily on lexis over grammar, with reliance on the L1 increasing over time. quarantine.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has prompted universities to reconsider how assessment can remain meaningful, valid and fit for an AI-integrated future. While institutional responses to GenAI are often framed as technical, policy or academic integrity challenges, they are also deeply human organisational change challenges, shaped by competing logics of risk, reform, infrastructure and operational efficiency. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with 11 learning designers (LDs) from six Australian and New Zealand universities, the paper addresses the following research question: How do LDs experience and navigate institutional responses to GenAI in assessment in higher education? The analysis identified five interrelated themes: navigating strategic ambiguity and policy lag; mediating compliance-driven and integrity-focused responses; translating GenAI disruption into assessment reform; bridging AI infrastructure and pedagogical practice; and advocating for educational purpose within operational constraints. The paper contributes to current debates on GenAI and assessment by shifting attention from assessment tasks and technologies to the institutional conditions that shape assessment change. It argues that in addition to policy statements and enterprise AI platforms, sustainable responses to GenAI require coordinated professional development, curriculum governance processes enabling timely change, and stronger recognition of LDs as strategic partners whose pedagogical expertise, institutional knowledge and change leadership are central to assessment transformation.

While tomographic volumetric bioprinting (TVBP) extends to print with living cells, allowing for fast fabrication of cell-laden 3D constructs. Our continuous work and the rapid developments on TVP/TVBP (TV(B)P) encourage us to review the current challenges faced by TV(B)P and the recent trend in algorithm-based optimization vs AI-based optimization. This review summarizes recent algorithmic advances in TV(B)P, with emphasis on algorithmic strategies for improving printing resolution and fidelity, including optimization of light refraction, scattering, and iterative reconstruction. Then, we further explore increasing attention on the emergence of AI-based TV(B)P, enabling automatic parameter optimization, adaptive exposure control, accelerated slicing, and automated quality assessment. Further, we compare the differences between algorithm-based and AI-based strategies, as well as the difference between AI-driven TV(B)P, by which the system is granted autonomous decision-making power at critical stages of manufacturing; and AI-assisted TV(B)P, by which efficiency, robustness, and interpretability are enhanced without replacing existing physical or algorithmic models. In summary, this review offers insights into the future directions of AI-based TV(B)P in materials science, biomedical engineering, and advanced manufacturing.

The study is designed to extend CAT into multilingual human–AI communication and to foreground the experiences of speakers of an indigenous/minoritized language in Pakistan. publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: Proprioceptive impairment is a common consequence of sports-related musculoskeletal injuries and is associated with altered neuromuscular control, impaired joint stability, delayed functional recovery, and an increased risk of reinjury. Conventional proprioceptive and sensorimotor assessments, including joint position sense testing, balance assessment, force-platform analysis, and isokinetic dynamometry, provide valuable clinical information, but they are often limited by laboratory dependence, intermittent measurement, cost, and reduced ecological validity. Wearable sensors, including inertial measurement units, pressure-sensing insoles, surface electromyography sensors, and sensor-integrated braces or smart textiles, provide portable quantitative measures of joint kinematics, postural control, gait, landing mechanics, and neuromuscular activation during functional tasks. This narrative review was informed by a structured, non-systematic literature search in PubMed, supplemented by targeted publisher searches and backward reference screening, updated through 31 August 2026, with an injury-focused PubMed update on 7 October 2026. English-language peer-reviewed studies and relevant reviews were prioritized, with direct evidence from sports-injury populations distinguished from indirect or transferable evidence from other populations. The review examines sensor modalities, their relationship to proprioceptive and broader sensorimotor outcomes, real-time biofeedback, home rehabilitation and remote monitoring, artificial intelligence-assisted analysis, and challenges in reliability, validity, and standardization. Current evidence supports technical feasibility and selected measurement and feedback applications, but many sensor-derived outcomes are influenced by pain, strength, fatigue, fear, attention, and compensatory strategies and should not be interpreted as direct measures of proprioceptive acuity. Evidence that wearable monitoring improves adherence, prevents reinjury, supports return-to-sport decisions, or enables clinically effective AI decision support remains limited. Clinical translation is further constrained by heterogeneous protocols, measurement error, limited external validation, small or selective datasets, privacy and usability concerns, and the absence of broadly accepted reference values. Future work should progress from analytical validation and reproducibility to prospective clinical validation, multicenter evaluation, and demonstration of athlete-relevant benefit.

quarantine.abstract_text: Chronic diseases are a major global public health concern and place a substantial burden on individuals, healthcare systems, and society. Their prevention and management depend not only on effective medical treatment but also on sustained engagement in health-promoting behaviors. These behaviors include regular physical activity, healthy dietary practices, medication adherence, self-monitoring, smoking cessation, and other disease-related self-management activities. However, initiating and maintaining such behaviors can be challenging, particularly because individuals differ in their health conditions, risk profiles, knowledge, motivation, behavioral readiness, and support needs. Therefore, accessible, personalized, and continuous interventions are needed to support health behavior change in both individuals at increased risk of chronic diseases and those already living with chronic conditions. Artificial intelligence (AI) agents have emerged as promising tools for supporting health behavior change. Through natural language interaction and other interactive functions, these agents may provide personalized health information, motivational support, goal setting, action planning, self-monitoring, feedback, reminders, and ongoing behavioral guidance. Advances in natural language processing, machine learning, and large language models have further expanded the potential capabilities of AI agents, enabling more flexible, context-sensitive, and personalized interactions. Nevertheless, the application of AI agents in chronic disease prevention and management is developing rapidly, and the available evidence remains diverse in terms of target populations, technological approaches, intervention strategies, theoretical foundations, and evaluated outcomes. A comprehensive mapping of this evidence is needed to understand the current state of the field and identify priorities for future research and development. This scoping review aims to systematically map the existing literature on the application of AI agents for health behavior change in chronic disease prevention and management. Specifically, it will examine the characteristics of the populations and chronic diseases addressed, the types and technological features of AI agents, the health behaviors targeted, the design and delivery of interventions, the behavioral theories and behavior change techniques employed, and the outcomes reported. Particular attention will be paid to how AI agents support behavior change through interactive communication, personalization, behavioral monitoring, feedback, motivational strategies, and other intervention components. The review will be guided by the Population–Concept–Context (PCC) framework. The population will include individuals living with chronic diseases and those at increased risk of developing chronic diseases. The concept will focus on AI agents that provide interactive communication and behavioral support, including AI-powered chatbots, large language model-based agents, virtual health assistants, virtual coaches, dialogue systems, and other relevant interactive AI systems. The context will encompass chronic disease prevention and management across healthcare, community, home-based, and digital health settings. publication_date_provenance.reason: HTTP None

quarantine.abstract_text: AI tools can generate code quickly, but developers still need to understand and check the results. We explore how the enriched multimodal context derived from the extended reality (XR) workspace might help developers manage this information. We first interviewed 13 experts in AI, XR, and related fields to identify opportunities and design challenges (Study 1). These interviews informed two prototypes explored with 12 professional developers (Study 2): four tried a version where the code faded to become invisible after it was looked at, and eight tried a version that replaced viewed code sections with short descriptions of their purpose. In the second prototype, head direction helped determine when to offer a change, while manual input let developers apply it and reopen the original code. A separate open-ended demonstration with seven software-engineering researchers provided complementary feedback. Participants' accounts suggested that descriptions could provide an overview of unfamiliar code and serve as reminders when revisiting it. However, difficulty comparing descriptions with source code, headset limitations, and controls that deviates from regular IDE routines could introduce additional effort. These exploratory findings identify requirements for attention support: make summaries easy to recognize and access, preserve straightforward inspection of the original code, and retain familiar navigation and editing practices. The study contributes to human-centered multimodal systems by showing how the coordination of input channels and AI-generated representations must account for users' attention, verification needs, and established ways of working.

It applies locally served models to agentic power electronics tasks, from the converter level to the system level, and measures their power, energy, token and time costs. The results are expected to provide practical insight for the use of agentic AI in power electronics and the power systems it serves.

We identify Efficacy Attribution as a potentially central mechanism determining whether AI-supported performance is internalized as evidence of teachers’ own professional capability or attributed primarily to the technological system. On this basis, we distinguish Augmented Efficacy, in which AI extends teachers’ capabilities while preserving professional agency, from Dependent Efficacy, in which perceived competence becomes increasingly contingent upon AI assistance. The framework further proposes that these processes are moderated by teacher characteristics, AI-system characteristics, teaching tasks, organizational context, and time. We conclude by outlining implications for measurement, teacher professional development, AI design, organizational policy, and future longitudinal and experimental research.

Through a critical analysis of primary and secondary sources, it finds that Bangladesh and its neighbours have adopted policies but lack adequate protections and binding laws to govern AI systems, leaving people living blindfolded.

quarantine.abstract_text: Large language models can now outperform human persuaders in controlled settings, and they do so in whichever direction they are instructed to persuade. Regulatory and ethical responses to this development nevertheless remain anchored in what this article calls the deception paradigm: the assumption that communicative influence becomes wrongful when, and because, it involves false assertion. The article argues that this paradigm systematically fails to capture AI hyperpersuasion. Drawing on the philosophical literature on manipulation, it shows that hyperpersuasion characteristically operates through true but selectively curated content, adaptive framing, simulated intimacy, and the exploitation of individually diagnosed cognitive dispositions – techniques that bypass rather than deceive rational agency. It then examines Article 5(1)(a)–(b) of the EU Artificial Intelligence Act. Although the prohibition is conceptually open to manipulation without deception, its operative test – material distortion, appreciable impairment of informed decision-making, counterfactual decision change, and significant harm – is inherited from unfair commercial practices law and reproduces the architecture of fraud, leaving paradigmatic cases of hyperpersuasion untouched. Extending the analysis from individual autonomy to democratic epistemology, the article contends that hyperpersuasion threatens democracy not primarily by aggregating individual harms but by degrading the epistemic conditions – independence of judgment formation, a shared space of reasons, and the contestability of public claims – on which collective self-government depends. Regulating hyperpersuasion therefore requires a shift from content-based tests of falsity and harm to process- and relationship-based criteria that target asymmetric epistemic power.
