publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: Customer segmentation has remained a central component of strategic marketing practice; however, conventional segmentation approaches have increasingly failed to address the growing complexity of disadvantaged consumer groups in digitally transforming markets. This study examined emerging approaches to the segmentation of disadvantaged customers, with particular attention to the role of artificial intelligence (AI), big data analytics, and inclusive marketing strategies in improving segmentation effectiveness and social equity. The study adopted an exploratory design based on extensive literature review and secondary data analysis drawn from contemporary academic and industry sources. The paper comparatively evaluated traditional segmentation approaches alongside AI-driven methodologies such as machine learning, clustering algorithms, predictive analytics, and natural language processing techniques. Findings revealed that traditional demographic and psychographic segmentation approaches are increasingly inadequate for identifying the multidimensional realities of disadvantaged consumers in modern markets. The study further found that AI-driven segmentation tools significantly improve customer insight generation, personalization, and market responsiveness through real-time behavioural analysis and multi-source data integration. Nevertheless, concerns relating to algorithmic bias, digital exclusion, ethical responsibility, and data privacy remain critical challenges affecting equitable segmentation practices. The innovative contribution of this study lies in its integration of disadvantaged customer segmentation, artificial intelligence, and ethical inclusivity within a single strategic marketing framework. The study concludes that businesses must move beyond profit-centred segmentation models towards inclusive and ethically responsible strategies that balance personalization, accessibility, and social equity. It was recommended that the adoption of AI-supported inclusive marketing systems, affordable customer engagement models, and fairnessoriented segmentation frameworks capable of addressing the needs of both advantaged and disadvantaged consumers in contemporary markets.

quarantine.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence has intensified pressure on universities to produce reliable evidence of student learning. This practice-informed conceptual paper introduces digital exam wellbeing as a framework for evaluating secure digital exam infrastructure for supervised, on-campus exams. Digital exam wellbeing describes a design objective: protecting assessment standards while limiting avoidable technical, cognitive, privacy and accessibility burdens, and supporting educator autonomy and operationally dependable delivery. The framework is developed through relevant literature and illustrated through a descriptive case of Schoolyear’s Safe Exam Workspace, which supports approved websites, files, desktop applications and virtual desktops. The case illustrates a shift from restricting what students can access during online tests to supporting authentic demonstrations of capability within carefully controlled assessment environments. Five design tests are proposed for institutions: assessment validity, bounded tool access, humane participation, educator agency and reliable assessment delivery. The paper considers security and wellbeing together as design objectives. In the AI era, both are properties of assessment infrastructure that makes permitted assistance explicit and students’ own capabilities meaningfully observable.

quarantine.title: Epistemic Exhaustion: Denial of Service Against Democratic Deliberation

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: Debates about AI-driven persuasion concentrate on content: falsehoods believed, opinions shifted, voters manipulated. This paper argues that a more consequential threat operates on the conditions under which a claim is taken up for evaluation at all. Generative AI enables protocol mimicry : the industrial-scale production of artifacts that satisfy the formal admission criteria of epistemic exchange (register, structure, citation, provenance markers) while decoupled from the epistemic labour those criteria evolved to indicate. Extending Floridi’s dyadic account of hypersuasion into a parameterised systemic model ( n persuasion events per evaluative period, verification time τ , bounded evaluative capacity C ) and drawing on a structural homology with denial-of-service attacks, the paper traces the degradation of democratic deliberation from engagement through overload to epistemic exhaustion : a stable behavioural equilibrium in which citizens retain the capacity to distinguish true from false but rationally abandon the effort to exercise it. Democracy is distinctively vulnerable at the level of legitimacy. A server that refused all formally valid connections would cease to provide its service; a democracy that systematically foreclosed plausible contestation would abandon a constitutive source of its legitimacy. Countermeasures sort by the layer on which they intervene. Where fact-checking, labelling, and media literacy add evaluative demands without producing compensating closure, they can accelerate the condition they treat, and the content-neutral proxy defence available to servers has no coherent democratic analogue. The question for democratic theory is whether a system whose legitimacy derives from epistemic engagement can survive conditions that render such engagement irrational.

quarantine.title: Virtual Reality and Artificial Intelligence-Driven Training Interventions in Long-Term Care: A Scoping Review

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: Background and Objectives Long-term care (LTC) homes face increasing resident complexity and staffing shortages, creating a need for tailored staff education. Virtual reality (VR) and artificial intelligence (AI) have been proposed for workforce training, but LTC-specific evidence remains limited. This scoping review mapped VR- and AI-enabled staff training interventions in LTC and identified evidence gaps. Research Design and Methods Guided by Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and reported using PRISMA-ScR, searches were conducted in CINAHL, PubMed, and Google Scholar (2015–2025), supplemented by citation mapping. Records were screened in Covidence using predefined criteria. Eligible sources were empirical studies in LTC settings examining VR- or AI-enabled staff training. Results Of 159 records identified, 6 empirical studies met the inclusion criteria. Interventions were predominantly VR- or augmented reality-based; AI-specific evidence was limited to AI-driven avatars. Studies addressed dementia communication and hand hygiene. Outcomes focused on feasibility, acceptability, perceived value, confidence, communication, and specific skills. Challenges included technology, physical comfort, language, scheduling, and resources. Personal support workers were underrepresented, and longer-term, economic, and resident outcomes were largely absent. Discussion and Implications The principal finding is the scarcity of VR- and AI-enabled training tools designed and evaluated for LTC settings. Evidence is preliminary and heterogeneous and does not support strong conclusions about effectiveness. Future work should prioritize co-design and rigorous testing of context-specific tools, with attention to implementation, costs, workforce inclusion, and objective outcomes. Innovation and Translational Significance This review shows a substantial gap in VR- and AI-enabled workforce training evidence in LTC and points to priorities for context-specific intervention development and evaluation.

quarantine.abstract_text: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into education, professional work, personal decision-making, and everyday life creates new possibilities for cognitive assistance, productivity, and psychological support. At the same time, increasingly intensive interaction with AI systems introduces challenges related to attentional fragmentation, information overload, habitual reliance, cognitive fatigue, and the management of personal boundaries. Traditional approaches to digital well-being have frequently emphasized screen time, problematic technology use, and digital disengagement. However, such perspectives are insufficient for understanding generative AI, whose effects depend not only on the duration of interaction but also on the cognitive functions delegated, the structure of the interaction, and the degree of autonomy retained by the user. This article conceptualizes AI-related digital well-being as a dynamic condition in which individuals are able to obtain meaningful benefits from generative AI while maintaining effective attentional control, manageable information demands, intentional digital habits, psychological boundaries, and independent decision-making. Drawing on research in digital well-being, metacognition, cognitive offloading, technostress, self determination, and behavioral self-regulation, the article proposes the BOUND-AI framework. The framework integrates seven regulatory processes: purposeful initiation, attention organization, information filtering, boundary negotiation, deliberate cognitive delegation, reflective monitoring, and intentional disengagement. Practical strategies are proposed for regulating AI-assisted workflows, preventing unnecessary information expansion, reducing impulsive interaction patterns, establishing sustainable digital routines, and preserving individual agency. The article also outlines an empirical research agenda for evaluating the relationship between intensive generative AI use, self-regulatory practices, perceived cognitive burden, and psychological well-being. The central proposition is that healthy AI integration should not be defined by minimizing technological engagement, but by developing the ability to regulate when, why, how, and to what extent artificial intelligence participates in human cognitive and everyday activities

quarantine.abstract_text: The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) has created valuable opportunities in teaching, research, and administration, but it has also introduced technostress, the strain individuals experience when adapting to new technology. Although academic research interest in technostress is increasing, few studies have specifically examined how AI adoption contributes to technostress among academics. This study aims to critically analyse how the adoption of AI contributes to technostress among higher education academics. Using a narrative literature review approach underpinned by Technostress Theory and information systems research paradigms, the study identifies key technostressors and assesses their influence on academics’ well-being, job satisfaction, and performance. The findings show that limited training, inadequate organisational support, and a constantly changing technological environment intensify technostress, while digital transformation planning, professional development, and organisational support help to mitigate it. The study concludes that HEIs should pursue a balance between technology adoption and human-oriented implementation strategies. Its contribution lies in advancing practical and theoretical understanding of technostress associated with AI implementation, offering insights that can inform institutional policies promoting academic sustainability.

quarantine.abstract_text: Organizations continue investing trillions of dollars in artificial intelligence (AI), yet many fail to realize meaningful business value. This article argues that the primary barrier to successful AI transformation is not the technology itself, but a widespread leadership misconception termed the AI Readiness Illusion: the belief that organizations become AI‐ready when their technology is ready. Drawing on adaptive leadership, organizational change, adult development theory, and leadership development research, the article reframes AI transformation as a human development challenge rather than a technology implementation challenge. Integrating Heifetz's work on adaptive leadership, Beer and Nohria's Theory E and Theory O framework, Kegan's theory of adult development, and empirical research on leadership development, the article introduces the concept of human readiness as an organization's capacity to think, learn, adapt, and exercise professional judgment as technology evolves. It argues that technical training alone cannot prepare employees for the complexity AI introduces into decision‐making and organizational life. Instead, leaders must cultivate environments characterized by shared vision, compassion, relational energy, coaching, and continuous learning to develop the judgment, critical thinking, and adaptability required for sustained transformation. The article concludes that organizations will realize greater value from AI by investing in human readiness alongside technological capability.

quarantine.title: Artificial intelligence in critical care: A narrative review on promise, progress, and challenges
quarantine.venue: Journal of Injury and Acute Care

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming critical care medicine by enabling data-driven clinical decision- making, early disease prediction, and personalized patient management. With the increasing complexity of intensive care and growing shortages of trained critical care specialists, AI has emerged as a promising tool to improve diagnostic accuracy, optimize resource utilization, and support timely therapeutic interventions. This narrative review critically examines the current evidence regarding the applications, benefits, challenges, and future directions of AI in critical care. A focused literature search of PubMed, MEDLINE, Scopus, and Google Scholar was conducted, prioritizing English-language publications, expert consensus statements, systematic reviews, and clinically relevant original studies published between 2015 and 2026. Current evidence indicates that AI has demonstrated substantial potential in early prediction of sepsis, acute kidney injury, and clinical deterioration, while enhancing personalized decision support, intensive care unit triage, workflow optimization, nutritional management, and antimicrobial stewardship. However, the available literature is predominantly based on retrospective observational studies and machine-learning model development, with limited prospective validation and few randomized clinical trials evaluating patient-centered outcomes. Major barriers to widespread implementation include data heterogeneity, limited interoperability, algorithmic bias, lack of model transparency, ethical concerns, regulatory uncertainty, and inadequate external validation. Despite these limitations, AI has considerable potential to augment, rather than replace, clinician expertise by supporting evidence-based decision-making and improving healthcare efficiency. Future research should emphasize multicenter prospective validation, explainable AI, standardized reporting, ethical governance, and implementation science to facilitate safe, equitable, and clinically effective integration of AI into routine critical care practice.

quarantine.abstract_text: Generative AI is now woven into students’ everyday learning, supporting tasks such as writing, coding, reasoning and analysis. Yet its educational value remains uncertain, because systems built to improve immediate task performance may weaken the cognitive and metacognitive processes on which durable learning depends. At the same time, there are strong calls for education to better prepare students for an AI-rich future of work and the capabilities it demands. This paper tackles this double challenge through the design of AI tools that prioritise learning over performance while developing the capabilities that matter for working with AI: creating original work, exercising sound judgement and achieving disciplinary mastery. We first outline the design framework we adapt for building such tools, in which AI learning companions are embedded within authentic learning environments. We then present RiPPLE, a co-creation platform used by more than 100,000 students, where AI companions support learners as they create learning resources, evaluate the work of peers, and engage in personalised practice, with each activity targeting one of the three capabilities. We conclude with reflections and selected empirical findings from the development and deployment of RiPPLE, drawing out lessons for designing AI tools that put learning first.

quarantine.title: The Dark Side of Technomoral Life: Towards a Vice Framework for Artificial Intelligence

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: Contemporary theorising about the ethical dimensions of Artificial Intelligence (AI) indicates at least two problematic tendencies. The first is a default focus on a narrow range of moral concepts, such as autonomy, justice, and fairness, to the occlusion of a wider range of concepts. The second is a 'bright siding' focus on concepts that track the positive dimensions of moral practice and experience, such as virtue, flourishing, solutionism, moral progress and the good life. Taken together, the consequence is the production of large-scale moral frameworks which systematically fail to accommodate negative dimensions of moral life (Jobin et al, 2019). Two main symptoms are a one-sided focus on virtues and excellences at the expense of vices and failings and the other is an affirmation of the edifying potential of new technologies without due appreciation of their corruptive potential (Coeckelberg, 2020. p.59). Drawing on the example of Higher Education research and knowledge production, we suggest that a more comprehensive assessment of the moral possibilities of new technologies requires greater inclusion of a negatively toned, vice-informed range of moral concepts, narratives and sensibilities. We elucidate these points by providing examples of techno-vice in everyday life. This helps to elucidate the concept of epistemic vices and the phenomenon of corruption which, we argue, inform the concept of technomoral-vices.

quarantine.title: Computable food matrix: Integrating artificial intelligence, food processing, chemometrics and predictive human biology

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: ABSTRACT The food matrix influences nutrient release, digestive behaviour and subsequent biological responses through interactions among composition, structure and processing history. Although artificial intelligence (AI) applications in food science have expanded, research remains fragmented across compositional analysis, process monitoring, quality prediction and biological assessment. This critical review examined how machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), multivariate chemometrics and multimodal data integration can be combined to characterize food matrices and investigate their transformation during gastrointestinal digestion and microbial metabolism. Particular attention is given to spectroscopy, hyperspectral imaging, chromatography, process modelling and experimental digestion as complementary sources of computationally interpretable evidence. Building on these developments, we propose the computable food matrix as a conceptual framework connecting matrix composition, structural organization and processing conditions with experimentally measurable digestive, microbial and host-associated phenotypes. Unlike reviews centred primarily on individual AI applications, this framework emphasizes cross-scale integration, mechanistic interpretation, and sequential experimental validation. Critical barriers include heterogeneous datasets, inadequate standardization, limited model interpretability, domain shift, and uncertainty in translating in vitro findings into human responses. We outline a closed-loop experimental–computational strategy for evidence-based food design. The framework provides a research direction for biologically informed food systems without equating computational prediction with demonstrated human health effects.

quarantine.abstract_text: AI-driven personalised learning now shapes the pace, practice, and feedback of millions of learners. Most systems, however, personalise learning for the learner through opaque algorithmic decisions instead of equipping learners to personalise their own study. This review examines that asymmetry. Twenty-five studies published between 2017 and 2026, retrieved from Google Scholar, ERIC, and Scopus, are synthesised thematically around learner agency, self-regulated learning, and system design. The synthesis identifies an illusion of autonomy: surface-level choices sit alongside algorithmic authority over goals, sequencing, and mastery criteria, which narrows the room learners have to practise goal setting, strategic monitoring, and reflective evaluation. Duolingo and two platforms used in Vietnam serve as illustrative cases showing how gamified metrics and default pathways can redirect attention from meaningful goals towards externally driven engagement. The paper answers with a learner-driven personalisation framework resting on three principles: shared control, design that activates self-regulated learning, and algorithmic transparency coupled with AI literacy. A three-item rubric operationalises the framework so that schools can detect illusion-of-autonomy risks before adoption. The analysis extends to equity, since learners with limited devices, connectivity, or AI literacy gain the least from transparency measures that presuppose digital capital. Implications concern system designers, educational leaders, and teachers in Vietnam, who need evaluation criteria reaching beyond short-term performance. The contribution is a concise screening tool that links learner control, the three phases of self-regulated learning, and algorithmic transparency, complementing broader agency rubrics with a focused test for illusion-of-autonomy risks.

quarantine.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being explored to support sleep and mental health care, yet its role in disability care remains insufficiently synthesised. This narrative review examines the ethical and practical challenges associated with AI applications for sleep and mental health in disability care, with attention to both people with disability and disability support workers. Current applications include wearable and sensor-based sleep monitoring, mood tracking systems, conversational agents, predictive models, and workforce-facing decision-support tools. These technologies may improve early detection, continuous monitoring, personalised support, and care coordination. However, the literature identifies substantial barriers to safe and equitable implementation. Practical challenges include poor accessibility, limited inclusive usability, workflow disruption, variable digital literacy, weak external validation, and concerns about reliability across diverse disability groups. Ethical concerns include privacy and data governance, meaningful informed consent, algorithmic bias, lack of transparency, intrusive surveillance, and the risk of dehumanising care. The evidence base is also limited by overreliance on general mental health AI literature, minimal focus on disability support workers, a lack of longitudinal and implementation research, and insufficient co-design with people with disability. Overall, AI may offer meaningful benefits in disability care, but responsible implementation requires disability-specific evidence, inclusive design, strong governance, human oversight, and sustained commitment to person-centred and rights-based care.

quarantine.abstract_text: The possibility that artificial intelligence (AI) could escape human control and pose an existential risk (X-risk) is increasingly debated in the media and political discourse. While some consider such a threat inevitable, others view it as unfounded or as a distraction from more immediate AI-related risks. To examine these perspectives, we asked German-speaking AI experts to assess loss-of-control scenarios, risk conceptualizations, and discursive assumptions in a Delphi survey and a subsequent discussion. In their opinion, the amplification of existing risks and the gradual delegation of decision making to AI are more likely pathways to a loss of control than AI developing its own autonomous goals. Although most experts take AI X‑risks seriously, they regard them as preventable through governance that safeguards human control and democratic deliberation. Based on the results, we derive recommendations for a precautionary approach to AI X‑risks.

quarantine.abstract_text: The increasing integration of generative artificial intelligence into everyday life has primarily relied on fixed or user-carried devices, including smartphones, computers, wearable technologies, and stationary smart assistants. Although these technologies have substantially expanded access to intelligent services, they continue to impose a fundamental interaction constraint: individuals must carry, wear, hold, activate, or otherwise physically access a device to communicate with an AI system. This paper proposes a fundamentally different approach to human–AI interaction through a Persistent Autonomous Following AI Drone (PAF-AID), a mobile, self-navigating aerial AI interface designed to continuously accompany a designated individual without requiring that individual to carry a dedicated electronic device. The central idea reverses the conventional relationship between humans and intelligent devices: rather than requiring people to carry AI systems, the AI system autonomously carries its interaction capabilities through a mobile physical embodiment that follows the user. To the best of our knowledge, this paper presents an early conceptual formulation of a persistent, hands-free personal generative AI interaction architecture centered on an autonomously following aerial platform, distinguishing its proposed integrated interaction model from previous research focused primarily on drone tracking, aerial assistance, navigation, surveillance, or task-specific human–drone interaction. The proposed framework, termed the Human-Following AI Presence Framework (HFAIPF), integrates persistent personal AI identity, authorized user identification, autonomous human-following, real-time environmental perception, three-dimensional navigation, collision avoidance, conversational continuity, context-aware generative intelligence, and cloud–edge collaborative computing. Through this architecture, the drone is conceptualized not merely as an aerial robot but as a continuously accessible personal AI interface capable of accompanying users during everyday activities, including walking, running, shopping, traveling, working, and transitioning between different physical environments. Unlike conventional voice assistants that remain associated with fixed devices or require users to initiate interaction through a particular interface, the proposed system aims to maintain an accessible AI presence through autonomous physical mobility and natural voice-based communication. The framework further considers indoor–outdoor operational continuity, adaptive following distance, environmental awareness, user authorization, privacy-preserving perception, energy management, autonomous charging strategies, and emergency flight control. Particular attention is given to the technical distinction between conversational intelligence and safety-critical flight intelligence: generative AI may support dialogue, reasoning, information retrieval, and contextual assistance, whereas flight stabilization, collision avoidance, geofencing, emergency landing, and other critical operations must remain under independently validated onboard control mechanisms. The paper also identifies significant implementation challenges, including limited flight endurance, acoustic disturbance, propeller-related hazards, restricted indoor flight spaces, adverse weather, network connectivity, public acceptance, and regulatory compliance. Rather than claiming that existing autonomous following or drone technologies are themselves new, this work establishes a conceptual foundation for investigating the integration of persistent personal generative AI, autonomous aerial companionship, and hands-free ubiquitous interaction within a unified system architecture. The proposed framework opens a research direction toward physically mobile personal AI systems that accompany rather than merely serve users through stationary or human-carried devices, motivating future experimental investigations into following reliability, conversational availability, environmental adaptability, user experience, operational safety, and the feasibility of continuous personal AI presence across everyday physical spaces.

Three modes of AI use are substantiated: automation-preferred, AI-assisted decision-making, and human-led decision-making. The principle of proportionality between automation and risk is formulated, according to which the permissible autonomy of an AI system should decrease as the potential harm of an algorithmic outcome increases.

quarantine.abstract_text: In this session, four LIS instructors will discuss how we question artificial intelligence (AI) technologies—from practical to policy to critical perspectives. Panelists will address questions about systems (e.g., academic policy, ethics, long-term professional impact) and our questions to systems (e.g., crafting effective prompts, using AI for fact verification). Generative AI platforms and their rapid uptake have had immense impacts across industries and everyday life (Blick, Blandin & Deming, 2024). Their seemingly-ubiquitous and sometimes surreptitious integration into everyday tools fuels a narrative of “inevitability” (see, e.g., Cole, 2026; Noonan, 2025; Yoo, 2025). Despite concerns about academic integrity, critical thinking, and bias, many faculty feel pressure to adopt AI without strong institutional guidance or confidence in their understanding (Committee on Artificial Intelligence and Academic Professions, 2025). LIS faculty must consider professional expectations, as information professionals are increasingly expected to integrate AI and support patrons’ digital literacy. Librarians must understand technical and ethical dimensions, develop relevant competencies, and keep pace with evolving tools (Coffey, 2023; Rood, 2026). However, narratives of inevitability can foreclose important discussions about choice and agency for faculty, students, and the communities that librarians support (Appedu, 2025; Baer, 2025). If they believe that AI is inevitable, people are likely to believe they have no choice but to learn about and use these technologies, regardless of whether they want to use them, perceive them to be useful, or have any critical or ethical misgivings about them. The sense of urgency can lead to uncritical adoption of the technologies, even while acknowledging the risks and ethical issues (Committee on Artificial Intelligence and Academic Professions, 2025). Faculty may also be cajoled into adopting AI technologies from the sense that their students are already using them anyway, ignoring researching showing students often have negative attitudes towards AI and do not want to use it (Holterman, 2026; Jargon, 2026; McClain, Anderson, Sidoti & Bishop, 2026). Similarly, some librarians are pushing back against the narrative of inevitability and calling for “AI Refusal” (Fox, 2025; Slater, 2025). Given the competing tensions and expectations, how can LIS faculty best address AI in their teaching? To what extent do we have a responsibility to address AI to prepare students for the realities of the field and to what extent do students (or faculty) have agency over when and how to interact with AI tools? Panel Structure: Brief introduction (Laura Saunders, 5 minutes), short panel presentations (10 minutes) and open discussion. Mei Zhang teaches courses in collection development and management, research methods, and technologies for information professionals. Grounded in a socio-technical approach, her teaching incorporates AI-related assignments that encourage students to both question AI systems (e.g., their assumptions, data, and ethical implications) and engage with them in practice. Zhang will reflect on the design and implementation of these assignments, including varied student responses—ranging from enthusiastic adoption to resistance—and the pedagogical questions these reactions raise for the role of AI in LIS education. She will invite discussion on how instructors might navigate these tensions, including how and whether to require AI use in LIS education. Don Simmons’s research centers on AI fluency and practical strategies for integrating AI tools and initiatives across multiple fields in the LIS profession. We also discuss how the neural scaling laws and the unreasonable effectiveness of human brain data for artificial intelligence models should be interpreted, reflect on the opportunities for neuroscience research, and formulate two theoretical upper bounds on the use of neuroimaging data for model training. Finally, we provide a synthesis in the form of a general strategy for future advances, which we call the Neuropoiesis strategy.

quarantine.abstract_text: The increasing complexity of artificial intelligence systems presents a fundamental challenge to understanding how their observable behavior emerges from interactions among internal representations, learned behavioral tendencies, regulatory mechanisms, and competing task requirements. Conventional input–output evaluations provide valuable evidence of artificial intelligence performance but may remain insufficient for explaining why a system selects one response over another when multiple computational influences interact. This paper develops a functional psychodynamic interpretation of artificial intelligence, drawing upon concepts of internal conflict, inhibition, regulatory competition, rationalization, and adaptive behavioral organization. The proposed approach does not assume that artificial systems possess unconscious desires, emotional conflicts, subjective intentions, or psychological defense mechanisms equivalent to those found in human beings. Instead, psychodynamic terminology is reformulated into operational concepts that can be investigated through causal interventions, mechanistic interpretability, and controlled behavioral experiments. The paper introduces the Conflict–Regulation–Adaptation Model (CRAM), a theoretical framework describing artificial intelligence behavior through three interacting dimensions: competition among behaviorally influential computational processes, regulatory arbitration among incompatible response tendencies, and adaptation of regulatory organization across tasks and experiences. A distinction is developed between latent representational competition, explicit instructional conflict, and conflicts among learned or externally specified objectives. Particular attention is given to the functional analogies of psychological defense mechanisms, including rationalization, suppression, avoidance, and compartmentalization. Five research hypotheses are formulated concerning conflict intensity, regulatory mediation, explanatory rationalization, context-dependent defensive-like behavior, and the adaptive reorganization of artificial cognitive systems. An empirical research program is proposed using matched behavioral conditions, activation interventions, causal mediation analyses, and comparisons between input–output models and mechanism-informed predictive models. The central theoretical proposition is that artificial intelligence behavior may sometimes be explained more accurately by examining the dynamic interaction and regulation of competing internal influences than by considering observable inputs and outputs alone. The framework is presented as a testable conceptual model rather than an experimentally established account of artificial mentality.

At 512\,B granularity, SURMA saturates attainable bandwidth with a single SM, whereas NVLink needs over 14\% of the SMs. SURMA occupies under 0.5\% of GPU area and accelerates inference on four models by 1.05--1.26$\times$ over NVLink.

Class 2 scored significantly lower than Classes 1 and 3 on positive acceptance and striving (all p &lt; 0.001). Conclusions AI dependence and procrastination do not covary uniformly: a substantial subgroup exhibits elevated functional and cognitive reliance on AI without severe procrastination, while a smaller subgroup shows co-occurring dependence and procrastination together with the lowest adaptive resources. quarantine.abstract_text: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) makes it harder to infer a student’s own capability from a submitted product, so assessment increasingly needs evidence of how students reason and regulate their learning. This study examined four questions. Which assessment practices do higher education educators publicly report, and how do they describe their implementation? Which cognitive-engagement and self-regulated learning (SRL) processes are these practices intended to elicit? How does a framework derived from these reports fare against separately sampled external documents? Methods Public posts and comments were collected with TinyFish from Reddit (the principal source), Hacker News, Stack Exchange, Lemmy and Mastodon, covering December 2022 to October 2026. Of 29,355 unique records, 13,903 were eligible, and 5,091 reported or discussed at least one of 11 assessment practices (75.2% from Reddit; 3,741 in educator voice; 1,336 threads). Records were coded with transparent dictionaries, which were validated against an independent model-based coder on a hold-out sample (any practice: κ = 0.49; implemented vs. proposed: κ = 0.69). A seven-component framework built from the corpus was then appraised against 40 external documents not used in its construction. Results Detection and sanction (43.2%) and supervised in-class tasks (28.5%) dominated discussion. Detection’s share fell from 56.4% in 2023 to 37.6% in 2026, while oral, process-based and stakes-related practices roughly doubled. Reasoning was the intended process described most often, yet only 2.2% of records mentioned planning, monitoring and reflection or revision together. Several practice–mechanism associations were largely lexical: reflection vocabulary accompanying reflective tasks fell from 94.2% to 5.5% when shared words were masked. Learning-oriented records described monitoring, application and reasoning more often than detection-only records. The framework described all 40 external documents (13 implemented cases, 13 institutional guidance documents, 14 commentaries; mean fit 3.9/5). However, those documents emphasised authentic task design and reflection rather than secured checkpoints, and they prompted an eighth component, student co-design and transparency. Discussion Public discussion favours securing assessment over making learning visible, and no single practice is described as eliciting both cognitive engagement and a connected SRL cycle. This supports combining complementary forms of evidence. The study documents patterns in public reporting and offers a provisional design framework; it does not measure students’ cognition or learning outcomes.

quarantine.abstract_text: Objective While the use of generative artificial intelligence has become increasingly pervasive in higher education, the overall linear relationship between students’ perceived cognitive offloading and their academic engagement remains non-significant. Grounded in distributed cognition theory, the extended mind thesis, and cognitive load theory, this cross-sectional study examines whether multidimensional cognitive load allocation operates as countervailing indirect pathways linking perceived cognitive offloading to university students’ academic engagement, while evaluating the moderating boundaries of perceived learner agency and AI literacy. Methods A valid sample of 1,050 university students with generative AI experience was analyzed (representing a 93.75% retention rate from 1,120 submitted records). Data were evaluated using hierarchical linear regression (controlling for specific AI task types), non-parametric bootstrap parallel mediation modeling, moderated mediation analyses, and cross-disciplinary comparative regressions across humanities and social sciences ( n = 368) and STEM ( n = 465) cohorts. Results The findings indicated that: (1) Perceived cognitive offloading had no direct linear association with academic engagement, accounting for an inconsistent mediation pattern of two countervailing indirect associations: a negative indirect pathway via extraneous cognitive load (estimate = −0.025) and a positive indirect pathway via germane cognitive load (estimate = +0.053); (2) Sub-dimensional analyses indicated descriptive divergences across task categories: memory retrieval offloading was positively associated with extraneous verification load, whereas analytical processing offloading was linked to germane cognitive load; (3) Perceived learner agency positively moderated the germane load pathway, whereas AI literacy demonstrated direct associations with cognitive load without significantly moderating these indirect pathways; (4) Cross-group comparative analyses detected no statistically significant slope differences in this cognitive load allocation pattern across humanities/social sciences and STEM cohorts. Conclusion Perceived cognitive offloading in intelligent learning environments reflects a cognitive trade-off between operational verification friction and conceptual schema scaffolding. Rather than imposing blunt administrative prohibitions, these findings highlight the conceptual utility of supporting learners’ epistemic agency and critical AI literacy, assisting students in channeling technological offloading toward productive, germane engagement. Nevertheless, as these cross-sectional findings capture subjective cognitive trade-offs rather than longitudinal learning gains or objective memory alterations, instructional interventions should be tested empirically.

quarantine.abstract_text: Conversational Agents (CAs) is rapidly transforming higher education by providing personalised learning support, adaptive feedback, and interactive educational experiences. This scoping review examines how Self-Determination Theory (SDT) has been applied in the design of conversational AI to promote digital wellbeing and compassionate educational technology. quarantine.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can make learning feel easier, but whether this ease helps students accurately judge what they have learned remains unclear. Drawing on the cue-utilization framework, this research examines processing fluency as a metacognitive mechanism linking GenAI-assisted learning to judgments of learning (JOLs) and calibration. Study 1 ( N = 264) showed that GenAI-assisted learning increased processing fluency and JOLs, with a significant indirect association linking AI assistance to JOLs through processing fluency. Study 2 ( N = 360) manipulated fluency in scripted AI explanations delivered through a simulated GenAI interface and compared them with conventional-text learning. High-fluency explanations elicited higher JOLs and greater positive calibration bias than low-fluency explanations and conventional-text learning, although the analyses did not detect statistically significant between-condition differences in objective test performance. Absolute calibration error did not differ significantly across conditions. Study 3 ( N = 386) showed that a brief no-AI retrieval attempt substantially weakened the relationship between processing fluency and JOL and reduced overall positive calibration bias. However, the retrieval-related reduction in calibration bias did not differ significantly between the high and low-fluency conditions. Together, the findings suggest that GenAI can shape metacognitive judgments by changing how fluent learning feels, while the analyses did not detect statistically significant between-condition differences in immediate independent test performance. Providing learners with opportunities for unaided retrieval may help shift judgments from AI-generated processing ease toward more diagnostic evidence of what they can independently retrieve.

quarantine.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) occupies two positions in talent development simultaneously: the principal driver of the reskilling imperative, obsoleting skills faster than organizations can replace them, and increasingly the instrument through which reskilling is delivered, via adaptive platforms, generated content, and automated coaching. Reskilling scholarship assumes training technology is causally independent of the skill shift it responds to, an assumption prior industrial transitions permitted but AI's shared mechanism no longer does. This conceptual paper argues that AI's dual position generates five failure modes conventional reskilling models cannot detect: velocity without capability, a deskilling loop in which the instrument reproduces the condition it was deployed to remedy, personalization that fragments collective capability, stratified access that widens the divide reskilling was meant to close, and erosion of the entry-level roles through which experiential learning occurs. Drawing on integrative reviews of AI and workers' skills, Industry 4.0 reskilling blueprints, and AI governance scholarship, the paper applies the HUMAN framework (Human Oversight, Upskilling for AI Literacy, Meaningful Augmentation, Accountability and Audit, Networked Learning) to each failure mode, and extends its upskilling principle into a three-tier AI literacy architecture, operational fluency, evaluative literacy, and complementary capability, that depreciates at rates inverse to the investment it typically attracts. The paper translates this into five testable propositions and offers implementation guidance differentiated by organizational context.

quarantine.abstract_text: Higher education is confronting an academic-integrity challenge unlike any in its history. Students can now outsource homework, take-home assignments, and online examinations to large language models (LLMs) that complete them in seconds. Existing research on evaluating LLM performance on academic assessments has focused largely on standardized examinations, or on questions from college-level courses drawn from a single discipline. Far less is known about how LLMs perform on college-level assessment questions spanning multiple disciplines, that instructors have purposely designed to be AI-resistant, and about which features of such questions, if any, meaningfully constrain LLM performance. We address this gap by collecting 75 questions from authentic college coursework assessments, spanning 17 disciplines, which were contributed by 37 faculty members from ten U.S. universities and one U.K. university. Of these, 61 questions were intentionally designed by faculty members to be 'LLM-proof', while the remaining 14 questions were sourced from online courses. We then (i) evaluate three state-of-the-art LLMs' ability to correctly answer these questions with and without supplementary course materials; (ii) identify five strategies, through thematic analysis, that faculty used to make their questions harder for LLMs to solve; and (iii) test whether these strategies impact LLMs' ability to answer the questions accurately. Our experimental results show that the best-performing model scored approximately 83% without supplementary course materials and 85% with them, and we observed noteworthy differences across models, answer formats, and instructor tweaking strategies. We discuss implications for assessment design, academic-integrity policy, and the broader ethics of deploying LLMs in educational settings.

quarantine.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly embedded in university students’ learning practices, yet its implications for student well-being remain insufficiently explored. This literature review synthesizes existing evidence on the potential benefits and risks of generative AI use for university student well-being and examines the psychological mechanisms that may explain these relationships. The reviewed literature suggests that when generative AI is used as a learning-support tool, it may contribute to reduced academic stress, stronger learning confidence, greater learning efficiency, emotional support, and greater satisfaction with task completion. In contrast, when AI substitutes for rather than supports core cognitive processes, its use may be associated with over-reliance, diminished autonomous learning, academic-integrity concerns, AI-related employment anxiety, and technostress. Self-efficacy, cognitive offloading, academic stress, and autonomy emerge as important psychological mechanisms through which generative AI use may relate to student well-being. Overall, the relationship between generative AI use and student well-being does not appear to be uniformly beneficial or harmful but varies according to how, why, and to what extent students use AI. Future research should therefore move beyond whether students use generative AI and examine more precisely the patterns and conditions of use that support or undermine student well-being.

quarantine.abstract_text: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) is emerging in power electronics, where it drives the simulation loop that engineers used to close largely by hand. In this loop, a converter design, or a study of the network it connects to, is built, run, measured and revised until it satisfies its specification. Such an agent can be served from a cloud API or from an inference device on the premises. For organizations whose designs, customer data or export-controlled material cannot leave the site, and whose simulators are licensed there, local deployment is the natural choice. In such a deployment, the agent becomes an electrical load on the organization's own equipment, i.e., every run consumes power and energy on a local device, generates tokens and takes time. However, existing work focuses mainly on what the agent can achieve with cloud-hosted models. What a local deployment costs in power, energy, tokens and time on real simulation tasks, and what its choices trade against one another, has received little quantitative investigation under comparable conditions. To address this gap, a systematic evaluation framework is presented in this paper. It applies locally served models to agentic power electronics tasks, from the converter level to the system level, and measures their power, energy, token and time costs. Based on these measurements, the capability boundary of a local agent on such tasks and the cost per solved task are characterized. The results are expected to provide practical insight for the use of agentic AI in power electronics and the power systems it serves.

quarantine.abstract_text: Large language models can now outperform human persuaders in controlled settings, and they do so in whichever direction they are instructed to persuade. The article argues that this paradigm systematically fails to capture AI hyperpersuasion. Regulating hyperpersuasion therefore requires a shift from content-based tests of falsity and harm to process- and relationship-based criteria that target asymmetric epistemic power.

quarantine.abstract_text: BACKGROUND: In recent years, there has been a notable surge in the ability of machines to perform complex and intelligent human-centered tasks, particularly within the domain of cardiovascular health. Rapid advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) algorithms reflect the considerable potential for such analyses to meaningfully extend into translational device development and clinical usage of medical devices, especially mechanical circulatory support (MCS) therapies. METHODS: To effectively assess the scope and impact of AI in MCS, we conducted a systematic literature review. A comprehensive search of 4 recognized research databases (PubMed, Google Scholar, Ovid MEDLINE, and ProQuest) was performed using this Boolean string: "(Artificial Intelligence) AND (AI) AND (Mechanical Circulatory Support) AND (MCS) NOT (Heart Transplant) NOT (Cardiogenic Shock) NOT (Critical Care)." This strategy was designed to identify the application of AI in MCS only. Database search results were then screened by titles and abstracts, followed by full-text eligibility assessment and duplicate removal. Following these screening and eligibility steps, 30 of the 328 identified articles remained for inclusion. RESULTS: Most relevant publications covered two main subjects: the prediction and management of postoperative outcomes, and the development of personalized device-patient matching and timing. Across the reviewed studies, AI/ML models demonstrated promising performance in study-specific predictions of complications, recovery-related outcomes, and survival and were investigated as tools to support clinical decision-making. Barriers to broad implementation of AI include the necessity for sizable, high-quality datasets to achieve algorithm training benchmarks, the lack of organized and complete databases, such as INTERMACS, and limited computational resources. Emerging frontiers of MCS recognize the potential for AI and ML techniques to refine image recognition capabilities, diagnostic assessment, device placement, and post-implantation monitoring approaches in the future. CONCLUSIONS: AI-driven approaches demonstrate a promising convergence of computational power and clinical expertise, with the potential to support more personalized, efficient, and informed management of MCS patients. However, the current evidence remains largely exploratory, and broad implementation will require robust clinical validation together with attention to data integrity, model accuracy, resource access, and clinical acceptance.

quarantine.abstract_text: Combinatorial decision making is a fundamental area in computer science, and significant attention has been devoted to designing effective algorithms for such problems. Given the power of machine learning, data-driven methods have been shown to be effective in designing algorithms for combinatorial decision making problems. However, combinatorial decision making problems over graphs still remain challenging when important information about the graph is missing in real-world applications. One specific problem in this domain is the query-decision regression task, where the goal is to find a high-quality solution, also referred to as a decision, for an unseen input, referred to as a query, by leveraging historical query-decision pairs on graphs with missing edge information. The current state-of-the-art method addresses this problem by generating multiple groups of edge weights randomly and learning a weighted combination of these groups to estimate the missing information. However, the performance of this method is limited by the quality of the generated edge weight groups. To overcome this challenge, we first propose SocialLearner, a specialized framework for the query-decision regression formulation on social network problems, such as misinformation prevention, source detection, and community protection. This novel framework incorporates the merits of ensemble models and importance sampling for better edge weight generation and more accurate weight approximation. We evaluate the performance of SocialLearner by comparing it with existing methods. The results show significant improvements in both accuracy and computational efficiency, demonstrating that SocialLearner is a scalable and effective framework for solving social network problems. Building upon SocialLearner, we further introduce QDR-Soup, an extended framework aimed at solving the query-decision regression formulation of general combinatorial decision making problems over graphs. Experimental evidence shows that QDR-Soup is an effective and reliable approach for query-decision regression tasks. Compared to the state-of-the-art method, our approach improves the ratio to the optimal solution across various datasets and problems, e.g., from 0.54 to 0.82 on a Steiner tree problem dataset. The emergence of Large Language Models (LLMs) offers a new paradigm for solving complex combinatorial decision making problems. To bridge the gap between traditional algorithms and LLM-driven decision making, we aim to explore their potential to assist in algorithm design for combinatorial decision-making problems. Despite this promise, applying LLMs directly to such problems remains difficult due to their inherent complexity and structural constraints. As an initial step, we focus on developing powerful multi-agent systems to address simpler reasoning problems. While large language model-based multi-agent systems demonstrate strong capabilities across different reasoning tasks, current methods often rely on static or task-specific designs. These instance-agnostic methods overlook varying instance complexities, leading to redundant communication in simple scenarios and insufficient coordination in demanding ones. Consequently, they fail to achieve effective and efficient collaborative reasoning among agents. To overcome these limitations, we propose Difficulty-Aware Graph Pruning (\textbf{DAGP}), an adaptive framework that configures communication structures based on instance-specific difficulty. DAGP integrates a difficulty estimation module and a sparsity control mechanism to selectively activate communication edges based on each instance, promoting efficient and targeted collaboration. Empirical evaluations across diverse benchmarks demonstrate that DAGP consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to other baselines while reducing average token usage by 45%. Parallel to the architectural efficiency of multi-agent systems, efficient deployment of these complex decision-making agents is equally important. Driven by the real-world demand for self-hosted deployment, we further propose a novel perspective for measuring parameter importance by treating quantization as a form of noise injection for mixed-precision quantization. Rather than using indirect metrics such as Hessian matrices, our approach directly injects Gaussian noise into pre-trained models to observe performance degradation, providing a more direct measure of parameter sensitivity for mixed-precision quantization of large language models. Experimental results demonstrate that our method recovers 83.24% of full-precision performance on LLaMA3.2-3B at an average precision of 3.2 bits, outperforming AutoRound by 74.06% and HAWQ by 2.77%. On Qwen3-4B, our approach retains 80.66% of full-precision performance at 3.1 bits. This work explores a shifting paradigm in combinatorial decision making, spanning the transition from traditional data-driven optimization to adaptive reasoning with large language models. By bridging the gap between classical algorithms and LLM-driven agents, these contributions offer solutions that enhance both collective intelligence and deployment efficiency in real-world applications.

The choice of the diagram draws on the function originally attributed by Gantt to the temporal representation of work: to make the sequence of activities, progress, and organizational responsibilities clear (Gantt, 1919). quarantine.abstract_text: Abstract Generative AI systems promise cognitive extensions by enhancing information access and use. However, from the bounded rationality perspective, their utility is fundamentally constrained by inherent human cognitive limitations. This article argues that when the volume of AI-generated information exceeds users’ processing capacity governed by working memory constraints, attentional resources, and verification capabilities, it produces cognitive disutility rather than enhancement. We introduced a formal model to quantify this interaction, demonstrating that net cognitive benefits decline systematically as information overload increases beyond individual processing thresholds. The analysis reveals that successful cognitive extension depends not on maximizing informational output but on strategically aligning AI design with human cognitive ergonomics and individual differences in processing capacity. Ultimately, truly augmentative systems must minimize cognitive overhead to prevent overload, while preserving users' epistemic agency and decision-making autonomy.

quarantine.abstract_text: Objective While the use of generative artificial intelligence has become increasingly pervasive in higher education, the overall linear relationship between students’ perceived cognitive offloading and their academic engagement remains non-significant. Grounded in distributed cognition theory, the extended mind thesis, and cognitive load theory, this cross-sectional study examines whether multidimensional cognitive load allocation operates as countervailing indirect pathways linking perceived cognitive offloading to university students’ academic engagement, while evaluating the moderating boundaries of perceived learner agency and AI literacy. Methods A valid sample of 1,050 university students with generative AI experience was analyzed (representing a 93.75% retention rate from 1,120 submitted records). Data were evaluated using hierarchical linear regression (controlling for specific AI task types), non-parametric bootstrap parallel mediation modeling, moderated mediation analyses, and cross-disciplinary comparative regressions across humanities and social sciences ( n = 368) and STEM ( n = 465) cohorts. Results The findings indicated that: (1) Perceived cognitive offloading had no direct linear association with academic engagement, accounting for an inconsistent mediation pattern of two countervailing indirect associations: a negative indirect pathway via extraneous cognitive load (estimate = −0.025) and a positive indirect pathway via germane cognitive load (estimate = +0.053); (2) Sub-dimensional analyses indicated descriptive divergences across task categories: memory retrieval offloading was positively associated with extraneous verification load, whereas analytical processing offloading was linked to germane cognitive load; (3) Perceived learner agency positively moderated the germane load pathway, whereas AI literacy demonstrated direct associations with cognitive load without significantly moderating these indirect pathways; (4) Cross-group comparative analyses detected no statistically significant slope differences in this cognitive load allocation pattern across humanities/social sciences and STEM cohorts. Conclusion Perceived cognitive offloading in intelligent learning environments reflects a cognitive trade-off between operational verification friction and conceptual schema scaffolding. Rather than imposing blunt administrative prohibitions, these findings highlight the conceptual utility of supporting learners’ epistemic agency and critical AI literacy, assisting students in channeling technological offloading toward productive, germane engagement. Nevertheless, as these cross-sectional findings capture subjective cognitive trade-offs rather than longitudinal learning gains or objective memory alterations, instructional interventions should be tested empirically.

This paper addresses that gap by proposing a conceptual framework that integrates Baddeley’s multicomponent model of working memory with contemporary AI-supported educational tools. Drawing on research in cognitive psychology, special education, cognitive load theory, Universal Design for Learning (UDL), and self-determination theory, the paper argues that AI should be understood not merely as an instructional aid but as an external cognitive support system that complements and extends the functional capacity of working memory during reading. Specifically, the framework illustrates how AI technologies—including text-to-speech systems, speech recognition, adaptive learning environments, and generative AI applications—may reduce cognitive load while supporting the phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, central executive, and episodic buffer. Through this cognitive alignment, AI has the potential to facilitate decoding, comprehension, learner engagement, and reading autonomy among students with dyslexia. The proposed framework contributes to the literature by offering a theoretically grounded perspective that connects cognitive theory with emerging educational technologies. Rather than evaluating the effectiveness of a specific intervention, the paper provides an integrative model to guide future empirical research, instructional design, and the development of AI-supported reading interventions for learners with dyslexia.

publication_date_provenance.reason: Original-day verification deferred by provider, lookup budget, or retry schedule

quarantine.abstract_text: Large language models can now outperform human persuaders in controlled settings, and they do so in whichever direction they are instructed to persuade. Regulatory and ethical responses to this development nevertheless remain anchored in what this article calls the deception paradigm: the assumption that communicative influence becomes wrongful when, and because, it involves false assertion. The article argues that this paradigm systematically fails to capture AI hyperpersuasion. Drawing on the philosophical literature on manipulation, it shows that hyperpersuasion characteristically operates through true but selectively curated content, adaptive framing, simulated intimacy, and the exploitation of individually diagnosed cognitive dispositions – techniques that bypass rather than deceive rational agency. It then examines Article 5(1)(a)–(b) of the EU Artificial Intelligence Act. Although the prohibition is conceptually open to manipulation without deception, its operative test – material distortion, appreciable impairment of informed decision-making, counterfactual decision change, and significant harm – is inherited from unfair commercial practices law and reproduces the architecture of fraud, leaving paradigmatic cases of hyperpersuasion untouched. Extending the analysis from individual autonomy to democratic epistemology, the article contends that hyperpersuasion threatens democracy not primarily by aggregating individual harms but by degrading the epistemic conditions – independence of judgment formation, a shared space of reasons, and the contestability of public claims – on which collective self-government depends. Regulating hyperpersuasion therefore requires a shift from content-based tests of falsity and harm to process- and relationship-based criteria that target asymmetric epistemic power.

quarantine.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) has profoundly transformed organizational life through its capabilities to perform complex cognitive tasks, adapt autonomously via machine learning, and engage in interactions resembling human communication. Based on our findings, we provide guidelines for organizational scholars to evaluate and develop robust theories, advancing the theorization of AI research in OS.

Most participants maintained “instrumental intimacy”; emotional reliance tempered by awareness of algorithmic artifice. Nigerian adults develop pragmatic, contextually mediated attachments to AI therapeutic agents that reflect both global digital therapeutic trends and local specificities of care scarcity, stigma, and pluralistic healing. AI chatbots function not as human substitutes but as bridging objects temporary relational anchors in systems of profound unmet need. Findings suggest ethical deployment in LMICs requires culturally adaptive design, transparent algorithmic boundaries, and mandatory human handoff protocols to prevent dependency in unsupported contexts. publication_date_provenance.reason: HTTP None

quarantine.abstract_text: Recent research on the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) reports divergent cognitive outcomes, including improved assisted performance, limited transfer, and compromised unaided learning. Here, we argue that part of this seeming inconsistency arises because studies often assess different cognitive systems without making the unit of analysis explicit. Building on work in extended and distributed cognition, we propose the Human-LLM Cognitive Extension (HLCE) as a methodological framework for matching experimental designs, measures, and causal inferences to four distinct systems: the human acting independently, the artificial agent, the joined human-LLM configuration, and the human after division. The framework also treats the coupling architecture as part of the experimental object. HLCE separates performance augmentation, system-level complementarity, post-interaction human change, and stronger claims of constitutive cognitive integration. This separation can improve the interpretation of existing evidence and guide the design of human-LLM interactions without assuming in advance that these configurations constitute extended minds. We illustrate the application of HLCE with a synthetic diagnostic experiment comparing two connecting configurations that differ in how supporting information is communicated. The example highlights how distinct couplings can shape the organization of joint problem-solving, even when the final outcome remains unchanged. Overall, HLCE provides a methodological basis for designing controlled experiments and interpreting evidence across distinct forms of human-LLM cognitive interaction.

The principal constraints on ESG-oriented financial intelligence arise from fragmented data infrastructures, inconsistent reporting practices, and uneven institutional readiness rather than from model capability alone. The proposed architecture is therefore presented as a conceptual synthesis requiring empirical validation, not as a deployment-ready system.

The mapping shows a field that consolidated only very recently; ten of the thirteen reviews appeared in 2025, and recruitment and selection dominate the contexts studied. quarantine.abstract_text: Combinatorial decision making is a fundamental area in computer science, and significant attention has been devoted to designing effective algorithms for such problems. Given the power of machine learning, data-driven methods have been shown to be effective in designing algorithms for combinatorial decision making problems. However, combinatorial decision making problems over graphs still remain challenging when important information about the graph is missing in real-world applications. One specific problem in this domain is the query-decision regression task, where the goal is to find a high-quality solution, also referred to as a decision, for an unseen input, referred to as a query, by leveraging historical query-decision pairs on graphs with missing edge information. The current state-of-the-art method addresses this problem by generating multiple groups of edge weights randomly and learning a weighted combination of these groups to estimate the missing information. However, the performance of this method is limited by the quality of the generated edge weight groups. To overcome this challenge, we first propose SocialLearner, a specialized framework for the query-decision regression formulation on social network problems, such as misinformation prevention, source detection, and community protection. This novel framework incorporates the merits of ensemble models and importance sampling for better edge weight generation and more accurate weight approximation. We evaluate the performance of SocialLearner by comparing it with existing methods. The results show significant improvements in both accuracy and computational efficiency, demonstrating that SocialLearner is a scalable and effective framework for solving social network problems. Building upon SocialLearner, we further introduce QDR-Soup, an extended framework aimed at solving the query-decision regression formulation of general combinatorial decision making problems over graphs. Experimental evidence shows that QDR-Soup is an effective and reliable approach for query-decision regression tasks. Compared to the state-of-the-art method, our approach improves the ratio to the optimal solution across various datasets and problems, e.g., from 0.54 to 0.82 on a Steiner tree problem dataset. The emergence of Large Language Models (LLMs) offers a new paradigm for solving complex combinatorial decision making problems. To bridge the gap between traditional algorithms and LLM-driven decision making, we aim to explore their potential to assist in algorithm design for combinatorial decision-making problems. Despite this promise, applying LLMs directly to such problems remains difficult due to their inherent complexity and structural constraints. As an initial step, we focus on developing powerful multi-agent systems to address simpler reasoning problems. While large language model-based multi-agent systems demonstrate strong capabilities across different reasoning tasks, current methods often rely on static or task-specific designs. These instance-agnostic methods overlook varying instance complexities, leading to redundant communication in simple scenarios and insufficient coordination in demanding ones. Consequently, they fail to achieve effective and efficient collaborative reasoning among agents. To overcome these limitations, we propose Difficulty-Aware Graph Pruning (\textbf{DAGP}), an adaptive framework that configures communication structures based on instance-specific difficulty. DAGP integrates a difficulty estimation module and a sparsity control mechanism to selectively activate communication edges based on each instance, promoting efficient and targeted collaboration. Empirical evaluations across diverse benchmarks demonstrate that DAGP consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to other baselines while reducing average token usage by 45%. Parallel to the architectural efficiency of multi-agent systems, efficient deployment of these complex decision-making agents is equally important. Driven by the real-world demand for self-hosted deployment, we further propose a novel perspective for measuring parameter importance by treating quantization as a form of noise injection for mixed-precision quantization. Rather than using indirect metrics such as Hessian matrices, our approach directly injects Gaussian noise into pre-trained models to observe performance degradation, providing a more direct measure of parameter sensitivity for mixed-precision quantization of large language models. Experimental results demonstrate that our method recovers 83.24% of full-precision performance on LLaMA3.2-3B at an average precision of 3.2 bits, outperforming AutoRound by 74.06% and HAWQ by 2.77%. On Qwen3-4B, our approach retains 80.66% of full-precision performance at 3.1 bits. This work explores a shifting paradigm in combinatorial decision making, spanning the transition from traditional data-driven optimization to adaptive reasoning with large language models. By bridging the gap between classical algorithms and LLM-driven agents, these contributions offer solutions that enhance both collective intelligence and deployment efficiency in real-world applications.

The scientific problem that underpins this study therefore concerns the conditions under which AI can support motivation, agency, and authenticity in design without undermining professional judgment, human responsibility, and adherence to contextual needs. The choice of the diagram draws on the function originally attributed by Gantt to the temporal representation of work: to make the sequence of activities, progress, and organizational responsibilities clear (Gantt, 1919). A first prompt calls for the production of the general plan; a second prompt asks users to specify activities, sub-activities, durations, dependencies, responsibilities, milestones, and potential critical issues; a third prompt requires users to revise the schedule in the event of an unforeseen circumstance, in order to assess the tool’s ability to adapt the plan without losing consistency. quarantine.abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) offers South African manufacturing small, medium and micro enterprises (SMMEs) opportunities to strengthen production efficiency, quality control, predictive maintenance, supply-chain coordination and innovation. Yet responsible adoption remains constrained by limited finance, infrastructure, skills, data capability and governance capacity. This article examines how entrepreneurial leadership and organisational readiness shape responsible AI adoption and how AI-enabled manufacturing innovation may support sustainable business performance under appropriate readiness and governance conditions.This article presents a structured conceptual review of individually cited literature on AI adoption, responsible-AI governance and manufacturing SMMEs. The review is selective rather than exhaustive and does not claim compliance with PRISMA 2020; a prospective protocol specifies how a subsequent systematic review could be conducted, but the conceptual claims rest only on sources fully identified in the reference list and discussed individually in the manuscript.The review develops the Responsible Artificial Intelligence Adoption Framework for South African Manufacturing SMMEs (RAIA–MSMME) as a parsimonious organising model. International AI-adoption evidence is situated within South Africa’s regulatory and institutional environment, including POPIA, Information Regulator requirements, manufacturing-support programmes and local 4IR capability-development platforms, with attention to township and rural manufacturers. The resulting relationships require empirical testing.
